questions.q: What kind of tool is Symfony Flex?

a.t: A Composer plugin that resolves aliases and applies recipes

questions.exp: Flex is a Composer plugin. It runs at Composer install/update time, resolving package aliases and applying recipes; it has no role during HTTP request handling.

questions.q: What does the symfony.lock file track?

a.t: Which recipes are installed and their versions

questions.exp: symfony.lock records applied recipes so Flex can detect updates and reverse them; it is distinct from composer.lock (package versions).

questions.q: How does a recipe auto-register a bundle?

a.t: By writing an entry into config/bundles.php

questions.exp: The bundles configurator adds the bundle class to config/bundles.php, which the kernel reads at boot via MicroKernelTrait::registerBundles().

questions.q: Which repository holds the community (opt-in) recipes?
questions.exp: Curated recipes live in symfony/recipes; community recipes live in symfony/recipes-contrib and require enabling extra.symfony.allow-contrib.

questions.q: Which statement about symfony.lock vs composer.lock is correct?

a.t: symfony.lock records applied recipes; composer.lock records resolved package versions — both are committed
symfony.lock replaces composer.lock and makes it optional
Both files should be git-ignored because Flex regenerates them
symfony.lock stores package versions and composer.lock stores recipes

questions.exp: The two files are complementary, not interchangeable. composer.lock pins resolved package versions (Composer's job); symfony.lock pins which recipe versions were applied (Flex's job) so every teammate/CI reproduces the same config and Flex can detect/rollback recipe changes. Both must be committed. The common trap is thinking one supersedes the other or that they should be ignored.

questions.q: At which point in a project's lifecycle does Symfony Flex actually run?

a.t: Only at Composer time — it subscribes to Composer events like post-install-cmd/post-update-cmd and package install/uninstall
On every HTTP request, as a high-priority kernel.request listener
At container compile time, as a Symfony compiler pass
At kernel.terminate, after the response is sent

questions.exp: Flex is a Composer plugin that hooks Composer's event system; when a package is installed/updated/removed it resolves aliases and applies (or reverses) the matching recipe's configurators. It writes files (config/, .env, bundles.php) but plays no part in the HTTP runtime, the DI compiler, or terminate — those read the files Flex produced.

questions.q: In Flex terminology, what is the difference between an alias and a recipe?

a.t: An alias is a short name that maps to a real package; a recipe is the automation (configurators) applied when that package is installed
They are two words for the same lookup on the recipe server
An alias applies config files; a recipe only renames the package

questions.exp: `composer require orm` uses the alias `orm`, which resolves to the real package `doctrine/orm`; the alias only affects the name written to composer.json. The recipe is the separate automation (bundles, copy-from-recipe, env, container configurators described in manifest.json) that wires the package into your app. Aliases are convenience; recipes are the work.

questions.q: Under which license is Symfony released?
questions.exp: Symfony components are released under the permissive, non-copyleft MIT license.

questions.q: What is the core obligation of the MIT license?

a.t: Retain the copyright and permission notice in copies

questions.exp: MIT only requires that the copyright and permission notice be kept in all copies or substantial portions; it is not copyleft.

questions.q: Does the MIT license grant rights to use the Symfony name and logo?

a.t: No — those are governed by the separate trademark policy
Yes — the license covers name and logo

questions.exp: The code license (MIT) and the trademark (name/logo) are separate legal instruments. Using the Symfony name/logo follows Symfony SAS's trademark policy.

questions.q: True or false: because Symfony is MIT-licensed, you must open-source any application you build on it.
questions.exp: False. MIT is permissive, not copyleft (unlike the GPL). You may ship Symfony inside closed-source, proprietary products without releasing your own source; the only condition is retaining the copyright/permission notice.

questions.q: A startup ships a closed-source SaaS built on Symfony and wants to market it as "SymfonyCloud". Which part is a problem?

a.t: The closed-source SaaS is fine under MIT, but naming it "SymfonyCloud" risks trademark infringement
Both are forbidden: MIT bans commercial use and the name is trademarked
Neither is a problem: MIT grants full rights to the Symfony name too

questions.exp: MIT permits commercial, closed-source use, so building the SaaS is fine. But the code license says nothing about names/logos: using \"Symfony\" in a product name is governed by Symfony SAS's trademark policy, so \"SymfonyCloud\" is the risky part. You may say \"built with Symfony\" but not brand as Symfony.

questions.q: What best describes a Symfony component?

a.t: A standalone, reusable PHP library shipped as its own Composer package
A configuration file loaded by the kernel
A bundle that can only run inside the framework

questions.exp: Components are decoupled libraries, each independently versioned and usable without the full framework.

questions.q: What do the symfony/*-contracts packages contain?

a.t: Stable interfaces and traits to depend on

questions.exp: Contracts packages hold interface-only definitions so consumers can depend on a stable API decoupled from a concrete implementation.

questions.q: Can symfony/routing be used without FrameworkBundle?

a.t: Yes — it is a standalone component

questions.exp: Components are decoupled; Routing can be installed and used on its own via UrlMatcher/UrlGenerator without the framework.

questions.q: Which mapping of term to definition is entirely correct?

a.t: Contract = interfaces/traits; Component = standalone library; Bridge = glue to a third-party lib; Bundle = framework wiring
Contract = compiled container; Component = a bundle; Bridge = a config file; Bundle = a PSR
Component = interfaces only; Contract = implementation; Bundle = third-party glue; Bridge = framework config

questions.exp: The four layers are distinct: contracts (e.g. symfony/service-contracts) ship only interfaces/traits; components (e.g. symfony/routing) are standalone implementations; bridges (e.g. symfony/twig-bridge) glue a component to one specific third-party library; bundles (e.g. symfony/framework-bundle) wire things into the framework with services and config. Confusing bridge with bundle, or contract with component, is the classic exam trap.

questions.q: Using only the Routing component standalone, what does $matcher->match('/hello/sf') return for a route defined as new Route('/hello/{name}') named 'hello'?

a.t: Nothing — UrlMatcher needs the kernel to resolve routes

questions.exp: UrlMatcher::match() returns an array of the matched route's parameters, including the special _route key with the route name and any placeholder values. No framework or kernel is involved — the component works standalone with a RouteCollection and a RequestContext. It returns parameters, never a Response (that is the framework's job).

questions.q: For a modern application, how should you depend on Symfony code?

a.t: Require the individual packages you need (e.g. symfony/routing); the symfony/symfony metapackage is discouraged
Always require the symfony/symfony metapackage to get everything at once
Require symfony/framework-bundle only, which contains every component's source

questions.exp: You should require only the individual component/bundle packages you use so the dependency graph stays minimal and each package versions independently. The old symfony/symfony monolithic metapackage is discouraged. Type-hinting contracts/interfaces further decouples you from concrete implementations.

questions.q: What is a Symfony bridge?

a.t: An integration layer between a component and a specific third-party library
A replacement for the service container

questions.exp: A bridge holds the glue coupling a Symfony component to one specific external library, keeping the component itself dependency-free.

questions.q: Where do bridges live in the Symfony monorepo?
questions.exp: Bridges have their own top-level directory, distinct from Component and Bundle.

questions.q: What typically activates a bridge inside a framework application?

a.t: A bundle that registers the bridge's classes as services
The bridge auto-registers itself at runtime

questions.exp: Bridges provide classes; a bundle wires them into the container and exposes configuration.

questions.q: Which statement distinguishes a bridge from a bundle correctly?

a.t: A bridge is a glue library (classes) coupling a component to one third-party lib; a bundle registers services and config in the framework
A bridge configures itself in the framework; a bundle only provides plain classes
They are the same thing under two names

questions.exp: A bridge is just a Composer library of adapter/glue classes that depends on a component plus one specific external library; it does not wire itself into any app. A bundle is the framework-integration layer that registers those classes as services and exposes configuration. Expecting a bridge to configure itself is the trap — that is a bundle's job.

questions.q: Why is the external library an optional dependency of the component but a required dependency of the bridge?

a.t: Keeping it optional on the component preserves the component's minimal, reusable dependency graph; the bridge exists precisely to depend on that library, so it requires it
Because Composer forbids components from having any required dependencies
Because the bridge is loaded at runtime while the component is loaded at compile time

questions.exp: A component must stay usable by everyone, so it must not hard-require any particular third-party library — that coupling is pushed into a separate bridge package. The bridge's whole reason to exist is to integrate that specific library, so it declares it as a required dependency. This keeps the component's graph minimal and the integration independently versioned.

questions.q: Which directory is the web root of a Symfony application?
questions.exp: public/ contains index.php and static assets and is the only web-accessible directory.

questions.q: Where are bundles enabled in a modern Symfony app?
questions.exp: config/bundles.php maps each bundle class to the environments where it is enabled; the kernel reads it via MicroKernelTrait.

questions.q: What supplies registerBundles() and registerContainerConfiguration() in a skeleton Kernel?
questions.exp: App\\Kernel uses MicroKernelTrait, which implements the boilerplate to load bundles from config/bundles.php and configuration from config/.

questions.q: In config/bundles.php an entry reads `WebProfilerBundle::class => ['dev' => true, 'test' => true]`. What does this mean?

a.t: The bundle is enabled only in the dev and test environments, not in prod
The bundle runs in all environments because at least one is true
The bundle is disabled everywhere until you add 'all' => true

questions.exp: config/bundles.php maps each bundle class to an array of environment => bool. The kernel enables the bundle only in the listed environments whose value is true. `['all' => true]` means every environment; `['dev' => true, 'test' => true]` means dev and test only (typical for debugging/profiling bundles).

questions.q: In prod, why is public/index.php fast and free of YAML parsing on the hot path?

a.t: config/ is parsed at compile time into a dumped container in var/cache/<env>/; runtime only loads that compiled container
The kernel re-parses config/packages/*.yaml on every request but caches the result in APCu
index.php inlines all YAML as PHP arrays that are re-evaluated per request

questions.exp: Configuration is compiled once into a dumped PHP container under var/cache/<env>/. In prod the kernel simply loads that compiled container, so no YAML parsing happens per request — that is why the front controller stays tiny and the hot path is fast. In dev, ConfigCache checks freshness and rebuilds when source config changes.

questions.q: How does a modern (Symfony 8) bundle inherit and override another bundle's resources?

a.t: It doesn't — bundle inheritance via getParent() was removed; you override each resource type individually
By implementing getParent() to return the parent bundle's name
By extending the parent bundle class and calling parent::build()

questions.exp: The getParent() bundle-inheritance mechanism was deprecated in 4.4 and removed in 5.0; it does not exist in Symfony 8. Modern apps override each resource type on its own (templates via templates/bundles/<Name>/, services via decoration/redefinition, config via config/packages/). Mentioning getParent() as a current mechanism is a planted trap.

questions.q: What does the default `App\:` service definition with `resource: '../src/'` and `exclude: '../src/{Kernel.php}'` achieve?

a.t: It auto-registers every class under src/ as a service (with autowire/autoconfigure defaults), excluding Kernel.php
It marks all src/ classes public so they can be fetched from the container
It imports src/ as a Composer autoload path at runtime

questions.exp: The resource glob discovers classes under src/ and registers each as a service whose id is its FQCN, inheriting the _defaults (autowire: true, autoconfigure: true). exclude keeps non-service classes (like Kernel.php, entities, DTOs) out. Unused private services are then pruned by the compiler. It does not make them public.

questions.q: For a controller that returns a Response, in what order do the kernel events fire?
questions.exp: kernel.view is skipped because a Response was returned; the remaining events follow the canonical order, then finish_request and terminate.

questions.q: When is kernel.view dispatched?

a.t: Only when the controller returns a value that is not a Response

questions.exp: If the controller returns a non-Response value, kernel.view listeners must convert it into a Response.

questions.q: When is kernel.terminate dispatched?

a.t: After the response has been sent to the client, for the main request

questions.exp: terminate() runs after send() and is not called for sub-requests; it is ideal for slow post-response work.

questions.q: A listener calls setResponse() on kernel.request. What happens next?

a.t: The controller is skipped and flow continues at kernel.response

questions.exp: Setting a response on kernel.request short-circuits controller resolution; the response still passes through kernel.response.

questions.q: What is the value of HttpKernelInterface::MAIN_REQUEST?
questions.exp: MAIN_REQUEST is 1 and SUB_REQUEST is 2; the old MASTER_REQUEST constant was removed.

questions.q: What is the full firing order of the linear kernel events when a controller returns a non-Response value that a listener then converts?

a.t: request → controller → controller_arguments → view → response → finish_request → (after send) terminate
request → controller_arguments → controller → response → view → terminate → finish_request
request → controller → view → controller_arguments → response → terminate
request → controller → response → view → finish_request → terminate

questions.exp: The canonical order is request, controller, controller_arguments, view (only when a non-Response is returned), response, finish_request; then after the response is sent, terminate. kernel.exception is the eighth KernelEvents constant but fires out of band, only on error. controller_arguments runs AFTER argument resolution, and view sits between the controller call and response.

questions.q: What are the respective jobs of ControllerResolverInterface and ArgumentResolverInterface?

a.t: ControllerResolver reads the _controller attribute and returns a callable; ArgumentResolver builds the ordered argument array via value resolvers
ControllerResolver builds the argument array; ArgumentResolver picks the route
Both resolve the route; the controller is chosen by the router directly

questions.exp: ControllerResolverInterface::getController(Request) reads the _controller request attribute (set by the router) and returns a PHP callable. ArgumentResolverInterface::getArguments() then runs a chain of ValueResolverInterface resolvers (request attributes, the Request object, #[MapRequestPayload], services, variadics, defaults) to build the ordered argument list passed to the controller.

questions.q: Relative to argument resolution, when does kernel.controller_arguments fire?

a.t: After ArgumentResolver has built the argument array — listeners edit an already-resolved array via setArguments()
Before argument resolution, so listeners provide the raw values the resolver will use
During controller execution, once per argument

questions.exp: kernel.controller_arguments is dispatched AFTER ArgumentResolverInterface::getArguments() has produced the final ordered array; listeners receive a ControllerArgumentsEvent and may mutate the already-built array with setArguments(). Assuming it runs before resolution (to feed the resolver) is a common misconception.

questions.q: A controller does its work but has no return statement (returns null) and no kernel.view listener handles it. What happens?

a.t: The kernel dispatches kernel.view; since no response is set, it throws ControllerDoesNotReturnResponseException
The kernel silently sends an empty 200 response
A fatal PHP TypeError is raised before any event fires

questions.exp: After the controller runs, handleRaw() checks whether the return value is a Response; if not, it dispatches kernel.view carrying the value. If no listener calls setResponse(), the kernel throws ControllerDoesNotReturnResponseException (a LogicException) with the familiar \"The controller must return a Response object but it returned null\" message. The fix is to return a real Response or register a view listener.

questions.q: Which statement about sub-requests is correct?

a.t: They run the same request→...→finish_request flow but never fire kernel.terminate; RequestStack push/pop restores parent state
They fire kernel.terminate once per sub-request, like the main request
They skip kernel.request and start directly at kernel.controller

questions.exp: A sub-request (HttpKernelInterface::SUB_REQUEST) runs the full linear flow from kernel.request through kernel.response and kernel.finish_request, but kernel.terminate fires only for the main request after send. handleRaw() pushes the sub-request onto the RequestStack before kernel.request and pops it after kernel.finish_request, restoring the parent request/locale.

questions.q: What is the signature of HttpKernelInterface::handle() and the role of its $catch argument?

a.t: handle(Request $request, int $type = self::MAIN_REQUEST, bool $catch = true): Response — with $catch=true, exceptions are caught and turned into a response via kernel.exception; with $catch=false they propagate
handle(Request $request): void — it prints the response directly and $catch controls output buffering
handle(string $env, bool $debug): Response — $catch enables the profiler

questions.exp: The contract is handle(Request, int $type = MAIN_REQUEST, bool $catch = true): Response. handle() wraps the private handleRaw() in a try/catch when $catch is true, so an escaped exception is routed through handleThrowable()/kernel.exception into a Response. With $catch=false (common in sub-requests and tests) the exception simply propagates to the caller.

questions.q: A listener is annotated #[AsEventListener(event: KernelEvents::RESPONSE, priority: -10)] and sets an X-Frame-Options header. When does it run?

a.t: On every response passing through kernel.response, after listeners with higher priority (since -10 is below the default 0)
Only when the controller returns a non-Response value
Before the controller is called, during kernel.request

questions.exp: kernel.response fires for every response (whether from the controller, a view listener, or a short-circuit). Listeners run high priority first; priority -10 is below the default 0, so this header listener runs relatively late. The #[AsEventListener] attribute is wired by RegisterListenersPass at compile time, replacing manual tagging.

questions.q: Which event is responsible for turning an exception into a response?
questions.exp: When an exception escapes handleRaw(), HttpKernel dispatches kernel.exception; listeners may set the response.

questions.q: What status code results from an uncaught plain \LogicException?
questions.exp: Only exceptions implementing HttpExceptionInterface carry a status; any other exception defaults to 500.

questions.q: At what priority is the default ErrorListener registered on kernel.exception?
questions.exp: ErrorListener runs at a low priority (-128) so your own exception listeners get the first chance to handle the throwable.

questions.q: Where do you override the default 404 error template?
questions.exp: TwigBundle resolves error templates from templates/bundles/TwigBundle/Exception/, falling back to error.html.twig.

questions.q: What does the default ErrorListener actually do when it handles a kernel.exception?

a.t: It logs the exception, forwards to the error controller as a sub-request, and sets the resulting Response on the event
It immediately calls exit() with the HTTP status code
It re-throws the exception so PHP's default handler renders it

questions.exp: ErrorListener (priority -128) logs the throwable, forwards to the error_controller (ErrorController) as a sub-request whose response carries the status/headers from HttpExceptionInterface, and sets that response on the ExceptionEvent. Because it runs last, any higher-priority listener that already set a response wins and ErrorListener does nothing.

questions.q: How do Security's AccessDeniedException and HttpKernel's AccessDeniedHttpException differ?

a.t: AccessDeniedHttpException implements HttpExceptionInterface (→ 403 directly); AccessDeniedException is a Security exception the firewall translates to 403 or a redirect to login
They are aliases of the same class in different namespaces
AccessDeniedException already carries a 403 status code via HttpExceptionInterface

questions.exp: They are different classes. Symfony\\Component\\HttpKernel\\Exception\\AccessDeniedHttpException implements HttpExceptionInterface and yields a 403 through the normal error flow. Symfony\\Component\\Security\\Core\\Exception\\AccessDeniedException is a Security exception that does NOT implement HttpExceptionInterface; the firewall's exception listener catches it and turns it into a 403 (or a redirect to the login page for unauthenticated users).

questions.q: A kernel.exception listener inspects getThrowable() and builds a JsonResponse, but the custom page never appears. What is the most likely bug?

a.t: The listener forgot to call $event->setResponse() on its branch, so the event's response stays null and the default handler wins
The listener has priority -128, which is impossible to register
kernel.exception cannot produce JSON responses, only HTML

questions.exp: ExceptionEvent::getResponse() returns null until some listener calls setResponse(). Reading getThrowable() and constructing a response is not enough — you must actually set it on the event. If a branch forgets setResponse(), the response stays null, ErrorListener's default page (or a 500) is used instead, and your custom page never shows.

questions.q: After kernel.exception is dispatched, what does the kernel do if no listener set a response?

a.t: handleThrowable() sees hasResponse() is false and re-throws the original throwable (which surfaces as a 500 when catch is true)
It returns an empty Response with status 204
It automatically retries the controller once more

questions.exp: If ExceptionEvent has no response after dispatch, handleThrowable() re-throws the original exception. In practice ErrorListener (priority -128) fills the gap, so this null case only bites when you replace or disable it. With catch:true the re-thrown error becomes a 500 to the client.

questions.q: Which built-in exception produces a 404 response?
questions.exp: NotFoundHttpException maps to 404. AccessDeniedHttpException maps to 403 and BadRequestHttpException to 400. All implement HttpExceptionInterface, so their status code and headers flow through to the produced response; a generic HttpException takes any status code from its constructor.

questions.q: What does a higher listener priority mean?
questions.exp: Listeners are sorted by priority in descending order, so higher priorities run first; the default priority is 0.

questions.q: What is the dispatch() signature in Symfony 8 (PSR-14)?

a.t: dispatch(Event $event, string $eventName) with a required name

questions.exp: Symfony follows PSR-14: the event object comes first, the name is optional (defaults to the event's class name).

questions.q: Which method must an event subscriber implement?
questions.exp: EventSubscriberInterface defines the static getSubscribedEvents() method returning event names mapped to handlers.

questions.q: What does $event->stopPropagation() do?

a.t: Prevents the remaining listeners of this event from running

questions.exp: It sets a flag the dispatcher checks before each listener; only the current event's remaining listeners are skipped.

questions.q: How does EventDispatcher store and order listeners internally?

a.t: It keeps listeners[eventName][priority][] and sorts by priority descending on first dispatch, memoising the sorted list until a listener is added/removed
It sorts listeners alphabetically by class name on every dispatch
It runs listeners in random order to prevent coupling

questions.exp: Internally the dispatcher stores listeners keyed by event name then priority. On the first dispatch of an event it sorts by priority descending (higher first; equal priorities preserve registration order) and caches the result in a sorted[] map, invalidated only when listeners change. This memoisation keeps repeated dispatches cheap.

questions.q: How are tagged listeners/subscribers and #[AsEventListener] attributes wired into the dispatcher?

a.t: RegisterListenersPass wires them at container compile time, and listener services are instantiated lazily only when their event fires
The kernel calls addListener() for each on every kernel.request
They are registered at runtime the first time getSubscribedEvents() is called

questions.exp: The RegisterListenersPass compiler pass scans services tagged kernel.event_listener/kernel.event_subscriber and #[AsEventListener] attributes and wires them into the dispatcher at compile time. Listeners are registered lazily — the service is only constructed when its event actually fires — which keeps boot cheap. You rarely call addListener() at runtime.

questions.q: Which are valid return values from getSubscribedEvents() for a single event? (choose all that apply)
questions.exp: getSubscribedEvents() maps event NAMES to handlers. The value may be a method name string, a [method, priority] pair, or a list of such pairs to register several handlers for the same event. Mapping method → event name (reversed) is wrong and a frequent mistake.

questions.q: What does dispatch(object $event) return, and how do you read a listener's result?

a.t: It always returns the same event object you passed in; results reach you only by listeners mutating that event (e.g. setResponse), never as a listener return value
It returns whatever the last listener returned
It returns null when no listener set a value

questions.exp: dispatch() returns the exact event object passed in — even with no listeners, or when all left it untouched. Listeners themselves return void; the only way data flows back is by mutating the event, which you then read from the returned object. Expecting dispatch() to hand back a listener's return value is the classic bug.

questions.q: Two listeners for the same event both use the default priority. In what order do they run?

a.t: In registration order — the default priority is 0 and equal priorities preserve the order they were added
In reverse registration order (last added runs first)

questions.exp: The default priority is 0. Listeners are sorted by priority descending, and ties (equal priority) keep their registration order. So two default-priority listeners run first-registered-first. To force an order, set explicit priorities rather than relying on registration order.

questions.q: What is the key difference between a listener and a subscriber?

a.t: A listener is registered against one event; a subscriber declares all the events it handles in getSubscribedEvents()
A subscriber can only handle one event; a listener handles many
Listeners run at runtime while subscribers run at compile time

questions.exp: A listener is a callable attached to a single event name (via #[AsEventListener] or the kernel.event_listener tag). A subscriber implements EventSubscriberInterface and declares all its events (and priorities) in the static getSubscribedEvents() method — handy when one class handles several related events. Both are wired by RegisterListenersPass.

questions.q: Where should business logic live according to the best practices?
questions.exp: Controllers should be thin and delegate to services, which keeps logic reusable and testable.

questions.q: What visibility should application services have by default?
questions.exp: Private services let the DI compiler inline and remove them, and discourage the service-locator anti-pattern.

questions.q: Where do sensitive credentials belong?
questions.exp: Secrets should be stored in the encrypted Secrets vault, while infrastructure config uses env vars and behaviour uses parameters.

questions.q: What does this services.yaml _defaults block enable: autowire: true, autoconfigure: true, public: false?

a.t: Constructor deps are injected by type, services are auto-tagged by the interfaces they implement, and services are private by default
All services become public singletons that can be fetched from the container
It disables the compiler so services are resolved at runtime

questions.exp: autowire resolves constructor arguments by type-hint; autoconfigure auto-tags services based on implemented interfaces/attributes (e.g. subscribers get kernel.event_subscriber); public: false keeps them private so the compiler can inline/prune them and you inject rather than fetch. This is the idiomatic Symfony 8 default.

questions.q: Where should each belong: a database URL, a feature toggle, and a third-party API private key?

a.t: Database URL → env var; feature toggle → parameter (or env var if it varies per env); API private key → Secrets vault
All three → hard-coded parameters in services.yaml
All three → the Secrets vault, committed to git

questions.exp: Infrastructure config that varies per environment (database URL) goes in env vars; application behaviour (feature toggle) goes in parameters, or an env var if it changes per environment; sensitive credentials (API private key) go in the encrypted Secrets vault — never committed as plain config.

questions.q: Why is making application services public "to be safe" discouraged?

a.t: Public services block the DI compiler from inlining/removing them and invite the service-locator anti-pattern; private + injected is preferred
Public services cannot be autowired at all
Public services are slower because they are re-instantiated on every request

questions.exp: Marking services public prevents the compiler from optimising them away or inlining them, and encourages fetching from the container (service location) instead of dependency injection. The best practice is private, autowired services injected via the constructor. Public visibility is only needed in a few edge cases (e.g. legacy get() calls).

questions.q: How often does a new Symfony minor version ship?

a.t: Every six months, in May and November

questions.exp: Symfony uses a fixed time-based cadence: a minor every May and November, a major every two years.

questions.q: Which Symfony 8.x version is the LTS?
questions.exp: The last minor of each major (X.4) is the LTS; it ships alongside the next major (9.0).

questions.q: What may a MINOR release NOT do?
questions.exp: Minors add features and deprecations but never break BC; breaks are reserved for major releases.

questions.q: What are the maintenance windows for a standard (non-LTS) release?

a.t: 8 months of bug fixes and 14 months of security fixes
3 years of bug fixes and 4 years of security fixes

questions.exp: Standard versions get 8 months bug fixes and 14 months security fixes; LTS versions get 3 years and 4 years respectively.

questions.q: How are bug fixes propagated across Symfony's maintained branches?

a.t: Fixes are merged UP from the oldest maintained branch to newer ones, so a patch to 8.0 also lands in 8.1, 8.2, etc.
Each branch is patched independently with no relationship between them
Fixes are merged DOWN from the newest branch into older ones

questions.exp: Symfony uses a merge-up model: a fix is committed to the lowest maintained branch that needs it and then merged upward into every newer branch. This keeps behaviour consistent across all maintained versions and avoids a fix being present in an old branch but missing in a newer one.

questions.q: What is the difference between a PATCH and a MINOR release?

a.t: A patch (8.0.1 → 8.0.2) contains bug fixes only; a minor (8.0 → 8.1) adds new features and deprecations but is still BC-safe
A patch can add small features; a minor is only for security fixes
Both may break BC as long as deprecations were added

questions.exp: Patch releases carry bug fixes only — no new features, no deprecations, no BC breaks. Minor releases add features and may introduce deprecations, but never break BC. Only majors break BC (by removing previously deprecated code). Confusing patch (bugs only) with minor (features) is a common trap.

questions.q: What is a MAJOR release uniquely allowed to do?

a.t: Remove deprecated code and break backward compatibility (only for APIs deprecated in the previous major line)
Add features without any deprecation path

questions.exp: A major (e.g. 8.x → 9.0) is the only release level permitted to break BC, and only for code that was deprecated during the previous major line. This is what lets you upgrade safely within a major and plan the jump across a major once you have cleared deprecations.

questions.q: When may Symfony break backward compatibility?

a.t: Only in a major release, and only after prior deprecation

questions.exp: BC breaks are reserved for majors and require the affected API to have been deprecated in the previous major line.

questions.q: What does the @internal marker mean for the BC promise?

a.t: The element is excluded from the BC promise and may change at any time

questions.exp: @internal marks implementation details not covered by BC, even if they are PHP-public.

questions.q: How should you customise a final Symfony class in a BC-safe way?
questions.exp: final classes must not be subclassed; wrap them via decoration so Symfony can change internals without breaking you.

questions.q: Is @experimental code covered by the BC promise?

a.t: No — experimental features (often whole components in their first release) are explicitly excluded until marked stable
Yes — everything shipped in a stable Symfony release is covered
Only their public methods are covered, not their properties

questions.exp: @experimental features are excluded from the BC promise until they are stabilised; they may change in any release. Building critical paths on experimental code is risky. Along with @internal and final, @experimental is one of the markers that carve exceptions out of the promise.

questions.q: Symfony adds a new method to one of its own interfaces in a minor release. Is this a BC break?

a.t: Not for code that only USES the interface, but it can break code that IMPLEMENTS it — so only implement interfaces Symfony marks as safe to implement
Yes, always — adding anything to an interface is forbidden between minors
No, never — interfaces are outside the BC promise entirely

questions.exp: The promise is written from two viewpoints. For USING code (calling methods, reading returns) adding a method is safe. For EXTENDING code (your class implementing that interface) a new method is a break, because your class no longer satisfies the contract. Symfony reserves the right to add methods to its interfaces, so you should only implement interfaces meant for implementation.

questions.q: Which of the following are covered by the BC promise? (choose all that apply)

a.t: A public method with no special annotation
The stable public constructor of a non-final, non-internal class

questions.exp: Stable public API without @internal/@experimental is covered — regardless of being a method or constructor. @internal is excluded even though PHP-public, and @experimental is excluded until stabilised. The classic misconception is equating PHP `public` with \"covered\"; @internal overrides that.

questions.q: True or false: a method declared public in PHP but annotated @internal is protected by the BC promise.
questions.exp: False. @internal explicitly removes an element from the BC promise even when it is PHP-public. Such methods/classes can change or disappear in any release, so you must not depend on them. PHP visibility and BC coverage are independent.

questions.q: Which function emits a Symfony deprecation notice, and from which package?

a.t: There is no helper; you must call trigger_error() directly

questions.exp: symfony/deprecation-contracts provides trigger_deprecation($package, $version, $message, ...$args), which formats an E_USER_DEPRECATED notice.

questions.q: When is deprecated code actually removed?
questions.exp: Deprecations survive the whole major line and are only removed in the next major, per the BC promise.

questions.q: Which tool lets you fail the test suite when new deprecations appear?
questions.exp: The PHPUnit bridge collects deprecations; SYMFONY_DEPRECATIONS_HELPER (e.g. max[total]=0) can make the suite fail on any deprecation.

questions.q: What is the argument order of trigger_deprecation()?
questions.exp: The signature is trigger_deprecation(string $package, string $version, string $message, mixed ...$args) with sprintf-style formatting.

questions.q: Which call correctly deprecates ReportBuilder::generate() (deprecated in your app version 8.1)?
questions.exp: The signature is (package, version, message, ...args) with sprintf-style formatting for the message. The first option passes the package, the version it was deprecated IN, a message with a %s placeholder, and self::class as the arg. Putting the message first, or misusing trigger_error with these arguments, is wrong.

questions.q: How do you mark a service as deprecated in config/services.yaml?

a.t: Add a `deprecated:` key with package, version and message under the service definition
Prefix the service id with an underscore

questions.exp: A service is deprecated via the `deprecated:` key (package/version/message), which maps to Definition::setDeprecated() and triggers a deprecation when the service is referenced. Container-level deprecations like this surface during cache:clear/compile time, whereas method-call deprecations fire at runtime.

questions.q: At what error level are Symfony deprecations emitted, and do they throw?

a.t: They are E_USER_DEPRECATED notices — they do not throw unless your test suite/CI is configured to fail on them
They throw a DeprecationException that halts execution immediately
They are E_USER_ERROR, so the request always dies with a fatal error

questions.exp: trigger_deprecation() ultimately calls @trigger_error(..., E_USER_DEPRECATED), producing a notice that is logged/collected but does not interrupt execution. Only when tooling (e.g. the PHPUnit bridge via SYMFONY_DEPRECATIONS_HELPER) is configured to fail on deprecations does a deprecation cause a failure.

questions.q: Which version string should you pass as the second argument of trigger_deprecation()?

a.t: The version in which the API was DEPRECATED (e.g. '8.1'), not the current running version
The current installed version at the time the notice fires
The version in which the code will be REMOVED (the next major)

questions.exp: The version argument records when the deprecation was introduced, producing the \"Since <package> <version>: <message>\" format tooling parses. A common mistake is passing the current version, or the removal version — both are wrong. Use the version the API was deprecated in.

questions.q: Where do you place a template that overrides a bundle template?
questions.exp: Twig resolves overrides from templates/bundles/<BundleName>/, which takes precedence over the bundle's own templates.

questions.q: What is the current mechanism to override an inherited bundle resource?

a.t: Per-resource overriding of templates, services, translations and config

questions.exp: Bundle inheritance via getParent() was deprecated in 4.4 and removed in 5.0; modern Symfony overrides each resource type individually.

questions.q: How do you augment a bundle service without replacing it?

a.t: Decorate it with #[AsDecorator] / the decorates: key
Make it public and fetch it

questions.exp: Decoration wraps the original service (injected as .inner), letting you add behaviour and delegate.

questions.q: When you decorate a service with #[AsDecorator(decorates: 'acme.mailer')], how do you access the original?

a.t: Inject the renamed original (the .inner service) via #[AutowireDecorated] and delegate to it
Instantiate a new copy of the original class with `new`
Fetch it from the container by making acme.mailer public

questions.exp: Decoration renames the original service to a .inner id and injects it into the decorator. The #[AutowireDecorated] attribute (or the special .inner reference in YAML) gives you that original instance so you can add behaviour and delegate. Re-creating it with `new` or fetching it publicly defeats the decoration pattern.

questions.q: A bundle ships translations/messages.en.yaml and your app defines the same domain/locale in translations/. Whose strings win?

a.t: The application's translations/ take priority over the bundle's translations
The bundle's translations always win because they load first
They merge alphabetically and the last key alphabetically wins

questions.exp: The application's translations/ directory has higher priority than any bundle's translations. Providing a catalogue with the same domain and locale overrides the bundle's strings — the same convention-based precedence used for template overrides.

questions.q: What happened to bundle inheritance (getParent()) and the legacy Resources/ folder?

a.t: getParent() inheritance was deprecated in 4.4 and removed in 5.0; modern bundles use top-level config/, templates/, translations/ instead of Resources/
getParent() is still the recommended way to override bundle resources in Symfony 8
Resources/ is now mandatory and getParent() was reinstated in 8.0

questions.exp: Bundle inheritance via getParent() is gone (deprecated 4.4, removed 5.0) and must not be presented as current. Modern bundles also drop the legacy Resources/ layout in favour of top-level config/, templates/ and translations/. Overriding is done per resource type instead.

questions.q: In which months do Symfony minor releases ship?
questions.exp: The cadence is fixed: a new minor every May and every November.

questions.q: When does 8.4 (LTS) release relative to 9.0?
questions.exp: The LTS (X.4) always ships together with the next major (X+1).0.

questions.q: How often is a new major (and its LTS) released?
questions.exp: Majors, and the accompanying LTS, come every two years.

questions.q: Which sequence correctly lists the Symfony 8.x release dates?
questions.exp: 8.0 opened the cycle in Nov 2025; a minor lands every six months (May/Nov): 8.1 May 2026, 8.2 Nov 2026, 8.3 May 2027, and 8.4 (LTS) Nov 2027 alongside 9.0. The pattern repeats for every major: X.0 opens, four minors follow, X.4 is the LTS shipping with (X+1).0.

questions.q: Which statement about the LTS timing is correct?

a.t: The LTS (X.4) ships at the same time as the next major (X+1).0, not before it
The LTS ships one year before the next major so people can migrate
8.0 is the long-term support release of the 8.x line

questions.exp: A frequent misconception is that the LTS precedes the next major. In fact X.4 (the LTS) and (X+1).0 release together (8.4 and 9.0 both Nov 2027). Another trap: 8.0 is a standard release, not the LTS — 8.4 is.

questions.q: A product must run 3+ years without a major upgrade. Which 8.x version should you target and why?

a.t: 8.4 (LTS) — it provides 3 years of bug fixes and 4 years of security fixes, the longest support window in 8.x
8.0 — being the first release it is supported the longest

questions.exp: Only the LTS (X.4) offers the long maintenance windows (3 years bug fixes, 4 years security fixes). Standard minors get 8 months bug + 14 months security, far short of 3 years. So a long-lived product should pin to 8.4 and plan the jump to the next major deliberately.

questions.q: Which PSR does Symfony's EventDispatcher implement?
questions.exp: Symfony's EventDispatcherInterface extends the PSR-14 Psr\\EventDispatcher\\EventDispatcherInterface.

questions.q: Is HttpFoundation's Request a PSR-7 message?

a.t: No — a psr-http-message bridge converts between them

questions.exp: HttpFoundation predates and differs from PSR-7; the psr-http-message bridge converts between HttpFoundation and PSR-7/15/17.

questions.q: Which PSR interface does Symfony's service container implement?
questions.exp: Symfony's ContainerInterface extends Psr\\Container\\ContainerInterface (PSR-11).

questions.q: Which PSR does Symfony primarily consume (rather than implement) so you can inject any implementation?
questions.exp: Components type-hint Psr\\Log\\LoggerInterface (PSR-3), so any compliant logger can be injected. PSR-11, PSR-14, PSR-6 and PSR-20 are implemented by Symfony.

questions.q: Which PSRs does Symfony IMPLEMENT (i.e. Symfony objects ARE valid PSR objects)? (choose all that apply)
questions.exp: Symfony implements PSR-6 (Cache pool), PSR-11 (Container), PSR-14 (EventDispatcher), PSR-16 (Simple Cache adapter) and PSR-20 (Clock) — its objects can be handed to any library expecting those interfaces. PSR-3 (Logger) is CONSUMED: Symfony type-hints LoggerInterface so you inject any implementation, but it does not ship the logger itself.

questions.q: What is the difference between PSR-6 and PSR-16 in Symfony's Cache?

a.t: PSR-6 is the pool/CacheItem model (CacheItemPoolInterface); PSR-16 is the simpler get/set SimpleCache API (Psr16Cache adapter)
PSR-6 is for HTTP caching and PSR-16 is for the container
They are the same interface at different versions

questions.exp: PSR-6 models caching as a pool of CacheItem objects (CacheItemPoolInterface::getItem()/save()); PSR-16 (Simple Cache) is a lighter get()/set()/delete() API, exposed by Symfony's Psr16Cache adapter. Confusing the pool/item model (PSR-6) with the simple key/value API (PSR-16) is a common trap.

questions.q: Which PSR does Symfony's Clock component implement, and why inject its interface?

a.t: PSR-20 via Psr\Clock\ClockInterface — injecting it makes time testable instead of calling new \DateTime() directly
PSR-7 — the clock produces HTTP timestamps
PSR-11 — the clock is fetched from the container by id

questions.exp: Symfony\\Component\\Clock\\Clock implements Psr\\Clock\\ClockInterface (PSR-20). Type-hinting ClockInterface lets you inject a MockClock in tests and control time deterministically, instead of hard-coding new \\DateTime()/now() calls that are impossible to freeze.

questions.q: What is the practical difference between Symfony implementing a PSR and consuming a PSR?

a.t: Implementing means a Symfony object satisfies the PSR (hand it to any PSR consumer); consuming means Symfony type-hints the PSR so you can inject any implementation
Implementing is done at runtime; consuming is done at compile time
There is no difference — both mean Symfony ships the concrete class

questions.exp: Implements: Symfony's class IS a valid PSR object (e.g. its Container is a PSR-11 container), usable by any library expecting that interface. Consumes: Symfony depends on the PSR interface as a type-hint (e.g. PSR-3 LoggerInterface) so you can plug in any compliant implementation. The direction of the dependency is what differs.

questions.q: How are application service IDs written in modern Symfony?
questions.exp: The service id is the FQCN; autowiring matches type-hints to these ids.

questions.q: What naming case do environment variables use?

a.t: UPPER_SNAKE_CASE, usually with an APP_ prefix

questions.exp: Env vars use upper snake case (APP_ENV, APP_DEBUG) and are read in config via processors such as %env(int:APP_PAGE_SIZE)%.

questions.q: Which is a correctly named route?
questions.exp: Route names use snake_case, conventionally entity_action.

questions.q: How is an abstract class conventionally named?

a.t: With an Abstract prefix, e.g. AbstractController
With an Abstract suffix, e.g. ControllerAbstract

questions.exp: Abstract classes take the Abstract prefix; interfaces use the Interface suffix and traits use the Trait suffix.

questions.q: Which set correctly fixes these names: httpClientInterface, Abstract_Controller, blogShow (route), app-page-size (parameter), app_env (env var)?
questions.exp: Interfaces are PascalCase with the Interface suffix (HttpClientInterface); abstract classes take the Abstract prefix in PascalCase (AbstractController); routes are snake_case (blog_show); parameters are snake/dot-separated lowercase (app.page_size); env vars are UPPER_SNAKE with APP_ prefix (APP_ENV).

questions.q: Why is the Interface suffix more than cosmetic in Symfony?

a.t: Autoconfiguration inspects implemented interfaces (e.g. EventSubscriberInterface) to auto-tag services, so correct interface naming/implementation is part of a working contract
The router requires interface names to end in Interface to build URLs
Composer's autoloader only loads classes whose interface ends in Interface

questions.exp: When autoconfigure is on, Symfony auto-tags services based on the interfaces they implement — e.g. implementing EventSubscriberInterface auto-adds the kernel.event_subscriber tag, and ServiceSubscriberInterface, and voter/command interfaces behave similarly. So the Interface suffix marks a real, functional contract that drives wiring, not just style.

questions.q: Which casing pair is correct for PHP class constants and bundle config keys?

a.t: Constants are UPPER_SNAKE_CASE (e.g. MAIN_REQUEST); bundle config keys are snake_case (e.g. framework.http_method_override)
Constants are camelCase; config keys are PascalCase

questions.exp: PHP constants follow UPPER_SNAKE_CASE (HttpKernelInterface::MAIN_REQUEST) and enum cases are PascalCase. Bundle configuration keys are snake_case under the extension's alias (e.g. framework.http_method_override). Mixing these up — camelCase config keys, for instance — is a planted mistake.

questions.q: Which of the following statements are true about Symfony Flex? (select all that apply)

a.t: Flex is a Composer plugin that resolves package aliases and applies recipes at install/update time
symfony.lock records which recipes are installed and should be committed to version control
Bundles enabled by recipes are registered in config/bundles.php, which the kernel reads at boot
Flex hooks into the kernel at runtime to auto-register bundles on each HTTP request
Installed recipes are recorded in composer.lock together with package versions

questions.exp: Flex is a Composer plugin that runs only at Composer install/update time, resolving aliases and applying recipes; it plays no role during request handling, so the runtime option is wrong. Applied recipes are tracked in symfony.lock (committed), not in composer.lock which only tracks package versions, and recipe configurators write bundle registrations into config/bundles.php for the kernel to read at boot.

questions.q: Which statements accurately describe the Symfony release process? (select all that apply)

a.t: Minor versions are released on a time-based schedule in May and November, and a new major arrives every two years
8.4 is the Symfony 8 LTS version and ships alongside 9.0
A minor version may break backward compatibility as long as the change was deprecated first
Standard (non-LTS) versions receive 3 years of bug fixes
The LTS of each branch is always the X.0 release of the major

questions.exp: Symfony follows a time-based schedule: minors in May and November and a new major every two years, with the last minor of a branch (X.4, e.g. 8.4) being the LTS that ships alongside the next major. BC breaks happen only in major versions, never in minors even after deprecation, and standard versions get 8 months of bug fixes / 14 months of security fixes — the 3-year bug-fix window belongs to LTS releases only.

questions.q: Which statements are true about Symfony's backward compatibility promise? (select all that apply)

a.t: Public API that is not marked @internal or @experimental stays stable within a major version
Existing behavior is removed only in the next major version, and only after being deprecated first
Classes marked @internal are covered by the promise as long as their methods are public
Extending framework classes through inheritance is the recommended way to customize Symfony

questions.exp: The BC promise guarantees that public, non-@internal, non-@experimental API remains stable within a major, and removals happen only in the next major after a deprecation phase. @internal and @experimental annotations carve exceptions out of the promise regardless of method visibility, and the recommended extension mechanisms are events, decoration and dependency injection rather than inheriting framework classes.

questions.q: Which statements about HttpKernel's request handling and its events are correct? (select all that apply)

a.t: kernel.view is dispatched only when the controller returns something other than a Response
kernel.terminate is dispatched after the response has been sent to the client
When handle() is called with catch: true, exceptions are caught and kernel.exception is dispatched
kernel.response is dispatched before kernel.controller so listeners can veto the controller
The controller callable itself is resolved by the ArgumentResolverInterface

questions.exp: kernel.view fires only for non-Response controller return values, and kernel.terminate runs after the response was already sent, which makes it suitable for heavy post-response work; with catch: true, HttpKernel catches throwables and dispatches kernel.exception. The event order puts kernel.controller before kernel.response, and the controller callable is resolved by ControllerResolverInterface — ArgumentResolverInterface only resolves the controller's arguments.

questions.q: Which statements about Symfony's relationship to the PSR standards are true? (select all that apply)

a.t: The service container implements PSR-11 and the Clock component implements PSR-20
Components type-hint the PSR-3 Psr\Log\LoggerInterface, so any PSR-3 logger can be injected
The psr-http-message bridge converts between HttpFoundation objects and PSR-7 messages
HttpFoundation's Request and Response natively implement the PSR-7 interfaces

questions.exp: Symfony implements PSR-6, PSR-11, PSR-14, PSR-16 and PSR-20 (the container is a PSR-11 ContainerInterface and Clock is PSR-20), and it consumes PSR-3 by type-hinting LoggerInterface so any compliant logger works. HttpFoundation predates and does not implement PSR-7 — the psr-http-message bridge converts between the two object models — and autoloading follows PSR-4, not PSR-0.

questions.q: Which statements about the EventDispatcher component are correct? (select all that apply)

a.t: Listeners for an event are invoked in descending priority order (highest priority first)
stopPropagation() prevents only the remaining listeners of the current event from running
Event subscribers must be registered manually with addListener() for every event they handle
dispatch() takes the event name as the first argument and the event object as the second

questions.exp: The dispatcher sorts listeners by priority in descending order, and stopPropagation() halts only the not-yet-called listeners of the event currently being dispatched — other events are unaffected. Subscribers declare all their events in getSubscribedEvents() and are wired automatically (autoconfiguration tags them), and dispatch() follows the PSR-14 signature: the event object first, then an optional event name.

questions.q: Which are valid ways to override parts of Symfony or a third-party bundle in an application? (select all that apply)

a.t: Override a bundle template by placing a file with the same path under templates/bundles/<BundleName>/
Override a service by decorating it or replacing its definition, e.g. via a compiler pass
Override translations by defining the same key in the application's translations/ directory, which wins over the bundle's
Create a child bundle and point getParent() at the bundle you want to override
Copy the entire bundle into src/ so your copy shadows the vendor code

questions.exp: Per-resource overriding is the supported model: templates placed under templates/bundles/<BundleName>/ shadow the bundle's own, application translations take precedence over bundle translations, and services can be redefined, decorated or altered through a compiler pass. Bundle inheritance via getParent() has been removed, and copying whole bundles into src/ is not an override mechanism at all.

questions.q: Which command runs when you execute `php bin/console` with no arguments?
questions.exp: The Application's default command is `list`, which prints all available commands grouped by namespace. `help` shows usage for a single command and must be given a name; `about` prints an environment summary; `debug:container` is a FrameworkBundle command. The classic trap is to assume `help` is the default — it is not.

questions.q: Which command is provided by an optional bundle (MakerBundle), not by Symfony core?
questions.exp: `make:*` generators ship with the optional symfony/maker-bundle dev dependency. `cache:clear` and `debug:router` come from FrameworkBundle, and `about` is a core Console command. Expecting `make:*` to be part of the core framework is a classic certification trick.

questions.q: How does `bin/console` obtain the console Application in Symfony 8?

a.t: It returns a closure that the Runtime component executes to build the kernel and Application
The web front controller instantiates it

questions.exp: bin/console requires vendor/autoload_runtime.php and returns a closure; the Runtime component reads $context (APP_ENV/APP_DEBUG), runs the closure to build the Kernel and FrameworkBundle Application, then calls Application::run(). There is no Application::create() factory, and the web front controller boots the HTTP kernel, not the console one.

questions.q: What does `php bin/console ca:cl` do when the abbreviation is unambiguous?
questions.exp: Application::find() resolves unambiguous abbreviations (per namespace segment) to the full command name, so `ca:cl` maps to `cache:clear`. If more than one command matched, it would raise an ambiguity error instead — abbreviations only work when the prefix resolves to exactly one command.

questions.q: Which commands exist in *every* Console application, independent of FrameworkBundle? (choose 2)
questions.exp: `list`, `help`, `about` and `completion` are core Console commands present in any Application, even a standalone one. `cache:clear` and `debug:container` are added by FrameworkBundle and only exist in a full-stack Symfony app. A frequent trap is believing `about` is a FrameworkBundle command — it is core Console.

questions.q: You want to inspect which service is registered for an autowired interface without rebuilding the cache. Which command fits?
questions.exp: `debug:autowiring` lists the types you can type-hint for autowiring and the service each resolves to — pure inspection, no cache rebuild. `cache:clear` rebuilds the container (a mutation, not inspection), `cache:warmup` fills caches without clearing, and `make:command` is a MakerBundle generator. Confusing the inspecting `debug:*` family with the rebuilding `cache:*` family is a common error.

questions.q: In Symfony 8 `bin/console` ends with `return static function (array $context): Application { ... };`. What consumes this returned closure?

a.t: The Runtime component (loaded via vendor/autoload_runtime.php), which invokes it with $context and calls run()
PHP itself auto-executes any returned closure at end of file
The Kernel's boot() method executes it
Composer's autoloader executes it during class discovery

questions.exp: `require vendor/autoload_runtime.php` installs the SymfonyRuntime, which captures the closure the file returns, builds a runner, injects $context (from $_SERVER / env), invokes the closure to get the Application, and calls its run() method. PHP does not auto-run returned closures, the Kernel does not, and Composer's autoloader only maps classes to files. This inversion is what lets the same Runtime handle web and console entry points.

questions.q: What integer value does `Command::INVALID` represent?
questions.exp: The return constants are SUCCESS=0, FAILURE=1, INVALID=2. INVALID signals bad input/usage as opposed to a runtime failure (FAILURE=1). 255 is a shell convention for a general error but is not a Command constant.

questions.q: In Symfony 8, what does an invokable command class require?

a.t: The #[AsCommand] attribute and an __invoke() method returning int
It must be registered manually in services.yaml

questions.exp: Invokable commands only need #[AsCommand] plus an __invoke() method returning int; they do not extend Command, yet still use its SUCCESS/FAILURE/INVALID constants for return codes. Autoconfiguration registers them, so no manual services.yaml tag is needed.

questions.q: How is a command normally registered in the service container?

a.t: You always add the 'console.command' tag manually
It is discovered purely by filename

questions.exp: Autoconfiguration applies the console.command tag to any service carrying #[AsCommand] or extending Command; AddConsoleCommandPass then builds a ContainerCommandLoader mapping name→service id for lazy loading. Manual tagging is redundant, filename plays no role, and you do not call Application::add() yourself in a framework app.

questions.q: What must a command's execute()/__invoke() return in Symfony 8?
questions.exp: The returned int becomes the process exit code; returning void/null triggers a type error in Symfony 8. A Response belongs to HTTP controllers, and a bool is not accepted — use Command::SUCCESS/FAILURE/INVALID.

questions.q: Given an invokable command `public function __invoke(SymfonyStyle $io, #[Argument] string $name, #[Option] bool $force = false): int`, how are `$name` and `$force` mapped to the input definition?

a.t: $name becomes a REQUIRED argument; $force becomes a VALUE_NONE (boolean flag) option
$name becomes an OPTIONAL argument; $force becomes VALUE_OPTIONAL
$force becomes a REQUIRED argument because it has no shortcut

questions.exp: The invokable adapter derives modes from the parameter: a #[Argument] with no default is REQUIRED; a #[Option] typed bool becomes a VALUE_NONE flag (present = true, absent = its default false). $name is not optional because it lacks a default, and $force is an option (declared with #[Option]), never an argument.

questions.q: Which statement about a modern invokable command is TRUE?

a.t: It does not extend Command, yet still uses Command::SUCCESS for the return value
It must extend Command to access SUCCESS/FAILURE
It cannot use SymfonyStyle because it has no HelperSet

questions.exp: An invokable command is a plain class; it does not extend Command, but the SUCCESS/FAILURE/INVALID constants are public class constants you can reference from anywhere. SymfonyStyle is injected by type-hint into __invoke(), and __invoke() is a normal (non-static) method. Assuming you must extend Command to reach the constants is the trap.

questions.q: A command's execute() ends with `$io->success('done');` and no return statement. What happens when it runs?

a.t: A TypeError — execute() is declared `: int` but returns null
It silently exits 0 because success() returns 0
It loops until a return is added

questions.exp: execute() is typed `: int`, so falling off the end (returning null) is a fatal TypeError. SymfonyStyle::success() returns void, so it cannot supply the exit code. There is no implicit SUCCESS/INVALID default — you must explicitly `return Command::SUCCESS;`. Forgetting the return is a very common mistake.

questions.q: Which class collects the `console.command` tags and builds the lazy command loader?

a.t: AddConsoleCommandPass, which builds a ContainerCommandLoader (name → service id)
The Kernel's registerCommands() method scans the filesystem

questions.exp: Symfony\\Component\\Console\\DependencyInjection\\AddConsoleCommandPass gathers every service tagged console.command and constructs a ContainerCommandLoader mapping each command name to its service id, so a command is instantiated only when its name is invoked. There is no CommandCompilerPass, commands are not instantiated eagerly at compile time, and Symfony 8 does not scan the filesystem for commands.

questions.q: When unit-testing a command with `CommandTester`, which call executes it and how do you assert the exit code?

a.t: You must boot the full HTTP kernel and issue a request

questions.exp: CommandTester::execute(array $input) runs the command in-memory; getStatusCode() returns the int exit code and getDisplay() returns the captured output. assertCommandIsSuccessful() is the convenience assertion. There is no run() returning a Response (that is HTTP) nor a handle()/getExitCode() pair, and testing a command does not require the HTTP kernel.

questions.q: What is the correct command lifecycle order?
questions.exp: configure() runs in the constructor; then run() binds input and calls initialize(), interact() (only if interactive), input validation, and finally execute(). initialize() always precedes interact() so shared state is ready before prompting.

questions.q: When is interact() called?

a.t: Only when the input is interactive

questions.exp: interact() is skipped for non-interactive input (e.g. -n / --no-interaction), so it is the wrong place for mandatory logic. It runs after initialize(), never before it, and always before execute() — never after.

questions.q: Why declare the command name in #[AsCommand] rather than only in configure()?

a.t: It lets the command loader know the name without instantiating the class (lazy loading)
configure() cannot set a name at all
It is required for execute() to run

questions.exp: The attribute exposes name/aliases at compile time so ContainerCommandLoader maps name→id and instantiates the command only when invoked. Putting the name only in configure() (via setName()) would force the Application to construct every command just to learn its name, defeating lazy loading.

questions.q: A command declared with hidden: true …

a.t: Does not appear in `list` but can still be executed
Only runs in the dev environment

questions.exp: The hidden flag only affects listing; the command stays registered and fully runnable by name or alias. It is not removed from the container and is not environment-scoped.

questions.q: Why can't you read an argument value inside configure()?

a.t: configure() runs in the constructor, before any input is bound
configure() runs after execute(), so input is already consumed
Arguments are only available to interact()
You can — getArgument() works in configure()

questions.exp: configure() is invoked from the Command constructor, long before run() binds the ArgvInput to the definition, so no argument values exist yet — configure() may only declare structure (name, arguments, options, help). Reading input there is a classic mistake; to act on values use initialize()/interact()/execute().

questions.q: A command sets `$this->io = new SymfonyStyle(...)` in initialize() and, in interact(), prompts for a missing `name` argument. Under `--no-interaction` with no `name` given, what happens?

a.t: interact() is skipped, so name stays null and validation fails for the required argument
interact() still runs and blocks waiting for input
initialize() is also skipped, causing a null $this->io

questions.exp: With --no-interaction, interact() is not called, so the prompt never fills the missing value; input->validate() then throws for the missing REQUIRED argument. initialize() always runs regardless of interactivity, so $this->io is set. This is why prompts belong in interact() but must not be the only way to satisfy required input.

questions.q: What does `#[AsCommand(name: 'app:report:generate', aliases: ['app:report'], hidden: false)]` configure?

a.t: The primary name, an alternative name (alias), and that it appears in `list`
Two independent commands sharing one class
A namespace restriction so it only runs under app:report

questions.exp: #[AsCommand] declares metadata: the canonical name, aliases (extra names that invoke the same command), and hidden (false = shown in list). It defines one command reachable by several names, not multiple commands, and aliases are names — not arguments or namespace filters.

questions.q: After moving the command name from #[AsCommand] into `setName()` in configure(), `bin/console list` becomes noticeably slower on a large app. Why?

a.t: The Application must now instantiate every command to learn its name, defeating lazy loading
configure() is called twice per command
list rebuilds the cache when names are dynamic

questions.exp: When the name lives only in configure(), the ContainerCommandLoader can no longer map name→id at compile time, so the Application constructs each command just to read its name — eager instantiation. Keeping the name in #[AsCommand] preserves lazy loading. configure() is not called twice, and setName() does not touch the container cache.

questions.q: Which mode declares a valueless boolean flag option?
questions.exp: VALUE_NONE takes no value; the option is false unless present, then true. It cannot carry a default. VALUE_OPTIONAL/REQUIRED expect a value, and InputArgument::OPTIONAL is an argument mode, not an option mode.

questions.q: What is the integer value of InputOption::VALUE_IS_ARRAY?
questions.exp: Option modes are VALUE_NONE=1, VALUE_REQUIRED=2, VALUE_OPTIONAL=4, VALUE_IS_ARRAY=8, VALUE_NEGATABLE=16. They are powers of two so they can be combined with a bitmask (e.g. VALUE_REQUIRED | VALUE_IS_ARRAY = 10).

questions.q: Which statement about an IS_ARRAY argument is correct?

a.t: There can be only one and it must be declared last
You may declare several per command
It cannot be combined with REQUIRED

questions.exp: An array argument greedily consumes all remaining tokens, so only one is allowed and it must come last. It may be combined as IS_ARRAY | REQUIRED or IS_ARRAY | OPTIONAL. Declaring it first or having several would make positional parsing ambiguous.

questions.q: Which option mode adds a `--no-foo` counterpart to `--foo`?
questions.exp: VALUE_NEGATABLE (16) generates the --no- twin: the value is true with --foo, false with --no-foo, and its default otherwise. VALUE_NONE is a plain flag with no negation, and the array/optional modes are unrelated.

questions.q: Which InputArgument mode value is OPTIONAL?
questions.exp: Argument modes are REQUIRED=1, OPTIONAL=2, IS_ARRAY=4. Note these differ from option modes (where 2 is VALUE_REQUIRED) — mixing the two integer scales is a common exam trap.

questions.q: `$this->addOption('force', 'f', InputOption::VALUE_NONE, 'Force it', true);` throws when the command is built. Why?

a.t: A VALUE_NONE option cannot have a default value
The shortcut 'f' collides with a reserved global shortcut
VALUE_NONE options require an array default
Options may not have both a shortcut and a description

questions.exp: A VALUE_NONE option is always false unless present (then true), so providing a default is meaningless and InputOption's constructor throws a LogicException. Passing null (or omitting the default) is correct. Shortcuts and descriptions are perfectly allowed together.

questions.q: In an invokable command, `#[Option] array $tags = []` on the __invoke() parameter produces which InputOption mode?

a.t: VALUE_IS_ARRAY (repeatable, e.g. --tags=a --tags=b), optional via the [] default
VALUE_NONE, because arrays are treated as flags
VALUE_REQUIRED with a single string value
It is rejected — arrays are only allowed for arguments

questions.exp: The invokable adapter maps an array-typed #[Option] to VALUE_IS_ARRAY, so the option is repeatable; the [] default makes it optional. A bool would map to VALUE_NONE, a scalar with no default to VALUE_REQUIRED. Arrays are valid for both options and (as the last) arguments.

questions.q: Which is true about shortcuts like `-f`?

a.t: Shortcuts belong to options only; arguments have no shortcuts
Every argument automatically gets a one-letter shortcut
Shortcuts are only for VALUE_NONE options
Shortcuts must be exactly two characters

questions.exp: Only options accept a shortcut (the 2nd argument of addOption); arguments are positional and have no shortcut. Shortcuts work for any option mode, not just VALUE_NONE, and are typically a single character (e.g. -f).

questions.q: What role does InputDefinition play during a command run?

a.t: $input->bind(definition) maps raw ArgvInput tokens to args/options; $input->validate() then throws if a REQUIRED value is missing
It renders help text only and has no effect on parsing
It executes the command after parsing
It stores the exit code after execution

questions.exp: InputDefinition is the ordered set of InputArguments plus the map of InputOptions. run() calls $input->bind($definition) to match raw tokens, then $input->validate() throws a Console RuntimeException if a REQUIRED argument or VALUE_REQUIRED option value is absent. It does not execute the command or hold exit codes; help rendering is a separate use of the same definition.

questions.q: Which argument declaration order is INVALID?

a.t: A REQUIRED argument declared after an OPTIONAL one
A REQUIRED argument followed by an OPTIONAL one
A REQUIRED argument followed by an IS_ARRAY argument

questions.exp: Because arguments are positional, a REQUIRED argument may not follow an OPTIONAL one — the parser could not tell which token filled which slot. Required-then- optional is fine, a lone optional is fine, and an array argument (last) may follow a required scalar.

questions.q: Which method returns the STDERR stream in a CLI command?
questions.exp: getErrorOutput() lives on ConsoleOutputInterface, not the base OutputInterface — so guard with `instanceof ConsoleOutputInterface` before calling it, or you risk a fatal type error. SymfonyStyle exposes getErrorStyle() (not stderr()), and input has nothing to do with error streams.

questions.q: Which two arguments does SymfonyStyle require?
questions.exp: SymfonyStyle wraps both input (for prompts like ask/confirm) and output (for styled writing), so its constructor is (InputInterface, OutputInterface). It creates its own QuestionHelper internally and needs neither an Application nor a Command.

questions.q: What does $output->section() return?

a.t: A ConsoleSectionOutput that can be overwritten or cleared independently

questions.exp: Output sections are independently re-writable regions (ConsoleSectionOutput): you can overwrite() or clear() one without disturbing others — the basis for multiple live progress bars. section() is only available on ConsoleOutputInterface (real CLI output).

questions.q: What is the difference between write() and writeln()?

a.t: writeln() appends a newline; write() does not
write() sends to STDERR, writeln() to STDOUT

questions.exp: writeln() is write() plus a trailing line break; neither changes the target stream (both go to STDOUT unless you fetch the error output) and neither toggles colours. Both accept an optional verbosity mask as a second argument.

questions.q: Why can a SymfonyStyle instance be passed to a method type-hinted OutputInterface?

a.t: SymfonyStyle implements OutputInterface (it decorates the underlying output)
The Console component casts it automatically
OutputInterface is a marker interface with no methods
It cannot — SymfonyStyle is unrelated to OutputInterface

questions.exp: SymfonyStyle implements both StyleInterface and OutputInterface, decorating the wrapped output, so it satisfies an OutputInterface type-hint directly — no cast needed. OutputInterface is a full contract (write/writeln/verbosity), not a marker.

questions.q: A command exports CSV to STDOUT so users can run `bin/console app:export > data.csv`, yet you still want a live progress message on screen. Where should the progress message go?

a.t: To STDERR via getErrorOutput(), keeping STDOUT clean for the piped CSV
To STDOUT interleaved with the CSV rows
To a log file only; the terminal cannot show it
Nowhere — progress bars break redirection entirely

questions.exp: Data belongs on STDOUT (what the redirection captures); status/progress belongs on STDERR, which still displays on the terminal when STDOUT is piped to a file. Writing progress to STDOUT would corrupt the CSV. This split-stream design is why getErrorOutput() exists.

questions.q: `execute(InputInterface $input, OutputInterface $output)` calls `$output->getErrorOutput()`. It works locally but fatals in a test. Likely cause?

a.t: The test passes a plain OutputInterface (e.g. BufferedOutput) that has no getErrorOutput(); guard with instanceof ConsoleOutputInterface
STDERR is unavailable during PHPUnit runs

questions.exp: getErrorOutput() is declared on ConsoleOutputInterface, not the base OutputInterface. Real CLI runs inject a ConsoleOutput (which implements it), but tests often inject a BufferedOutput, so the call fatals. Guarding with `if ($output instanceof ConsoleOutputInterface)` fixes it. The method still exists in Symfony 8 and needs no setter.

questions.q: Which InputInterface method reports whether the command may prompt the user?
questions.exp: InputInterface::isInteractive() returns false under -n/--no-interaction, and the runner uses it to decide whether interact() runs; guard prompts with it. isVerbose() is an output verbosity check, not interactivity, and there is no built-in 'interactive' argument/option to read.

questions.q: How does a classic command obtain the QuestionHelper?
questions.exp: Helpers are fetched by their string name from the command's HelperSet, so getHelper('question') returns the QuestionHelper. QuestionHelper's constructor takes no input, there is no Application::question(), and SymfonyStyle exposes ask()/confirm() rather than a helper() accessor.

questions.q: Which question class offers a fixed list of selectable answers?
