questions.exp: ChoiceQuestion presents a list of options and supports single or multi-select. Question is free text, ConfirmationQuestion is yes/no, and there is no HiddenQuestion class — hidden input is Question::setHidden(true).

questions.q: What does ProgressBar::setRedrawFrequency(100) do?

a.t: Redraws the bar only every 100 steps to reduce terminal I/O
Sets the total number of steps to 100
Caps the bar width at 100 characters

questions.exp: Redraw throttling avoids expensive terminal writes on every micro-step — a performance knob, not cosmetic. The total is set via the constructor/ start($max), width is a separate format setting, and it never sleeps.

questions.q: Which class moves or hides the terminal cursor?
questions.exp: Cursor issues ANSI escape sequences to move/hide/show the cursor and clear lines. FormatterHelper formats text blocks, Table renders data, and ProgressBar shows progress — none of them is the cursor primitive.

questions.q: Why can't an invokable command call `$this->getHelper('question')`?

a.t: It does not extend Command, so it has no HelperSet accessor — inject services or use SymfonyStyle instead
Helpers only exist for progress bars
Invokable commands run without an Application

questions.exp: getHelper() is a protected method on the Command base class; an invokable command extends nothing, so it has no HelperSet accessor. The idiomatic solution is to type-hint SymfonyStyle in __invoke() (which wraps QuestionHelper) or inject the collaborators you need. getHelper() still exists for classic commands.

questions.q: You need the user to pick several roles at once from a list. How do you configure a ChoiceQuestion?

a.t: Create the ChoiceQuestion and call setMultiselect(true) so it returns an array of selections
Pass an array as the default; multiselect is automatic
Multiselect requires a separate MultiChoiceQuestion class

questions.exp: ChoiceQuestion::setMultiselect(true) lets the user choose comma-separated values and returns them as an array. Without it, only one selection is returned. There is no MultiChoiceQuestion class, and passing an array default does not enable multiselect on its own.

questions.q: How is the HelperSet organised and populated for a classic command?

a.t: The Application populates it with default helpers keyed by name (question, formatter, process, debug_formatter)
Each command builds its own empty HelperSet in configure()
Helpers are keyed by their FQCN, not a short name
The container autowires helpers into command properties

questions.exp: The Application seeds each command's HelperSet with default helpers, addressable by short string keys (question, formatter, process, debug_formatter), which is why getHelper('question') works. They are keyed by name, not FQCN, and are not autowired container services.

questions.q: What is the dispatch order for a successful framework command?
questions.exp: COMMAND fires before execution and TERMINATE always fires last. ERROR fires only when a Throwable is raised, so a successful run dispatches just COMMAND → TERMINATE (no ERROR).

questions.q: Which event lets you change the exit code regardless of outcome?

a.t: It cannot be changed after execution

questions.exp: ConsoleTerminateEvent::setExitCode() runs on every command (success or failure) and is the last chance to alter the process exit code. COMMAND runs before execution, and SIGNAL only fires when a subscribed OS signal arrives.

questions.q: What exit code results from ConsoleCommandEvent::disableCommand()?
questions.exp: Disabling the command in the COMMAND event skips execution and returns ConsoleCommandEvent::RETURN_CODE_DISABLED, which is 113 — neither SUCCESS (0), FAILURE (1), nor 255.

questions.q: Which interface lets a command react to OS signals such as SIGTERM?
questions.exp: Implement SignalableCommandInterface's getSubscribedSignals() and handleSignal(); it requires the pcntl extension. SignalHandlerInterface and TerminableInterface do not exist for this, and EventSubscriberInterface is generic event wiring, not signal handling.

questions.q: A command's execute() throws a RuntimeException. What is the event sequence?

a.t: COMMAND → ERROR → TERMINATE (TERMINATE still runs after ERROR)
COMMAND → TERMINATE only (ERROR is skipped for RuntimeException)
ERROR only; the process aborts before TERMINATE

questions.exp: COMMAND fires before execution; the thrown Throwable triggers ERROR (ConsoleErrorEvent, where a listener can change the exit code or swap the exception); TERMINATE always fires last, even after an error. ERROR never runs before COMMAND, and it does not suppress TERMINATE.

questions.q: What is the correct signature of handleSignal() in Symfony 8's SignalableCommandInterface?
questions.exp: handleSignal receives the signal number and the previous exit code, returning an int to set the exit code or false to let the process continue running. The method is named handleSignal (not onSignal), takes an int signal (not a Signal object), and returns int|false rather than a plain bool/void.

questions.q: When are ConsoleEvents actually dispatched?

a.t: Only when the Application has an EventDispatcher (as in the framework); a bare Console app fires none
Always, even in a standalone Console component with no dispatcher
Only for commands that implement EventSubscriberInterface

questions.exp: ConsoleEvents require an EventDispatcher wired into the Application via setDispatcher(). The full-stack framework does this automatically, but a bare Console app without a dispatcher fires no COMMAND/ERROR/TERMINATE events. It is not environment-scoped, and command interfaces do not gate dispatching.

questions.q: A command returns 300 as its exit code. What does the process actually exit with?

a.t: 44 — exit codes are clamped to 0–255 via % 256 (300 % 256 = 44)
1 — out-of-range codes fall back to FAILURE

questions.exp: POSIX exit codes are a single byte (0–255), so Symfony normalises out-of-range values with % 256; 300 % 256 = 44. It is not passed through, not capped at 255, and not coerced to FAILURE. By convention a signal-terminated process exits with 128 + signalNumber.

questions.q: What does `#[AsEventListener(event: ConsoleEvents::TERMINATE)]` on an `__invoke(ConsoleTerminateEvent $event)` class achieve?

a.t: Registers the class as a listener that runs after every command, able to read/set the exit code
Registers a new console command named terminate
Subscribes the class to HTTP kernel.terminate instead
Runs the listener only when a command fails

questions.exp: #[AsEventListener] autoconfigures the class as an event listener for ConsoleEvents::TERMINATE, so __invoke() runs after every command with a ConsoleTerminateEvent exposing getExitCode()/setExitCode(). It is a console event, distinct from kernel.terminate, runs on success and failure alike, and does not define a command.

questions.q: Which flag maps to VERBOSITY_VERY_VERBOSE?
questions.exp: -v is VERBOSE (64), -vv is VERY_VERBOSE (128), -vvv is DEBUG (256), and -q is QUIET (16). The number of v's maps directly to the level.

questions.q: What is the integer value of VERBOSITY_NORMAL?
questions.exp: The constants are QUIET=16, NORMAL=32, VERBOSE=64, VERY_VERBOSE=128, DEBUG=256. NORMAL is 32, not 0 (0 is not used) — memorising this 16/32/64/128/256 ladder is exam-critical.

questions.q: Where is the current verbosity level stored?

a.t: On the OutputInterface, set by the Application from the flags

questions.exp: The Application parses -v/-vv/-vvv/-q before dispatching and calls $output->setVerbosity(); verbosity is a property of the output, queried via isVerbose()/isDebug(). Reading it from the input is a classic mistake — the input carries the raw flags, but the resolved level lives on the output.

questions.q: A message written with VERBOSITY_VERBOSE is displayed at which levels?
questions.exp: A message prints when the current level is >= the message's level. VERBOSE is 64, so it shows at -v (64), -vv (128) and -vvv (256), but not at normal (32) or quiet (16).

questions.q: Which of these VERBOSITY constant/value pairs are correct? (choose 2)
questions.exp: The ladder is QUIET=16, NORMAL=32, VERBOSE=64, VERY_VERBOSE=128, DEBUG=256, so QUIET=16 and DEBUG=256 are correct. NORMAL is 32 (not 0) and VERBOSE is 64 (not 100). The values are powers of two starting at 16.

questions.q: `$output->writeln('trace', OutputInterface::VERBOSITY_DEBUG);` — when is 'trace' printed?

a.t: Only at -vvv (DEBUG), because the line prints only when the current level >= DEBUG
At every level, since a mask only affects colour
Never, because writeln ignores the second argument

questions.exp: The second argument is a verbosity mask; the line prints only if the output's current level is >= the message level. DEBUG (256) is the highest, so 'trace' appears only under -vvv. writeln does honour the mask, and the mask governs visibility, not colour.

questions.q: What does passing -q (VERBOSITY_QUIET) actually do?

a.t: It silences normal output but the command still runs and returns its exit code
It forces the command into non-interactive mode
It suppresses the exit code so the shell always sees 0

questions.exp: -q sets QUIET (16), which suppresses normal output; the command executes fully and returns its real exit code (scripts can still branch on it). It does not skip execution, does not change interactivity (that is -n), and does not alter the exit code. Assuming -q skips work is a common trap.

questions.q: Which guard should wrap a full payload dump so it only shows at -vvv?
questions.exp: isDebug() is true only at -vvv (DEBUG=256), the right guard for the most verbose diagnostics. isVerbose() is true from -v upward (too broad here), isInteractive() is about prompting not verbosity, and isQuiet() is the opposite end of the scale.

questions.q: Which statements about console arguments and options are correct? (select all that apply)

a.t: Arguments are positional, while options are named and may define a one-letter shortcut
An option defined with InputOption::VALUE_NONE acts as a flag: it accepts no value and has no default
InputOption::VALUE_NEGATABLE makes the option also accept a --no-* variant
Options are positional and must be passed in the order they were defined
An InputArgument::IS_ARRAY argument can be followed by additional arguments in the definition

questions.exp: Arguments are bound by position while options are named (with optional -x shortcuts) and can appear anywhere on the command line, so options are never positional. VALUE_NONE options are pure presence flags with no value or default, and VALUE_NEGATABLE (16) adds the negated --no-* form. An IS_ARRAY argument swallows all remaining input, so it must be the last argument defined.

questions.q: Which statements about console verbosity are true? (select all that apply)

a.t: -q suppresses normal output, but the command still executes fully and returns its real exit code
$output->isDebug() returns true only at the -vvv (DEBUG) level
Verbosity is a property of the input object, read via $input->getVerbosity()
-q also forces the command into non-interactive mode, exactly like -n
-v, -vv and -vvv only change the logger's log level, not what the console prints

questions.exp: Quiet mode silences output only — execution and the exit code are untouched — and isDebug() is the guard that matches exactly the -vvv/DEBUG level. Verbosity is a property of the output (OutputInterface constants 16 to 256), not of the input; non-interactivity is controlled separately by -n; and the verbosity flags directly govern what the console output prints.

questions.q: Which statements about console events and exit codes are correct? (select all that apply)

a.t: The TERMINATE event is dispatched whether the command succeeds or throws
Calling disableCommand() in a COMMAND event listener skips execution and yields exit code 113
A ConsoleErrorEvent listener can replace the throwable or set a custom exit code
The ERROR event is dispatched on every command run, right before TERMINATE
Exit codes returned by commands can be any integer and are passed to the shell unchanged

questions.exp: ConsoleTerminateEvent always runs, after success and after errors alike, and ConsoleErrorEvent listeners may swap the throwable or call setExitCode(). disableCommand() short-circuits execution with ConsoleCommandEvent::RETURN_CODE_DISABLED (113). The ERROR event fires only when a Throwable is thrown, and exit codes are clamped to the 0-255 range before reaching the shell.

questions.q: Which statements about command configuration and the command lifecycle are true? (select all that apply)

a.t: configure() is called from the command's constructor, before any input is available
Putting the command name in the #[AsCommand] attribute keeps command loading lazy
interact() runs after execute() so it can ask follow-up questions about the result
initialize() is only invoked when the command runs in interactive mode

questions.exp: configure() runs in the constructor, which is why it cannot read input, and declaring the name in #[AsCommand] lets the application know the command without instantiating it, enabling lazy loading. The lifecycle order is configure, then initialize, then interact, then execute — interact() runs before execute(), and initialize() runs on every execution regardless of interactivity.

questions.q: Which statements about writing custom commands in Symfony 8 are correct? (select all that apply)

a.t: Invokable commands using __invoke() are the modern default; extending Command still works
Commands should return Command::SUCCESS (0), Command::FAILURE (1) or Command::INVALID (2)
With autoconfiguration, command classes are automatically tagged console.command
Commands must extend ContainerAwareCommand to access services
execute() may return null and the framework converts it to a success exit code

questions.exp: Symfony 8 favors invokable commands built around __invoke() while the classic extends-Command style remains valid, exit statuses use the SUCCESS/FAILURE/INVALID constants (0, 1, 2), and autoconfiguration applies the console.command tag so commands are registered and loaded lazily. ContainerAwareCommand no longer exists — services are injected through the constructor — and execute() must return an int, not null.

questions.q: Which statements about the commands available in bin/console are true? (select all that apply)

a.t: Running bin/console with no command name executes the default list command
The make:* commands come from MakerBundle, not from Symfony core
cache:clear and the debug:* commands are added by FrameworkBundle, not by the standalone Console component
The completion command must be installed through a separate Composer package
help can only display documentation for built-in commands, not custom ones

questions.exp: list is the default command (so a bare bin/console prints the command list), make:* generators ship with MakerBundle rather than core, and cache:clear, cache:warmup and debug:* come from FrameworkBundle on top of the component. completion is one of the commands present in every Console application without extra packages, and help works with any registered command, including custom ones.

questions.q: Which statements about console input and output handling are correct? (select all that apply)

a.t: SymfonyStyle wraps the input and output and provides styled helpers such as title(), table() and ask()
STDERR is reached through ConsoleOutputInterface::getErrorOutput(), keeping pipeable data clean on STDOUT
Output sections allow parts of the output to be updated independently while the command runs
$output->writeln() writes to STDERR by default so it never pollutes piped output
Console sections require re-running the command to refresh their content

questions.exp: SymfonyStyle is constructed from the input and output and is the go-to styled UI layer; error/diagnostic text belongs on the dedicated error output obtained via ConsoleOutputInterface::getErrorOutput(); and output sections can be overwritten live and independently during a single run. writeln() targets the normal STDOUT stream, which is exactly why diagnostics should be sent to the error output instead.

questions.q: How is an invokable single-action controller referenced in the `_controller` attribute? (choose one)

a.t: The fully-qualified class name only (Symfony calls __invoke)

questions.exp: For an invokable controller you reference only the class; the ControllerResolver detects the __invoke() method automatically.

questions.q: Is the `Action` method suffix required for controller actions in Symfony 8?

a.t: No — it is a legacy convention with no meaning under attribute routing
Yes, the router matches methods ending in Action
Yes, but only for invokable controllers

questions.exp: Attribute routing binds a specific method explicitly, so the Action suffix is purely historical and can be dropped.

questions.q: What visibility must a controller action method have to be invoked by the kernel?
questions.exp: The kernel invokes the controller callable externally, so the method must be public.

questions.q: Which statement best defines a Symfony controller?

a.t: Any PHP callable that returns a Response
A method whose name ends in Action

questions.exp: A controller is any callable (method, invokable object, closure) the kernel runs to produce a Response; extending AbstractController is optional.

questions.q: A route is declared as `#[Route('/', name: 'home')]` on the class `App\Controller\HomeController`, which defines a `public function __invoke(): Response`. Which YAML `controller:` value targets it correctly?
questions.exp: For an invokable controller the `_controller` value is the class name alone; the resolver detects `__invoke()`. Adding `::__invoke` also works but is not idiomatic, and `#invoke` / a made-up service id are invalid.

questions.q: Which of these are valid `_controller` formats the ControllerResolver accepts? (choose 3)
questions.exp: The resolver normalises `Class::method`, an invokable `Class`, a `service_id::method`/`service_id`, or a closure into a callable. The `Class#method` syntax is not a recognised format.

questions.q: A controller must extend `AbstractController` to be usable in Symfony 8. True or false?
questions.exp: Extending `AbstractController` is optional convenience. A controller is any callable returning a Response; a plain invokable class with no base class is perfectly valid.

questions.q: How does AbstractController obtain its helper services?

a.t: Via a lazy service locator injected through setContainer(), driven by getSubscribedServices()
Through constructor injection of each service
The full application container is injected

questions.exp: AbstractController implements ServiceSubscriberInterface; the compiler builds a per-controller locator containing only the subscribed services.

questions.q: What does `$this->container` hold inside an AbstractController?

a.t: Only the subscribed services (a restricted service locator)

questions.exp: The injected locator exposes exactly the services returned by getSubscribedServices(), not the whole container.

questions.q: What happens if you call `$this->render()` without Twig installed?

a.t: A clear LogicException telling you Twig is required
A container 'service not found' fatal error
It silently returns an empty Response

questions.exp: The twig service is subscribed with the optional '?' prefix, so the helper guards its absence with a descriptive LogicException.

questions.q: When overriding getSubscribedServices() to add a service, what must you do to keep the built-in helpers?

a.t: Spread parent::getSubscribedServices() into the returned array

questions.exp: Returning only your service replaces the list; merge the parent's subscriptions so render/getUser/etc. still resolve.

questions.q: You extend AbstractController and override getSubscribedServices() to add a `ReportGenerator`. Which body keeps `render()`, `getUser()`, etc. working?
questions.exp: The subscription list fully replaces the inherited one, so you must spread `parent::getSubscribedServices()` alongside your own entry. Returning only your service drops router/twig/security and breaks every helper.

questions.q: In getSubscribedServices(), what does prefixing a service with `?` (e.g. `'?'.Environment::class`) mean?

a.t: The service is optional; if absent the locator returns null instead of failing to compile
The service is lazily proxied but always required
The service is private and cannot be fetched
It marks the service as deprecated

questions.exp: The `?` marks the subscription optional, letting the controller boot even when (say) Twig or the form factory is not installed; the helper then throws a clear LogicException rather than a container error.

questions.q: A developer fetches an application service with `$this->container->get(InvoiceMailer::class)` inside a controller and gets a 'service not found' error. What is the correct fix?

a.t: Inject InvoiceMailer via the constructor — $this->container only holds subscribed helper services
Register InvoiceMailer as public in services.yaml
Add InvoiceMailer to the kernel's global container

questions.exp: `$this->container` is the restricted subscriber locator; it only exposes the framework helper services, not your domain services. Inject your own dependencies through the constructor instead of using the locator as a service-locator anti-pattern.

questions.q: Which AbstractController helpers directly return a Response (or subclass)? (choose 3)
questions.exp: render/json/redirectToRoute (and file/stream/forward) return a Response or subclass. createNotFoundException() returns a NotFoundHttpException you must throw — it is not a Response and does not abort on its own.

questions.q: On a public (no-firewall) route, `return new Response($this->getUser()->getEmail());` fatals with 'Call to a member function getEmail() on null'. Why?

a.t: getUser() returns ?UserInterface and is null when no one is authenticated
getUser() always throws on public routes
The token storage service is not subscribed
Response cannot accept a string built from getUser()

questions.exp: getUser() reads security.token_storage; with no authenticated token it returns null. Guard with denyAccessUnlessGranted()/#[IsGranted] first, or read defensively with `$this->getUser()?->getEmail()`.

questions.q: Which value resolver supplies a `Request` type-hinted controller argument?
questions.exp: RequestValueResolver (priority 120) injects the current Request; RequestAttributeValueResolver handles named route parameters.

questions.q: In which parameter bag do matched route parameters appear?
questions.exp: The router writes matched parameters into the attributes bag; query is GET data and request is the POST body.

questions.q: How should a service (not a controller) access the current Request?
questions.exp: The Request is request-scoped and cannot be injected directly; inject the RequestStack service instead.

questions.q: For the URL `/search` (no `?page=`), what does `(int) $request->query->get('page')` evaluate to, and what is the safer call?

a.t: 0, because get() returns null which casts to 0; use getInt('page', 1) instead
null, and the cast is skipped

questions.exp: InputBag::get() returns null for a missing key (default default is null), and (int) null is 0 — rarely the intended fallback. getInt('page', 1) coerces and guarantees the type with an explicit default.

questions.q: What does the `$request->request` bag actually contain?
questions.exp: Despite the name, `$request->request` is the InputBag of POST body fields, not 'the request object'. Query lives in `$request->query`, route params in `$request->attributes`.

questions.q: `$request->getContent()` is called on a JSON API request. What does it return?

a.t: The raw request body as a string — it is not JSON-decoded
An associative array decoded from the JSON body
A stdClass of the JSON payload

questions.exp: getContent() returns the raw body; it does not decode JSON. Use #[MapRequestPayload] (serializer + validator) or json_decode() yourself to get a structured value.

questions.q: The `Request` object can be autowired directly into a service constructor. True or false?
questions.exp: The Request is request-scoped and created per HTTP call, so it is not an autowireable service. Inject RequestStack and call getCurrentRequest().

questions.q: What must a controller ultimately produce?

a.t: A Response object (or a value converted to one by a kernel.view listener)
An array that Symfony auto-serializes to JSON
A string that becomes the body

questions.exp: If a controller returns a non-Response, the kernel fires ViewEvent; if no listener produces a Response a LogicException is thrown.

questions.q: When does a StreamedResponse produce its body?

a.t: During send(), by invoking its callback

questions.exp: The callback runs at send time and streams output; you cannot change headers once streaming has begun.

questions.q: Which response class best serves a resumable (range-request) file download?
questions.exp: BinaryFileResponse supports HTTP range requests and X-Sendfile/X-Accel offloading for efficient downloads.

questions.q: An action does `return ['id' => 1, 'name' => 'Ada'];` expecting Symfony to auto-serialize it to JSON, but the request fails. Why?

a.t: Symfony does not auto-serialize arrays by default; with no kernel.view listener the kernel throws a LogicException
Arrays are silently rendered as a 200 with an empty body
The array is cast to a string body
It returns a 500 with the array var_dump()ed

questions.exp: A non-Response return fires ViewEvent; without a listener that builds a Response, the kernel throws 'The controller must return a Response'. Return $this->json($data) explicitly.

questions.q: Inside a StreamedResponse callback, code echoes rows and then calls `$response->headers->set('Content-Type', 'text/csv')`. What is wrong?

a.t: Headers cannot be changed after output has started; set Content-Type before returning the response
The callback must return the header array
You must use JsonResponse for CSV

questions.exp: The callback runs at send time; once bytes are flushed the headers are already sent, so header changes are ineffective. Set headers on the StreamedResponse before returning it from the action.

questions.q: You already hold a valid JSON string. Which avoids double-encoding it in a JsonResponse?
questions.exp: new JsonResponse($json) / $this->json($json) would JSON-encode the string again (double-encoding). fromJsonString() sets the body verbatim and the application/json Content-Type.

questions.q: Where does a controller read incoming cookies from?
questions.exp: The cookies ParameterBag wraps $_COOKIE; responses set cookies via $response->headers->setCookie().

questions.q: A cookie sent with SameSite=None also requires which attribute?
questions.exp: Modern browsers reject SameSite=None cookies unless they are marked Secure (HTTPS-only).

questions.q: Why might clearCookie('token') fail to delete the cookie?

a.t: The path/domain do not match those used when the cookie was set
Cookies cannot be removed from the server side

questions.exp: Deletion sends an expired Set-Cookie scoped by path/domain; a mismatch targets a different cookie and leaves the original intact.

questions.q: `Cookie::create('t','v')->withSameSite(Cookie::SAMESITE_NONE)` is set without calling `withSecure(true)`. What is the effect in modern browsers?

a.t: Browsers reject the cookie because SameSite=None requires Secure
The cookie is accepted but treated as SameSite=Lax
The cookie is silently upgraded to Secure

questions.exp: SameSite=None mandates the Secure attribute; without it the browser drops the cookie. Chain ->withSecure(true) so it is sent only over HTTPS.

questions.q: In Symfony's Cookie value object, `httpOnly` defaults to true. True or false?
questions.exp: Cookie defaults are security-first: httpOnly=true (hidden from JS, mitigating XSS token theft) and sameSite='lax'. JS-readable cookies must opt out explicitly with withHttpOnly(false).

questions.q: An action sets a `theme` cookie on the response, then in the same action reads `$request->cookies->get('theme')` and gets the old value. Why?

a.t: A cookie set on the response is only sent to the browser and readable on subsequent requests
setCookie also updates the request bag synchronously
clearCookie must be called before re-reading

questions.exp: Response cookies go out as Set-Cookie headers; the request's cookies bag reflects what the browser already sent. A newly set cookie is only visible on the next request.

questions.q: What is the recommended way for a service to access the session?
questions.exp: The session is request-scoped; RequestStack::getSession() is the stable entry point in services.

questions.q: When does a lazy Symfony session actually start (session_start + Set-Cookie)?

a.t: Only when the session is first read or written

questions.exp: Lazy sessions avoid emitting a session cookie for requests that never touch the session, preserving cacheability.

questions.q: Which method regenerates the session id after login to prevent session fixation?
questions.exp: migrate() issues a new session id while keeping data; invalidate() also wipes data. Symfony authenticators call migrate() on login.

questions.q: What is a caching side effect of touching the session on a public page?

a.t: A Set-Cookie header makes the response uncacheable by shared proxies
Nothing; sessions never affect HTTP caching

questions.exp: Shared caches must not store responses carrying a per-user Set-Cookie, so touching the session prevents shared caching.

questions.q: A console command injects RequestStack and calls `getSession()`, which throws SessionNotFoundException. What is the cause and fix?

a.t: There is no current request in the CLI; guard with getCurrentRequest() and hasSession() before reading
getSession() returns null in CLI; check for null instead
Sessions require enabling framework.session in the console
You must call session_start() manually first

questions.exp: getSession() throws SessionNotFoundException (it does not return null) when called outside a request or on a request with no session. Guard the request first: check getCurrentRequest() and hasSession().

questions.q: Why is injecting `SessionInterface` directly into a service constructor discouraged in Symfony 8?

a.t: The session is request-scoped; inject RequestStack and call getSession() so it resolves per request
SessionInterface is deprecated in favour of $_SESSION
It forces the session to start eagerly on boot, which is fine

questions.exp: Directly autowiring the request-scoped session into a long-lived service is discouraged/removed; RequestStack::getSession() is the stable entry point. You can still type-hint SessionInterface on a controller action (resolved by SessionValueResolver, priority 120).

questions.q: Merely type-hinting SessionInterface on an action starts the session. True or false?
questions.exp: Sessions are lazy: SessionValueResolver injects the session object, but session_start() and the Set-Cookie header only fire on the first read or write. Merely receiving the session does not start it.

questions.q: What happens the first time you read a flash message (get/all or app.flashes)?

a.t: It stays until the session expires
It is copied to the next request

questions.exp: Reading consumes flashes; use peek()/peekAll() to read without removing them.

questions.q: `$this->addFlash('notice', 'Saved')` is shorthand for which call?
questions.exp: addFlash() is an AbstractController convenience over the session flash bag.

questions.q: Why are flash messages typically paired with a redirect?

a.t: They display on the next (GET) request, matching the Post/Redirect/Get pattern
Redirects are required to write to the session
Flashes cannot be added during a GET request

questions.exp: Flashes are built to survive exactly one redirect and be shown on the following request, then discarded.

questions.q: A controller reads `app.session.flashbag.get('success')` for logging, then the Twig template shows no flash. What happened?

a.t: get() consumed (drained) the messages, so nothing remains for Twig; use peek() to read without consuming
Flashes only render on POST requests
The template must call addFlash() again
The session expired between the two reads

questions.exp: get()/all() consume the flash bag. Reading in the controller drains the messages before Twig can show them. Use peek()/peekAll() when you must read without removing.

questions.q: Which method reads flash messages WITHOUT consuming them?
questions.exp: peek()/peekAll() return messages while leaving them in the bag. get()/all() both return and remove. There are no read()/keep() methods on FlashBag.

questions.q: Which Twig loop renders all flash types, consuming them once?

a.t: {% for label, messages in app.flashes %}{% for m in messages %}{{ m }}{% endfor %}{% endfor %}
{% for m in app.session.flash %}{{ m }}{% endfor %}
{% for m in flashbag() %}{{ m }}{% endfor %}

questions.exp: app.flashes yields a map of type => messages; iterating it calls all() under the hood, which consumes the bag so each message shows exactly once.

questions.q: What is the default HTTP status code of redirectToRoute()?
questions.exp: RedirectResponse defaults to 302 Found; pass a status argument to change it.

questions.q: Which redirect status codes preserve the original HTTP method and body?
questions.exp: 307/308 must not change the request method; 303 always forces GET and 301/302 may downgrade to GET.

questions.q: What is the difference between redirect() and redirectToRoute()?

a.t: redirect() takes a URL; redirectToRoute() takes a route name and parameters

questions.exp: redirect() is URL-based; redirectToRoute() builds the URL from the router. Both return a RedirectResponse (default 302).

questions.q: After creating a resource in a POST action, you want the browser to issue a GET to the show page. Which call is correct?
questions.exp: 303 See Other forces the follow-up request to GET, the strict form of Post/Redirect/Get. 307 would preserve POST; forward() is internal (no URL change); redirect() takes a URL, not a route name + params.

questions.q: A checkout POST persists an order and redirects to the confirmation page to avoid duplicate submissions on refresh. Which status best fits?

a.t: 302 (or the stricter 303) — a temporary, non-cached redirect for PRG

questions.exp: PRG needs a temporary redirect that ends on a GET. 302 (default) or 303 are correct; 301/308 are cached (wrong and hard to undo), and 307 would replay the POST.

questions.q: Why is accidentally using 301 (or 308) for a temporary redirect dangerous?

a.t: 301/308 are cached by browsers, so the redirect sticks and is hard to undo
301/308 always force a GET, losing the body

questions.exp: 301 and 308 signal a permanent move and are cached by browsers; if used by mistake the client keeps redirecting even after you fix the server. Use 302/303 for temporary redirects.

questions.q: `redirect()` accepts a route name as its first argument. True or false?
questions.exp: redirect() takes a URL (string). To redirect by route name (plus params), use redirectToRoute(), which builds the URL via the router.

questions.q: What does AbstractController::forward() do?

a.t: Runs another controller in a sub-request and returns its Response, without a new client request
Sends a 302 redirect to another route

questions.exp: forward() dispatches a sub-request through the kernel; the browser URL does not change and no 3xx is sent.

questions.q: During a forwarded sub-request, what does Request::isMainRequest() return?
questions.exp: The sub-request is dispatched with HttpKernelInterface::SUB_REQUEST, so isMainRequest() is false and some listeners (e.g. the firewall) skip.

questions.q: After a forward(), what does the user's address bar show?
questions.exp: Forwarding is server-internal within the same request, so no new client navigation occurs.

questions.q: How does `forward()` pass a `month` value so the target action can receive it as an `int $month` argument?
questions.exp: The second argument to forward() becomes the sub-request's attributes (the $path array), which the argument resolver then maps to the target's named parameters — not through query.

questions.q: Two controllers need the same 'latest news' logic. Which reuse approach is usually preferable to forwarding?

a.t: Extract the logic into a shared service and inject it into both controllers
forward() from one controller to the other
Duplicate the code in both controllers

questions.exp: Forwarding runs a full kernel pass and couples controllers. A shared service reuses just the logic without routing/events/resolver overhead. Forward when you need another controller's whole Response embedded.

questions.q: Which constant does forward() pass to HttpKernel::handle(), and what is a consequence for the security firewall?

a.t: HttpKernelInterface::SUB_REQUEST — the firewall does not re-authenticate (isMainRequest() is false)
HttpKernelInterface::MAIN_REQUEST — a fresh security context is built

questions.exp: Sub-requests are dispatched with SUB_REQUEST (the old MASTER_REQUEST constant was removed; MAIN_REQUEST is used for the main request). Because isMainRequest() is false, listeners like the firewall skip re-authentication.

questions.q: How do you correctly produce a 404 from a controller?
questions.exp: createNotFoundException() returns a NotFoundHttpException you must throw; the kernel then renders the error page.

questions.q: A controller throws a plain \RuntimeException. What status code results?
questions.exp: Only exceptions implementing HttpExceptionInterface set a specific status; any other exception becomes a 500.

questions.q: Where do you place a custom production 404 template?
questions.exp: The Twig error renderer looks up per-status templates in that path in the prod environment.

questions.q: Which kernel event lets a listener turn an exception into a Response?
questions.exp: ExceptionEvent listeners can call setResponse(); otherwise the error controller renders the page.

questions.q: `$this->createNotFoundException('Missing');` is written on its own line, then the action continues and fatals with 'member function on null'. Why?

a.t: createNotFoundException() only builds and returns the exception; without throw the action keeps running with the null entity
createNotFoundException() logs the error but never stops execution by design of the 404 flow
The exception is thrown but caught silently by the kernel
You must return the exception, not throw it

questions.exp: The helper is a factory: it returns a NotFoundHttpException and does not abort. You must `throw` it. Written alone, the exception is created, discarded, and execution continues on the null value.

questions.q: Which one-liner raises a 404 when a repository lookup returns null?
questions.exp: The throw expression (PHP 8) combines with `??` so a null lookup throws the 404. Without `throw` the exception is merely assigned/discarded; `?:` and `abort()` are wrong (abort() is not a Symfony helper).

questions.q: createNotFoundException() aborts the action as soon as it is called. True or false?
questions.exp: It only returns a NotFoundHttpException object; nothing happens until you `throw` it. Treating it as self-aborting is the classic trap.

questions.q: An API must return problem+json error bodies for every HttpException. What is the cleanest app-wide approach?

a.t: A kernel.exception listener (or a custom framework.error_controller) that maps exceptions to a JSON Response
Wrap every action body in try/catch and build JSON manually
Return new Response('', 404) from each action

questions.exp: A single kernel.exception listener calling setResponse(), or a custom error_controller, centralises error rendering with content negotiation — far cleaner than per-action try/catch or per-status Twig templates.

questions.q: Which value should you trust to determine an uploaded file's real type?
questions.exp: Client-supplied name/MIME are spoofable; getMimeType()/guessExtension() inspect the actual file content.

questions.q: What does UploadedFile::move() do when it fails?

a.t: Returns null and logs a warning

questions.exp: move() throws FileException on failure rather than returning a status value.

questions.q: With #[MapUploadedFile] and a failing File constraint, what happens?

a.t: An HTTP exception is thrown before the action body runs
The argument is set to null

questions.exp: The resolver validates the upload and aborts with an HTTP error when a constraint fails, so the body never executes with invalid input.

questions.q: A user uploads a file larger than `post_max_size` and the action crashes on a null `$request->files->get('avatar')`. What is the underlying cause?

a.t: Exceeding post_max_size can yield an empty files bag (no exception), so the get() returns null — always null-check
move() threw a FileException that was swallowed
getMimeType() returns null for large files
Symfony automatically rejects the request with a 413

questions.exp: When post_max_size is exceeded, PHP may discard the POST data, leaving an empty files bag rather than raising an exception. Guard the result with an instanceof UploadedFile / isValid() check before using it.

questions.q: Which signature binds and validates a PDF upload straight into a controller argument?
questions.exp: #[MapUploadedFile] (handled by RequestPayloadValueResolver) binds the UploadedFile and applies inline File/Image constraints, throwing an HTTP exception on failure. The other attributes target payloads/query/user.

questions.q: Why must uploaded files be stored outside the web root (or with execution disabled)?

a.t: An uploaded .php in a served directory can be executed — remote code execution
The web root has a strict file-count limit
Symfony refuses to move files into public/
Files in the web root are automatically deleted on cache clear

questions.exp: A script (e.g. .php) saved into a publicly served directory could be requested and executed, yielding RCE. Store uploads outside public/ or disable script execution there, and always use a safe generated name.

questions.q: Which built-in controller renders a Twig template purely from route config?
questions.exp: TemplateController::__invoke() renders the 'template' default and can set HTTP cache headers, needing no custom class.

questions.q: RedirectController configured with permanent: true returns which status?
questions.exp: permanent selects the permanent status code; combined with keepRequestMethod it becomes 308 to preserve the method.

questions.q: What status does RedirectController return when the target route/path is empty?
questions.exp: An empty target signals the resource is permanently gone, so the controller responds 410.

questions.q: Which route config serves `/terms` from a template with a one-day shared cache and no PHP class?

a.t: controller: TemplateController with defaults { template: 'static/terms.html.twig', sharedAge: 86400 }
controller: TemplateController with defaults { path: '/terms', ttl: 86400 }

questions.exp: TemplateController accepts template plus optional maxAge/sharedAge/private to set HTTP cache headers. sharedAge sets the shared-cache TTL (s-maxage). RedirectController/CacheController are wrong for rendering.

questions.q: A route sets `controller: ...\\RedirectController` (class only) and the request errors. What is missing?

a.t: RedirectController is not invokable; reference ::redirectAction (route) or ::urlRedirectAction (URL)
It needs a permanent: true default to work
RedirectController must be registered manually as a service
You must add an __invoke default to the route

questions.exp: Unlike TemplateController, RedirectController has no __invoke; you must pick the matching action — redirectAction for a route target, urlRedirectAction for a path/URL target.

questions.q: A RedirectController route sets `permanent: true` and `keepRequestMethod: true`. What status does it return?
questions.exp: permanent alone gives 301; adding keepRequestMethod upgrades it to 308 so the HTTP method (e.g. POST) is preserved across the permanent redirect.

questions.q: Which interface does a custom value resolver implement in Symfony 8?
questions.exp: The split supports()/resolve() interface was removed; resolve() now returns an iterable and yielding nothing declines the argument.

questions.q: How does a value resolver signal that it does not handle an argument?

a.t: It yields nothing (returns an empty iterable)

questions.exp: Yielding no value passes the argument to the next resolver in priority order.

questions.q: Which resolvers have the highest default priority (120) in Symfony 8?
questions.exp: Request and Session resolvers run first at priority 120; the attribute, enum, uid and datetime resolvers sit at 100.

questions.q: A #[MapRequestPayload] argument fails validation. Which status is thrown?

a.t: 422 Unprocessable Entity (400 if the body itself is malformed)

questions.exp: RequestPayloadValueResolver deserializes then validates; validation errors throw UnprocessableEntityHttpException (422).

questions.q: How do the #[MapRequestPayload]/#[MapQueryParameter] resolvers get activated?

a.t: They are targeted resolvers that run only when their attribute is present on the argument
They always run first in the priority chain
They require manual registration in services.yaml

questions.exp: These resolvers carry the controller.targeted_value_resolver tag and are invoked only for arguments bearing the matching attribute.

questions.q: What binds a single typed query parameter such as ?page=2 to an int argument?
questions.exp: #[MapQueryParameter] binds one query value with casting; #[MapQueryString] maps the whole query string into a DTO.

questions.q: In a custom resolver, an argument's type does not match. What should `resolve()` do to decline it correctly?

a.t: return []; (yield nothing) so the next resolver handles it
return null; to indicate no value
return false; to skip the argument

questions.exp: resolve() is typed `: iterable`, so `return null` is a TypeError and `return false` is invalid. Decline by returning an empty array (or a generator that never yields).

questions.q: In a resolver, what is the difference between yielding nothing and `yield null`?

a.t: Yielding nothing declines (next resolver runs); yield null binds a real null value to a nullable parameter
They are identical — both bind null
yield null declines; yielding nothing binds null
Both throw because null is not iterable

questions.exp: 'Yields nothing' means 'not my argument' and passes control on; 'yield null' is a deliberate null bound to the parameter. Confusing them is the classic resolver bug.

questions.q: Which tag registers a resolver in the ordered chain, and how is its order controlled?

a.t: controller.argument_value_resolver with an optional priority (higher runs first); autoconfigure adds it automatically

questions.exp: Chain resolvers are tagged controller.argument_value_resolver; a higher priority runs earlier. Autoconfiguration tags implementing classes; set an explicit priority only when ordering matters (targeted resolvers use the controller.targeted_value_resolver tag instead).

questions.q: Which resolvers/attributes are targeted (activated only by their attribute), not part of the priority chain? (choose 3)
questions.exp: MapRequestPayload/MapQueryString, MapQueryParameter, MapUploadedFile (and #[CurrentUser]) are targeted resolvers, run only when the attribute is present. RequestValueResolver is a priority-120 chain resolver, not targeted.

questions.q: An action needs the authenticated user injected as an argument (not via $this->getUser()). Which attribute does this?
questions.exp: #[CurrentUser] injects the authenticated user via the security UserValueResolver. MapRequestPayload builds a DTO from the body, MapEntity is Doctrine (out of scope), and Autowire is for services.

questions.q: A resolver copied from an old project implements `ArgumentValueResolverInterface` with supports()+resolve() and no longer works in Symfony 8. Why?

a.t: ArgumentValueResolverInterface was removed; implement ValueResolverInterface with a single resolve(): iterable
supports() must now return an iterable
The resolver just needs a higher priority

questions.exp: The split supports()/resolve() interface no longer exists in Symfony 8. Use ValueResolverInterface::resolve(Request, ArgumentMetadata): iterable and decline by yielding nothing instead of a supports() check.

questions.q: Is #[MapEntity] a core HttpKernel value resolver you should study for this syllabus area?

a.t: No — #[MapEntity] is a DoctrineBundle feature, not a core HttpKernel resolver
Yes — it is one of the built-in HttpKernel resolvers at priority 100
Yes — it is a targeted core resolver like MapRequestPayload
No — because it was removed in Symfony 8

questions.exp: #[MapEntity] belongs to DoctrineBundle and is out of scope for the core HttpKernel resolver chain. The core built-ins are Request/Session (120), BackedEnum/Uid/DateTime/RequestAttribute (100), plus the targeted mapping attributes and #[CurrentUser].

questions.q: Which statements about HTTP redirects in Symfony controllers are true? (select all that apply)

a.t: redirectToRoute() returns a RedirectResponse with a 302 status by default
307 and 308 redirects preserve the original HTTP method and request body
301 and 308 are permanent redirects that browsers may cache
redirect() performs an internal sub-request, so the browser never makes a second request
Flash messages are lost across a redirect because a new request is made

questions.exp: redirectToRoute() and redirect() both return a RedirectResponse defaulting to 302; 307/308 keep the method and body intact, and the permanent codes 301 and 308 may be cached by browsers. A redirect is a real 3xx response triggering a brand-new client request (internal sub-requests are what forward() does), and flash messages are session-backed precisely so they survive that redirect in the Post/Redirect/Get pattern.

questions.q: Which statements about forward() (internal redirects) are correct? (select all that apply)

a.t: forward() creates a sub-request handled inside the same HTTP request, and the browser URL does not change
Inside the forwarded controller, $request->isMainRequest() returns false
forward() sends a 307 response so the client replays the request to the other controller
The forwarded sub-request passes through the security firewall again

questions.exp: forward() duplicates the request and runs another controller as a SUB_REQUEST within the same HTTP request, returning its Response directly — the client sees no new round-trip and the URL stays the same, which is also why isMainRequest() is false inside the target controller. No 3xx response is involved (that is an external redirect), and the firewall does not run again for the sub-request.

questions.q: Which statements about sessions in Symfony are true? (select all that apply)

a.t: Sessions are lazy: they are started and the cookie is sent only when the session is first used
migrate() regenerates the session id while keeping the data, which defends against session fixation
Flash messages are stored outside the session so they survive session invalidation
You must call $session->start() manually in every controller before reading attributes
In a service, the recommended way to get the session is injecting the 'session' service directly

questions.exp: Symfony sessions start lazily on first use, so no cookie is sent for visitors that never touch the session, and migrate() issues a new id while preserving data (invalidate() additionally wipes the data). The flash bag lives inside the session itself, explicit start() calls are unnecessary because access triggers the start, and services should inject RequestStack and call getSession() rather than a 'session' service.

questions.q: Which statements about AbstractController are correct? (select all that apply)

a.t: Extending AbstractController is optional — any callable can serve as a controller
Its helpers get their services from a lazy service locator whose entries are listed in getSubscribedServices()
Its helper methods like render() and redirectToRoute() are protected, usable only from within the controller
It injects the full service container, so $this->container->get() can fetch any service in the app
Extending it is required for constructor autowiring to work in a controller

questions.exp: AbstractController is optional convenience built on the service subscriber pattern: a lazy locator, scoped to the services declared in getSubscribedServices(), backs its protected helper methods. The container it holds is that limited locator, not the full application container, and autowiring works for any controller registered as a service — your own dependencies should be constructor-injected regardless of the base class.

questions.q: Which statements about argument value resolvers are correct? (select all that apply)

a.t: ValueResolverInterface::resolve() returns an iterable, and a resolver declines an argument by yielding nothing
Attribute resolvers like #[MapRequestPayload] and #[CurrentUser] are targeted: they act only when their attribute is present
All resolvers in the chain run for every argument and their yielded values are merged
A custom resolver must implement a supports() method that is called before resolve()

questions.exp: The ArgumentResolver walks the ordered resolver chain and the first resolver that yields a value wins — resolvers opt out by yielding nothing, which replaces the old supports() mechanism removed with ArgumentValueResolverInterface. The targeted resolvers (MapRequestPayload, MapQueryParameter, MapUploadedFile, CurrentUser) activate only when their attribute decorates the argument; results are never merged across resolvers.

questions.q: Which statements about controller responses are true? (select all that apply)

a.t: An action must return a Response; any other return value needs a kernel.view listener to convert it
A StreamedResponse generates its content at send time, making it suitable for large outputs
Response::HTTP_* constants (e.g. Response::HTTP_NOT_FOUND) are the idiomatic way to set status codes
Returning an array from an action is automatically serialized to JSON by the framework core
You can still modify the response headers after streaming of a StreamedResponse has begun

questions.exp: Controllers must produce a Response object — a non-Response return value triggers kernel.view, and without a listener handling it an error occurs, so arrays are not auto-serialized by core. StreamedResponse executes its callback when the response is sent, which is why headers cannot be changed once streaming starts, and Response::HTTP_* constants keep status codes readable and typo-free.

questions.q: Why are Symfony services private by default?

a.t: So the compiler can inline/remove them and to enforce proper dependency injection
Because public services are deprecated in Symfony 8
To make them read-only value objects
So that get() runs faster at runtime

questions.exp: Private services can be inlined into their single consumer and pruned when unreferenced, shrinking the compiled container, and it discourages the service-locator anti-pattern of pulling from the container.

questions.q: Calling $container->get() on a private service id results in what?
questions.exp: Private services are not fetchable by id from the public container; they may only be injected. Fetching one throws ServiceNotFoundException.

questions.q: What is written to var/cache/prod/ after compilation?

a.t: A dumped, optimised PHP container class produced by PhpDumper

questions.exp: PhpDumper writes a compiled PHP class with a method per service; the runtime uses it directly, never the ContainerBuilder.

questions.q: Which objects exist only at build time, not at runtime? (choose one)

a.t: Definition, Reference, Alias and Parameter metadata objects

questions.exp: Definition/Reference/Alias/Parameter are build-time recipes held by the ContainerBuilder; the runtime container holds instances.

questions.q: True or False: a service being public and a service being shared mean the same thing.
questions.exp: They are independent flags. Public means fetchable by id via get(); shared means the same instance is reused across get() calls. The default service is private and shared. A common trap confuses the two — a service can be public and non-shared, or private and shared, in any combination.

questions.q: A service is defined with shared: false. What happens on repeated $container->get() calls for it?

a.t: A brand-new instance is returned on every call
The same cached instance is returned each time
A ServiceNotFoundException after the first call
It is inlined and can no longer be fetched

questions.exp: shared defaults to true, so the first get() builds and caches the instance and later calls return the same object. shared: false disables caching, so the container rebuilds the service on every request. This is orthogonal to public/private — the misconception is thinking non-shared implies private.

questions.q: A developer calls $this->container->get(MailerInterface::class) inside a service and gets a ServiceNotFoundException, even though the mailer works elsewhere. Why?

a.t: MailerInterface resolves to a private service, which is not fetchable by id — inject it via the constructor instead
MailerInterface is not registered anywhere in the container
The container has not been compiled yet
get() only accepts string literals, not ::class constants

questions.exp: The mailer service is private (the default), so it can only be injected, not fetched by id from the public container — get() therefore throws. The fix is constructor injection/autowiring, not making it public. It is registered and the container is compiled; the misconception is treating get() as a general-purpose lookup instead of using DI.

questions.q: Which sequence correctly describes container compilation?

a.t: ContainerBuilder::compile() runs the PassConfig passes, freezes parameters, then PhpDumper writes the cached class
PhpDumper runs first, then the compiler passes, then parameters freeze
Parameters freeze before any pass runs, then the class is dumped, then passes run
Passes run lazily at runtime on the first get() call

questions.exp: compile() executes the passes in PassConfig phase order, then freezes the parameter bag (making it a FrozenParameterBag), then PhpDumper writes the optimised class to var/cache. It all happens at build time; nothing about compilation is deferred to runtime, which is the key misconception.

questions.q: How should you access the current request inside a service?
questions.exp: The Request is per-cycle and can change across sub-requests, so it is not injectable directly. Inject RequestStack and read the current request.

questions.q: Which command lists what a given type-hint autowires to?
questions.exp: debug:autowiring shows the types you can type-hint and which service each resolves to; debug:container inspects a definition by id.

questions.q: By default, debug:container hides which services?
questions.exp: debug:container lists public services and aliases; add --show-private to include private ones.

questions.q: A service injects RequestStack and calls $this->requestStack->getCurrentRequest()->getLocale(); it fatals when run from a console command. Why?

a.t: getCurrentRequest() returns null when there is no active request (e.g. CLI), so use the nullsafe operator ?->
RequestStack is not autowirable in commands
getLocale() does not exist on the Request object
The request stack is cleared after the controller runs

questions.exp: Outside the HTTP cycle (console commands, Messenger workers) there is no current request, so getCurrentRequest() returns null and the method call fatals. Guard with getCurrentRequest()?->getLocale() or an early null check. RequestStack is autowirable everywhere; the trap is assuming a request always exists.

questions.q: For the router, which statement about id, class and autowiring alias is correct?

a.t: The id is 'router', the class is a concrete Router, and an Alias maps RouterInterface to the id
The id, class and alias are all the string 'router'
The autowiring alias is the class FQCN pointing at the interface
There is no alias; autowiring matches the id string directly

questions.exp: These are three distinct keys. FrameworkExtension registers the service under the id 'router' with a concrete class, then adds an autowiring alias from the interface FQCN (RouterInterface) to that id so type-hints resolve. debug:autowiring lists those aliases; debug:container inspects the id.

questions.q: Which are correct ways to obtain framework services in your code? (choose 2)

a.t: Autowire by type-hinting the interface, e.g. LoggerInterface
Use debug:autowiring to discover which type resolves to which service
Type-hint a concrete Request to receive the current request

questions.exp: Autowiring by interface is the idiomatic path, and debug:autowiring is the discovery tool for finding the right type-hint. A raw Request cannot be injected (use RequestStack), and pulling services with $container->get() in business code is the service-locator anti-pattern.

questions.q: When is %env(DATABASE_URL)% resolved?

a.t: At runtime, via an env-var processor
At compilation, frozen into the cache
When .env is parsed at deploy time only
Never; it is a literal string

questions.exp: Env placeholders resolve at runtime so a single compiled container works across environments; parameters (%x%) are frozen at compile time.

questions.q: What does the expression %env(int:MAX)% produce?

a.t: The value of MAX cast to an integer
The raw string value of MAX

questions.exp: The int: processor casts the raw env string to an integer. Processors chain right-to-left.

questions.q: Which attribute injects the container parameter app.name into a constructor argument?
questions.exp: param: names a container parameter; a bare string without %% is a literal, and env: reads an environment variable.

questions.q: How do you write a literal percent sign inside a parameter value?
questions.exp: A doubled percent escapes to a single literal % so it is not treated as a parameter reference.

questions.q: What does %env(int:default:app.timeout:TIMEOUT)% do?

a.t: Reads TIMEOUT, falls back to the app.timeout parameter when unset, then casts the result to int
Casts app.timeout to int and ignores TIMEOUT entirely
Casts TIMEOUT to int, then defaults to app.timeout only if the cast fails

questions.exp: Env processors chain right-to-left. The innermost segment reads the env var TIMEOUT; default:app.timeout supplies the app.timeout parameter as a fallback when TIMEOUT is unset; int: then casts the resolved value. The misconception is reading it left-to-right, which inverts the meaning.

questions.q: A constructor arg is #[Autowire('%env(MAX)%')] int $max, but you hit a type error because a string was passed. What is wrong?

a.t: %env(MAX)% yields a string; add a cast processor: %env(int:MAX)%
Environment variables cannot be injected into constructors
MAX must be declared as a parameter before it can be read

questions.exp: Raw env values are always strings until a processor casts them, so %env(MAX)% is a string while the argument expects int. Use %env(int:MAX)%. #[Autowire] fully supports env placeholders and no prior parameter declaration is needed; the trap is assuming env values are already typed.

questions.q: After ContainerBuilder::compile(), what happens to the parameter bag?

a.t: It stays mutable so parameters can change at runtime
It is discarded and every parameter is inlined only
It is serialized into the .env file

questions.exp: During build the ContainerBuilder uses a mutable ParameterBag; compile() freezes it into a FrozenParameterBag, after which parameters are read-only. This is why parameters are compile-time constants — the misconception is expecting to mutate parameters at runtime.

questions.q: What does ParameterBagInterface::get('app.missing') do for an undefined parameter?

a.t: Throws ParameterNotFoundException — use has() first for optional lookups

questions.exp: Reading a missing parameter throws ParameterNotFoundException; it never returns null. Guard optional lookups with has() before get(). The common bug is assuming an absent parameter silently becomes null.

questions.q: True or False: environment variables referenced with %env(...)% are frozen into the compiled container cache at compile time.
questions.exp: The compiler replaces %env(...)% with a placeholder and the EnvVarProcessor resolves it at runtime, which is exactly why one compiled container works across environments and changing an env var needs no cache rebuild. Only plain parameters (%x%) are frozen at compile time.

questions.q: Using the App\: resource glob, what is a service's id?
questions.exp: PSR-4 auto-registration creates one definition per class using the FQCN as the service id.

questions.q: What does autoconfigure: true do (as opposed to autowire)?

a.t: Applies tags/flags based on implemented interfaces and attributes

questions.exp: Autoconfigure adds tags automatically (e.g. event subscriber); autowire is the separate flag that fills arguments by type.

questions.q: How do you make an interface type-hint resolve to a concrete class?

a.t: Type-hint the class instead of the interface
Add a tag to the class

questions.exp: An alias from the interface id to the concrete service lets autowiring resolve the interface type-hint.

questions.q: Given _defaults with autowire: true, autoconfigure: true, public: false and an App\: resource glob, what is true of a class under src/?

a.t: It is registered private, with arguments autowired by type and tags applied by interface
It is public and must be fetched with get()
Only classes carrying an attribute are registered
Its id is a snake_case short name

questions.exp: _defaults sets the baseline: public: false makes it private, autowire fills constructor arguments by type, and autoconfigure applies tags based on implemented interfaces. The id is the FQCN. The glob registers every class in the directory, not just annotated ones.

questions.q: The App\: glob registers a class, and a later named block redefines the same id. Which definition wins?

a.t: The later, more specific block overrides the glob for that id
The glob always wins over named blocks
They are merged field-by-field with the glob taking precedence

questions.exp: Registration order matters: the glob first registers everything, then a later, more specific entry for the same id overrides it. This is the idiomatic way to tweak one autowired service. It is not an error and the glob does not win.

questions.q: Which argument cannot be supplied by autowiring and must come from bind, #[Autowire], or a parameter?

a.t: A scalar string such as a directory path
An object dependency identified by an interface type-hint
A service aliased from its interface
The single implementation of an interface

questions.exp: Autowiring resolves objects by type-hint; it can never guess scalars (strings, ints, arrays). Those must be bound explicitly via bind, #[Autowire], or a parameter. Objects, aliases, and single implementations all autowire fine.

questions.q: You add the alias App\Report\ReporterInterface: '@App\Report\Missing' but the target service does not exist. What happens?

a.t: A compile-time error — an alias to a non-existent target breaks the build; it is not a silent null
The interface silently resolves to null at runtime
A ServiceLocator is injected in its place

questions.exp: An alias must point at an existing service id; a dangling alias fails the container build. Optional dependencies use nullable constructor args or NULL_ON_INVALID_REFERENCE, not a broken alias. The misconception is expecting a missing target to become null.

questions.q: In a decorator definition, what does @.inner reference?

a.t: The original (decorated) service, renamed by the compiler
A private alias of the container

questions.exp: DecoratorServicePass renames the decorated service and exposes it as .inner so the decorator can delegate to it.

questions.q: Which attribute injects the decorated (inner) service into a decorator?
questions.exp: #[AsDecorator] declares the decoration; #[AutowireDecorated] resolves the parameter to the .inner service.

questions.q: With two decorators on one id, a higher decoration_priority means the decorator is...

a.t: Applied first and sits closer to the original (innermost)
Applied last and is the outermost

questions.exp: Higher priority decorators are applied first and end up innermost; consumers receive the lowest-priority, outermost decorator.

questions.q: decoration_on_invalid: ignore does what when the decorated service is missing?
questions.exp: ignore drops the decorator; null would inject null; exception (the default) throws when the target is absent.

questions.q: Two decorators target the same service. You need caching wrapped directly around the original and logging on the outside so consumers hit logging first. How do you set decoration_priority?

a.t: Caching gets the higher priority (e.g. 20), logging the lower (e.g. 10)
Logging gets the higher priority, caching the lower
Both must be equal so ordering is deterministic
Priority has no effect on the chain order

questions.exp: Higher decoration_priority is applied first and ends up innermost (closest to the original), so caching needs the higher number to sit directly around the original, and logging the lower number to become the outermost wrapper consumers hit first. Assuming lower priority runs first inverts the chain.

questions.q: A decorator injects the service by its own (decorated) id instead of .inner and hits infinite recursion. What is the fix?

a.t: Inject @.inner (or use #[AutowireDecorated]) to reference the renamed original

questions.exp: Because the decorator takes over the decorated service's public id, referencing that id inside the decorator injects the decorator itself, causing infinite recursion. You must reference the renamed original via .inner or #[AutowireDecorated]. Visibility and priority are unrelated to the loop.

questions.q: decoration_on_invalid: null is set, but .inner is typed as non-nullable MailerInterface and the decorated target is absent. What happens?

a.t: A TypeError — null is injected as .inner but the non-nullable argument rejects it; type it ?MailerInterface and guard with ?->
An exception is thrown at compile time
An empty stub mailer is created

questions.exp: With null, the compiler injects null as .inner; if the argument type is not nullable this becomes a TypeError at instantiation. The fix is a nullable type (?MailerInterface) and nullsafe delegation. ignore (not null) is what removes the decorator; exception is the default that throws at build.

questions.q: What does a tagged_locator argument inject?

a.t: A lazy ServiceLocator keyed by an index

questions.exp: tagged_locator injects a ServiceLocator that instantiates services on demand, keyed by the configured index; tagged_iterator yields instances.

questions.q: A higher priority on a tag places the service where in the tagged iterator?

a.t: Earlier (tagged collections are sorted by descending priority)
It has no effect on order

questions.exp: Tagged services are ordered by descending priority, so higher priority comes first.

questions.q: How can every implementation of an interface receive a tag automatically?

a.t: Use #[AutoconfigureTag] on the interface or _instanceof in YAML
Only by writing a compiler pass

questions.exp: Autoconfiguration maps an interface to a tag so all implementers are tagged without manual annotation.

questions.q: What is the key difference between tagged_iterator and tagged_locator?

a.t: tagged_iterator yields already-instantiated services; tagged_locator gives a lazy ServiceLocator built on get()
Both eagerly instantiate every tagged service
tagged_iterator is lazy while tagged_locator is eager

questions.exp: tagged_iterator injects an iterable of instances (use it when you always iterate all of them), while tagged_locator injects a ServiceLocator that builds each service lazily on get() and is keyed for pick-one-of-many. The trap is swapping their laziness.

questions.q: How is the key of each tagged_locator entry determined?

a.t: From an index_by tag attribute, a default_index_method static method (e.g. getName), or #[AsTaggedItem(index:)]
It is always the service id
It is always the class FQCN
It is assigned randomly at compile time

questions.exp: The locator key comes from the index_by tag attribute, a static method named by default_index_method (commonly getName/getDefaultIndexName), or an #[AsTaggedItem(index:)] attribute — not the service id by default. If two services resolve to the same key, the later one silently overwrites the earlier.

questions.q: True or False: adding a tag to a service changes its behaviour automatically, even with no collector consuming that tag.
questions.exp: A tag is inert build-time metadata; on its own it does nothing. Something — a tagged_iterator/tagged_locator argument or a compiler pass calling findTaggedServiceIds() — must consume the tag for it to have any effect.

questions.q: What does #[AutowireIterator('app.handler')] on an iterable $handlers argument inject?

a.t: An iterable of all app.handler-tagged services, ordered by descending priority
An array of the tag's attribute sets

questions.exp: #[AutowireIterator] is the attribute form of tagged_iterator: it injects an iterable of the instantiated tagged services, ordered by descending priority. #[AutowireLocator] would give the lazy keyed locator; the attribute does not filter down to one service.

questions.q: Which class validates and defaults a bundle's configuration schema?
questions.exp: Configuration defines allowed keys, types, defaults and validation; Extension::load() only consumes the processed result.

questions.q: When does prepend() run relative to the extensions' load() calls?
questions.exp: Prepend runs first so a bundle can inject default configuration into other bundles before they load.

questions.q: Which command prints a bundle's configuration reference tree?
questions.exp: config:dump-reference dumps the schema defined by Configuration; debug:config shows the currently resolved values.

questions.q: In a Symfony 8 AbstractBundle, where do the config schema and the service wiring live?

a.t: configure() defines the tree and loadExtension() wires services — both on the bundle class, with no separate Extension file
Only in a separate Extension class

questions.exp: AbstractBundle streamlines bundles by folding the schema (configure) and the extension logic (loadExtension) onto the bundle class itself, so a separate Configuration/Extension pair is no longer required. Kernel::build() registers compiler passes, not bundle semantic config.

questions.q: Which command shows the currently resolved configuration values (not the schema) for a bundle?
questions.exp: debug:config prints the merged, resolved values in effect; config:dump-reference prints the schema (allowed keys, types, defaults) defined by Configuration. Confusing the two is a common trap — one shows what is set, the other what is allowed.

questions.q: Your bundle must set a default framework option before FrameworkBundle loads. What do you call, and when does it run?

a.t: prependExtensionConfig('framework', [...]) inside prepend()/prependExtension(), which runs before all load() calls
setParameter() inside load(), which runs first
prependExtensionConfig() inside load(), after the other bundles

questions.exp: PrependExtensionInterface::prepend() (or prependExtension() on AbstractBundle) runs before every extension's load(), and prependExtensionConfig() injects config into another bundle's namespace. Doing it in load() would be too late, and setParameter() sets a parameter, not another bundle's config.

questions.q: A bundle named AcmeBlogBundle exposes its configuration under which root key by convention?

a.t: acme_blog (snake_case of the bundle name minus 'Bundle')

questions.exp: The root key is derived from the extension/bundle name: the class name minus the Bundle suffix, converted to snake_case, giving acme_blog. The misconception is using the class name verbatim or keeping the Bundle suffix.

questions.q: For a factory-built service, where are its arguments passed?
questions.exp: With a factory, the container calls the factory and passes the definition's arguments to it, not to a constructor.

questions.q: How do you configure a factory produced value via attributes?
questions.exp: There is no dedicated #[Factory] attribute; factories are configured with #[Autowire(factory:)] or in YAML/PHP config.

questions.q: How is an instance-method factory referenced in YAML?
questions.exp: An array of [reference, method] denotes a method call on a service; a static factory uses the 'Class::method' string form.

questions.q: factory: '@svc::method' throws an error. What is the correct instance-method form?
questions.exp: The '@svc::method' string is invalid syntax for an instance-method factory; use the array form ['@svc', 'method']. The 'Class::method' string form is reserved for static factories. The other forms are not recognised.

questions.q: How is an invokable factory service referenced in YAML?
questions.exp: A bare service reference '@service' as the factory means the container calls the service's __invoke() and stores the return value. Explicitly naming __invoke via the '::' string form is invalid; the array form is used for named instance methods, not required for invokables.

questions.q: Ledger has a private constructor and a static open(string $path). How do you register it as a service?

a.t: factory: 'App\Payment\Ledger::open' with the path in arguments passed to open()
Pass the path in arguments to the constructor as usual
It cannot be registered as a service

questions.exp: A static factory in the 'Class::method' string form bypasses the private constructor, and arguments are passed to open(), not a constructor. The instance-method array form would require an existing service instance, which the private constructor prevents.

questions.q: Which attribute registers a compiler pass? (choose one)

a.t: There is no attribute; register it via addCompilerPass() in Kernel/bundle build()

questions.exp: Compiler passes are registered programmatically via ContainerBuilder::addCompilerPass(), typically in Kernel::build() or a bundle's build(). There is no core attribute for this.

questions.q: What is the default phase for a compiler pass registered without one?
questions.exp: PassConfig runs passes in phase order; unspecified passes run in the before-optimization phase.

questions.q: What does ContainerBuilder::findTaggedServiceIds('t') return?

a.t: A map of service id => array of that tag's attribute sets

questions.exp: It returns definitions' ids each mapped to the attributes of every occurrence of the tag, used to wire collectors at compile time.

questions.q: Inside a compiler pass process() method, what should you manipulate?
questions.exp: Compilation deals only with definitions; nothing is instantiated yet, so calling get() inside a pass is wrong.

questions.q: In which phase should a pass that removes a service run, and why not TYPE_BEFORE_OPTIMIZATION?

a.t: TYPE_REMOVING — removing earlier could delete a service that autowiring (the optimization phase) still needs to reference
