TYPE_BEFORE_OPTIMIZATION is fine; phase order never matters
TYPE_AFTER_REMOVING, because removal always happens last

questions.exp: Removal belongs in TYPE_REMOVING. Doing it before optimization would delete a service that the autowiring/optimization phase might still reference, breaking resolution. AFTER_REMOVING runs once pruning is done, and mixing it into OPTIMIZATION races with autowiring.

questions.q: Two passes are registered in the same phase with priorities 10 and 100. Which runs first?

a.t: The priority-100 pass — higher priority runs earlier within a phase

questions.exp: Within a phase, addCompilerPass orders by priority with higher running first. The trap is assuming lower numbers run first (as some other Symfony orderings work); for compiler passes higher priority is earlier.

questions.q: Inside process(), a pass calls $container->get(SomeService::class) and it fails. Why?

a.t: Compilation deals only with Definitions; nothing is instantiated yet — use findDefinition()/Reference instead
get() requires the service to be public first
get() is only available inside the Kernel

questions.exp: A compiler pass runs before any service exists, so you manipulate build-time Definition objects (findDefinition, addMethodCall, new Reference), never live instances. Calling get() during compilation is the classic mistake; visibility and spelling are not the cause here.

questions.q: Which are valid places to register a compiler pass? (choose 2)

a.t: A #[CompilerPass] attribute on the pass class

questions.exp: Passes are registered programmatically with addCompilerPass() in the application Kernel::build() or a bundle's build(). There is no #[CompilerPass] attribute and no services.yaml tag that registers a pass — those are common invented answers.

questions.q: In addCompilerPass(new MyPass(), PassConfig::TYPE_BEFORE_OPTIMIZATION, priority: 5), what do the 2nd and 3rd arguments control?

a.t: The compilation phase and the ordering priority within that phase
The service id and its visibility
The tag name and its index
The environment and the debug flag

questions.exp: addCompilerPass(pass, phase, priority) takes the phase constant that determines when in PassConfig the pass runs, and a priority that orders passes within that phase (higher first). It has nothing to do with service ids, tags, or environments.

questions.q: What can autowiring resolve automatically?

a.t: Object dependencies identified by their type-hint

questions.exp: Autowiring maps a type-hint to a service; scalars and env vars must be bound explicitly with bind or #[Autowire].

questions.q: Two services implement one interface with no default alias. Autowiring by that interface...

a.t: Throws an ambiguity error at compile time

questions.exp: Ambiguity is a hard build error; you disambiguate with a named alias, #[Target], #[Autowire(service:)] or bind.

questions.q: What does the #[Target('requestLogger')] attribute do?

a.t: Selects the named autowiring alias explicitly, decoupled from the parameter name
Adds a tag to the service

questions.exp: #[Target] binds to a named autowiring alias by name, so renaming the constructor parameter does not break wiring.

questions.q: What is the literal id of a named autowiring alias, e.g. for a Monolog channel logger?

a.t: Literally 'Psr\Log\LoggerInterface $requestLogger' — matched by the parameter name

questions.exp: A named autowiring alias id is the full type followed by the variable name, 'Type $paramName'. Autowiring matches it when your constructor parameter is named identically — which is fragile, so #[Target('requestLogger')] states the intent explicitly and survives parameter renames.

questions.q: A parameter has #[Autowire('app.foo')] and receives the literal string "app.foo" instead of the service. Why?

a.t: A bare string is a literal value; to inject a service use #[Autowire(service: 'app.foo')]
The app.foo service must be made public first
Service ids need an @ prefix inside attributes

questions.exp: In #[Autowire], a bare string is interpreted as a literal value (or a %param% / %env()% expression), not a service reference. Use the named argument service: to pin a service id. Visibility is irrelevant and no @ prefix is used in attributes.

questions.q: A constructor type-hints an interface that has no implementation and no alias. What does the container build do?

a.t: Fails with a compile-time 'Cannot autowire ... no such service' error — not a silent null

questions.exp: Autowiring an unregistered type is a hard build failure. Silent null only happens if you explicitly opt in with a nullable argument and default (?Type $x = null). Autowiring never guesses an arbitrary class or defers to runtime — the misconception is expecting null.

questions.q: Which techniques resolve autowiring ambiguity when several services implement one interface? (choose 3)
questions.exp: Ambiguity is resolved by explicitly choosing an implementation: a named alias, #[Target], #[Autowire(service:)], or bind. Making services public only affects fetchability by id and does nothing to disambiguate autowiring.

questions.q: How does a ServiceLocator differ from injecting the whole container?

a.t: It exposes only an explicitly declared, whitelisted set of services
It is eager while the container is lazy

questions.exp: A locator's set is explicit and analysable; injecting the whole container hides dependencies and is an anti-pattern.

questions.q: When does a ServiceLocator instantiate the services it holds?
questions.exp: A locator defers construction until a service is actually requested, which is its main advantage over injecting all candidates.

questions.q: What interface does Symfony's ServiceLocator implement?
questions.exp: ServiceLocator is a PSR-11 container exposing get() and has() over a fixed, compile-time set of services.

questions.q: What does ServiceSubscriberInterface::getSubscribedServices() declare?

a.t: The set of services the subscriber may lazily use, injected as a locator

questions.exp: It declares a whitelist; the container injects a matching ServiceLocator so services are built only when requested.

questions.q: Which trait should a Symfony 8 service subscriber use with #[SubscribedService] methods?
questions.exp: The older ServiceSubscriberTrait was deprecated in 6.4; Symfony 8 uses ServiceMethodsSubscriberTrait together with #[SubscribedService] methods whose return type names the service. ServiceLocatorTrait builds a locator class, and ContainerAwareTrait is the removed container-injection anti-pattern.

questions.q: With #[AutowireLocator(['stripe' => StripeGateway::class, 'paypal' => PayPalGateway::class])] ContainerInterface $gateways, what happens on $gateways->get('stripe')?

a.t: Only StripeGateway is instantiated (lazily); PayPalGateway is never built
Both gateways are instantiated up front
It throws unless both gateways are public

questions.exp: #[AutowireLocator] builds a PSR-11 locator that instantiates a service only when get() requests it, so fetching 'stripe' builds StripeGateway and leaves PayPalGateway cold. Locators do not require member services to be public, and they build instances, not return strings.

questions.q: A locator built for keys 'stripe' and 'paypal' is called with a user-supplied key 'unknown'. What happens?

a.t: It throws ServiceNotFoundException — validate with has() before get()
It returns the first declared service
It builds a new empty service on the fly

questions.exp: A locator's set is fixed at compile time, so get() on a key outside the whitelist throws; unlike the main container there is no NULL_ON_INVALID mode. Guard untrusted keys with has() first. It never returns null or falls back to another service.

questions.q: You have five heavy payment gateways but use exactly one per request, chosen by name. What is the best tool?

a.t: A service locator (e.g. #[AutowireLocator]) so only the chosen gateway is built
A tagged_iterator, iterating all five every request
Injecting all five gateways in the constructor

questions.exp: Pick-one-of-many with heavy dependencies is the textbook case for a lazy locator: only the selected gateway is instantiated. A tagged_iterator or constructor-injecting all five would eagerly build every gateway, and injecting the whole container is the anti-pattern the locator replaces.

questions.q: In Symfony 8 (PHP 8.4), what does the container inject for a concrete service marked lazy: true?

a.t: A native lazy ghost — an uninitialized instance whose constructor runs in place on first use
null, replaced by the real instance on first get()

questions.exp: Symfony 8 runs on PHP 8.4, whose engine provides native lazy objects. For a concrete class the dumped container creates a lazy ghost: the very same instance, handed out uninitialized, with the real constructor run in place on first state access. No external proxy library is involved.

questions.q: Which statements about PHP 8.4 native lazy objects as used by Symfony are true? (select all that apply)

a.t: A lazy ghost is initialized in place, so it is === the initialized object
final classes can be lazy ghosts, since no subclass is generated
First interaction with the object's state triggers initialization
A lazy service's constructor never runs, even when used

questions.exp: Native ghosts are created from the class itself: identity is preserved, final classes work (unlike old inheritance-based proxies), and the engine runs the initializer on first state access. No external proxy package is needed, and the constructor does run — just later.

questions.q: A service is declared with lazy: 'App\Payment\GatewayInterface'. A test asserts the injected object is === the real gateway instance after first use. What happens?

a.t: The assertion fails — interface laziness creates a proxy that delegates to a distinct real instance
The assertion passes — all lazy objects preserve identity
The container throws: lazy only accepts true or false
The proxy is replaced by the real instance after initialization, so it passes

questions.exp: Setting lazy to an interface name produces a lazy proxy implementing that interface. Unlike a ghost, a proxy is a separate object that forwards to the real instance it creates on first use, so proxy !== real instance. Identity is only preserved with ghosts (lazy: true on a concrete class).

questions.q: Which are valid ways to make a service lazy in Symfony 8? (select all that apply)

a.t: lazy: true under the service in services.yaml
->lazy() on the service in a services.php configurator

questions.exp: Laziness is a definition flag settable in every config format: the YAML lazy key, the Autoconfigure attribute's lazy argument, or the fluent ->lazy() call in PHP configuration. There is no LazyInterface contract to implement.

questions.q: Between two requests in a long-running worker runtime, what does the services_resetter service do?

a.t: Calls the configured reset method on every kernel.reset-tagged service that was instantiated
Destroys the container and reboots the kernel
Re-runs the constructor of every tagged service
Instantiates all tagged services, then resets them

questions.exp: ServicesResetter iterates only the tagged services that were actually initialized during the request and invokes their configured method(s); the container and the instances themselves survive. Never-instantiated services are skipped so laziness is not defeated.

questions.q: Which statements about resettable services are true? (select all that apply)

a.t: Implementing Symfony\Contracts\Service\ResetInterface autoconfigures the kernel.reset tag
Only services already instantiated during the request/message get reset
The messenger:consume worker resets services between messages unless --no-reset is passed
Resetting replaces the service with a brand-new instance
A service must be public to be resettable

questions.exp: Autoconfiguration tags ResetInterface implementors with kernel.reset; the resetter only touches initialized services; and Messenger workers reset between messages by default (--no-reset opts out). Reset calls a method on the same instance — it does not rebuild it — and visibility is irrelevant since the resetter receives the services internally.

questions.q: Under FrankenPHP worker mode, a shared service memoizes the current user's preferences in a private array and users start seeing each other's data. What is the idiomatic fix?

a.t: Implement ResetInterface (or tag kernel.reset with a method) that clears the memoized array between requests
Nothing — PHP resets all objects after every request
Mark the service lazy: true so it is rebuilt per request
Call cache:clear at the end of every request

questions.exp: In worker runtimes the container — and thus shared service state — survives across requests; the PHP-FPM "everything dies" assumption no longer holds. The reset mechanism exists exactly for this: clear the request-scoped state in reset(). Laziness only defers construction and cache:clear rebuilds compiled artifacts, not in-memory service state.

questions.q: After cache warmup, which artifacts does the dumped container leave in var/cache/{env}/? (select all that apply)

a.t: A Container{hash}/ directory with the compiled container class and per-service factory code
A generated .preload.php file for OPcache preloading
A serialized ContainerBuilder object loaded on each request
Copies of every services.yaml re-parsed at runtime

questions.exp: PhpDumper writes plain PHP: the container class with its getXxxService() factories (split per service or inlined depending on the dump settings) plus a preload script to reference from opcache.preload. The ContainerBuilder and the YAML files are build-time inputs only — nothing re-parses or unserializes them at runtime.

questions.q: debug:container shows a private service, yet the dumped container code contains no factory for it. Why?

a.t: The removing passes inlined or pruned it; debug:container reads a build-time snapshot, not the dumped code
The cache is stale and must be cleared
Private services never get factories, even when referenced by many consumers
debug:container invents entries for autowiring candidates

questions.exp: During the removing phases a private service with a single consumer is inlined into that consumer's factory (and unreferenced ones are removed), so it has no standalone factory in the dump. debug:container works from the pre-dump ContainerBuilder snapshot where the definition still exists — the asymmetry is expected, not a stale cache.

questions.q: You edit a service argument in services.yaml directly on a prod server. Requests keep using the old value. Why?

a.t: Prod executes the dumped PHP container and does not track config resources — the change needs a cache rebuild
YAML changes require restarting the database
The container watches services.yaml and applies changes after a short delay
Service arguments can only be changed through environment variables

questions.exp: In prod the container was compiled once and dumped to var/cache/prod as plain PHP; the runtime never re-reads services.yaml. Only rebuilding the cache (cache:clear / cache:warmup) re-runs extension loading, the compiler passes and the PhpDumper dump with the new configuration.

questions.q: Which two methods do you typically override in an AbstractType?
questions.exp: buildForm() adds fields to the builder; configureOptions() declares the type's options via OptionsResolver. getName() was removed; buildView() exists but is not the primary pair.

questions.q: A compound form with no data_class set returns what from getData()?

a.t: An associative array keyed by child field name

questions.exp: Without data_class the data mapper maps children into and out of an array. Set data_class to bind the form to an object instead.

questions.q: Where should field-adding logic live in a form type?

a.t: In configureOptions(), returning an array of fields

questions.exp: buildForm() receives the builder and is where ->add() calls belong. configureOptions() only declares options via OptionsResolver.

questions.q: A developer writes `public function configureOptions(OptionsResolver $resolver): void { return ['data_class' => Contact::class]; }`. Why does the form type fail to compile / behave?

a.t: configureOptions() returns void; you must call $resolver->setDefaults([...]), not return an array
data_class must be a string literal, never a ::class constant
You must call parent::configureOptions() first or it throws
Options can only be declared inside buildForm()

questions.exp: configureOptions() has a void return type and configures the injected OptionsResolver imperatively via setDefaults()/setRequired()/setAllowedTypes(). Returning an array does nothing. ::class constants are perfectly valid option values, and there is no requirement to call the parent (AbstractType's is empty).

questions.q: When you call $this->createForm(RegistrationType::class, $data), which object resolves the type's parent chain and extensions before the builder tree is built?

a.t: FormFactory::create() asks FormRegistry for a ResolvedFormType, which builds the FormBuilder and walks buildForm() parent→child
The controller instantiates the FormInterface tree directly
OptionsResolver builds the form tree from the declared defaults
The DataMapper creates the child forms from data_class metadata

questions.exp: createForm() delegates to FormFactory::create(), which via FormRegistry obtains a ResolvedFormType wrapping the type, its resolved parent chain and applicable type extensions. The resolved type creates a FormBuilder and runs each buildForm() from parent to child; getForm() then produces the immutable FormInterface tree. OptionsResolver only resolves options; the DataMapper maps data at submit/view time.

questions.q: Inside buildForm(FormBuilderInterface $builder, array $options), can you read the user's submitted values (e.g. $builder->getData() as posted input)?

a.t: No — buildForm() runs at build time on a FormBuilderInterface; the form is not submitted yet, so there is no request data to read

questions.exp: buildForm() receives a FormBuilderInterface, not a submitted FormInterface. The form does not exist yet and handleRequest()/submit() have not run, so submitted input is unavailable. To react to submitted values, add a PRE_SUBMIT listener, which fires later with the raw view data. There is no $builder->getRequest().

questions.q: What determines the Twig block name used to theme a custom form type?

a.t: getBlockPrefix() (defaults to the snake_cased class name without the Type suffix)
getName(), which returns the block name
The value passed as the field's second ->add() argument

questions.exp: getBlockPrefix() drives Twig block naming; it defaults to the snake-cased short class name minus the Type suffix. getName() was removed long ago — the FQCN is now the type identifier, but the FQCN is not used verbatim for block names.

questions.q: What is the canonical order of the controller form-handling calls?

a.t: handleRequest(), then isSubmitted() && isValid(), then getData()

questions.exp: handleRequest() inspects the request and submits the form; only then are isSubmitted()/isValid() meaningful, after which getData() holds the model.

questions.q: For a PATCH submission, handleRequest passes which clearMissing value?

a.t: false, enabling partial updates (absent fields keep their value)

questions.exp: handleRequest passes clearMissing: false for PATCH so fields missing from the payload retain their current value, enabling partial updates.

questions.q: Which service does FormInterface::handleRequest() delegate to under FrameworkBundle?
questions.exp: With HttpFoundation available, the form's request handler is HttpFoundationRequestHandler; NativeRequestHandler is the fallback when working with PHP superglobals directly.

questions.q: Why redirect after a successful POST (POST-redirect-GET)?

a.t: So a browser refresh re-fetches a GET instead of re-submitting the form
Because forms cannot render on a POST response
It is required for isValid() to return true

questions.exp: Without the redirect, refreshing re-POSTs the data and duplicates side effects. Redirecting lands the browser on a safe GET.

questions.q: What happens if you call $form->isValid() on a form that was never submitted?

a.t: It throws a LogicException ('Cannot check if an unsubmitted form is valid')
It returns true because there are no errors yet
It implicitly submits the form first

questions.exp: isValid() is only meaningful after submission, so calling it on an unsubmitted form throws a LogicException. Always guard with isSubmitted() first (isSubmitted() && isValid()). It does not auto-submit or silently return a value.

questions.q: A form posts to a controller and the browser gets a 405 Method Not Allowed on submit, though the page renders fine on GET. What is the most likely cause?

a.t: The route restricts methods to GET (missing POST in methods: ['GET','POST'])
data_class is not set on the form

questions.exp: A 405 comes from the router rejecting the HTTP method before the controller runs, so the route must allow POST as well as GET. A missing handleRequest() or CSRF token would let the request through and manifest as a form not submitting or an invalid-token error, not a 405; data_class is unrelated.

questions.q: Which accessor returns each of a field's three data representations after submit?

a.t: getData() = model, getNormData() = normalized, getViewData() = view
getData() = view, getViewData() = model, getNormData() = raw
All three return the same array

questions.exp: A field holds data in three shapes: model (your PHP value), normalized (transport-neutral canonical), and view (strings for HTML). They are read with getData()/getNormData()/getViewData() respectively; transformers convert between adjacent shapes. There are no getModelData()/getRenderedData() methods.

questions.q: What does a form type's getParent() return?

a.t: The parent type's fully-qualified class name (a string)

questions.exp: getParent() returns a class string (default FormType::class). The registry resolves it into the parent chain of a ResolvedFormType.

questions.q: Which object bundles a type with its parent chain and applicable extensions?
questions.exp: FormRegistry produces a ResolvedFormType wrapping the type, its resolved parent, and every type extension that applies.

questions.q: In what order do configureOptions() run along the type hierarchy?

a.t: Parent first, then child (child can override parent defaults)

questions.exp: The resolved type walks the chain top-down, so parent defaults are set before the child's, letting the child override them.

questions.q: A custom type does `public function getParent(): string { return new TextType(); }`. What is wrong?

a.t: getParent() must return a class-string (TextType::class), not an instance
Nothing — Symfony instantiates the returned object as the parent
It should return an array of parent FQCNs

questions.exp: getParent() is declared to return string; returning an object violates the return type and the registry expects an FQCN to resolve. Use TextType::class. It is not static and returns a single string, not an array.

questions.q: In configureOptions(), which OptionsResolver call derives one option's value from the values of others?
questions.exp: setNormalizer() receives the resolved Options plus the raw value, letting one option depend on others (e.g. force expanded when multiple is false). setAllowedTypes validates a type, setRequired marks an option mandatory, and a default closure cannot read sibling options the way a normalizer can.

questions.q: How are custom form types made available by their FQCN and able to receive injected services?

a.t: FrameworkBundle autoconfigures FormTypeInterface implementers with the form.type tag
You must register each type manually in config/services.yaml with form.type
Types are discovered by a #[AsFormType] attribute
The FormFactory scans the Form/ directory at runtime

questions.exp: Service autoconfiguration tags any class implementing FormTypeInterface with form.type, so it is usable by FQCN and can autowire constructor dependencies. There is no #[AsFormType] attribute and no runtime directory scan; manual tagging is only needed when autoconfiguration is disabled.

questions.q: What does form_row(form.email) render?

a.t: Label, widget, errors and help for that field

questions.exp: form_row composes the label, widget, errors and help via the *_row theme block. form_widget renders only the control.

questions.q: How is the hidden CSRF token normally emitted into the HTML?

a.t: By form_rest, which form_end calls by default
It is never rendered inside the form

questions.exp: The CSRF token is a hidden child rendered by form_rest; form_end triggers form_rest unless you pass render_rest: false.

questions.q: Which call renders form-level (non-field) errors?
questions.exp: Passing the root form view to form_errors renders errors attached to the form itself; per-field errors use form_errors(form.field).

questions.q: A template renders each field manually and ends with `{{ form_end(form, {'render_rest': false}) }}`. Submissions now fail with an invalid CSRF token. Why?

a.t: render_rest: false suppresses form_rest, so the hidden _token is never emitted; render form_rest(form) yourself
form_end always drops the token; you must add it in form_start
CSRF only works with form(form), never with manual layouts
The token expired because manual rendering is slower

questions.exp: form_end normally calls form_rest, which renders un-rendered fields including the hidden CSRF token. Passing render_rest: false skips that, so the _token is absent and PRE_SUBMIT validation fails. Render form_rest(form) (or the token) manually. Manual layouts are fully CSRF-capable; the token has nothing to do with speed.

questions.q: How do partial rendering (form_row on some fields) and form_rest avoid rendering the same field twice?

a.t: Each FormView carries an isRendered() flag; form_row/form_widget set it, and form_rest skips already-rendered views
form_rest re-renders everything and Twig de-duplicates the HTML
The renderer diffs the output string to remove duplicates
Fields can only be rendered once per request globally

questions.exp: Rendering operates on the FormView tree. Each view has an isRendered() flag set when form_row/form_widget renders it, so form_rest emits only the leftover (un-rendered) fields — including hidden and CSRF fields. There is no string diffing.

questions.q: Which Twig call is wrong for rendering a single field's widget?

a.t: form(form.email) — form() is for the whole form; use form_widget/form_row for a field

questions.exp: form() renders an entire form (start, rows, end). For an individual field use form_row (label+widget+errors+help) or the granular form_widget/form_label/ form_errors/form_help. Calling form() on a child view is a common mistake.

questions.q: In which order does the renderer try candidate theme blocks?

a.t: Most specific (unique field id) down to least specific (form_widget)

questions.exp: The block-prefix hierarchy is walked from the unique per-field name down to the root form_* block; the first existing block wins.

questions.q: What does the built-in bootstrap_5_layout.html.twig provide?

a.t: Twig blocks producing Bootstrap-compatible markup (a theme only)

questions.exp: Built-in layouts are theme templates (markup only). You still load the CSS framework yourself; the Form component ships no assets.

questions.q: When two global form themes define the same block, which wins?

a.t: The theme listed last in twig.form_themes

questions.exp: Themes in twig.form_themes are applied in order; later entries override earlier ones on a block clash.

questions.q: Which twig.yaml block applies a Bootstrap theme app-wide, then lets your own file override its blocks?
questions.exp: form_themes are applied in order and the last wins on conflicts, so your file must come after the Bootstrap layout to override its blocks. The key is twig.form_themes (a list), not twig.theme or a framework.* key.

questions.q: What is required to theme a form with {% form_theme form _self %}?

a.t: The template must NOT {% extends %} another template
You must also list the template in twig.form_themes
The blocks must be defined in a macro
_self only works for the CSRF field

questions.exp: _self references the current template's own blocks, which requires that the template does not extend another (extending re-scopes blocks). It works for any field's blocks, not just CSRF, and does not need a form_themes entry or macros.

questions.q: A field with block prefix 'rating' (parent 'integer') ignores your integer_widget override, but rating_widget works. Why?

a.t: The renderer tries rating_widget before integer_widget; the more specific block exists and wins, so integer_widget is never reached
integer_widget is a reserved block that cannot be overridden
Parent-prefix blocks are ignored unless you set inherit_data
You must clear the Twig cache for parent blocks to apply

questions.exp: Block-name resolution goes most-specific to least-specific along the block-prefix chain (rating → integer → form). Since rating_widget exists, it wins and the more generic integer_widget is never consulted. Override rating_widget (or remove it to fall through). inherit_data and caching are unrelated.

questions.q: At which form event is the CSRF token validated?
questions.exp: CsrfValidationListener runs on PRE_SUBMIT: it pops the _token field from the raw submitted data and validates it, adding a form error on failure.

questions.q: What does the csrf_token_id option control?

a.t: The token intention/namespace used to generate and validate it
The HTML name of the hidden field

questions.exp: csrf_token_id is the intention string. csrf_field_name sets the HTML field name (default _token); csrf_protection toggles the feature.

questions.q: Stateless CSRF (Symfony 7.2+/8) primarily removes the need for what?

a.t: A server-side session to store the token

questions.exp: With framework.csrf_protection.stateless_token_ids, the SameOriginCsrfTokenManager validates via a double-submit cookie plus origin checks, so no token is stored in the session.

questions.q: Which configuration enables stateless CSRF for the login and logout token ids?
questions.exp: Stateless CSRF is enabled per token id by listing them under framework.csrf_protection.stateless_token_ids; forms whose csrf_token_id is in that list use SameOriginCsrfTokenManager. There is no boolean stateless/session flag, and the key lives under framework, not security.

questions.q: When a submission arrives with a missing or invalid _token, what does CsrfValidationListener do?

a.t: It adds a form error (so isValid() returns false) — it does not throw an exception
It returns a 403 response before the controller runs
It silently regenerates a fresh token and continues

questions.exp: On PRE_SUBMIT the listener pops _token from the raw data and validates it; a missing/invalid token results in a form error, so isValid() is false and you re-render with csrf_message. It does not throw or short-circuit with a 403 — that is the pattern for the manual isCsrfTokenValid() helper in a controller.

questions.q: If csrf_token_id is not set explicitly on a form, what is its default value?

a.t: A random value regenerated every request

questions.exp: The default csrf_token_id is the form's block prefix; setting it explicitly makes the intention stable regardless of the class name. '_token' is the default csrf_field_name (the HTML name), not the id, and the token is not the app secret nor regenerated per request within a namespace.

questions.q: How do you read the value of an unmapped FileType field?
questions.exp: mapped => false excludes the field from the data mapper, so it is not written to the model; you fetch it directly from the child form.

questions.q: Which UploadedFile value is safe to trust for validating file type?
questions.exp: Client-supplied name and MIME are spoofable. Content-based guessing (used by the File/Image constraints) is authoritative.

questions.q: When does form_start emit enctype="multipart/form-data"?

a.t: When the form contains a file field
Never — you must add it yourself

questions.exp: The form's multipart view variable is set when a child (e.g. FileType) requires it, and form_start renders the enctype accordingly.

questions.q: On an optional upload field, the controller calls $file->move(...) and occasionally crashes with a fatal error. What is the fix?

a.t: Guard with `if ($file instanceof UploadedFile)` — getData() is null when no file was uploaded
Set required => true so getData() is never null
Call handleRequest() a second time to populate the file

questions.exp: An optional FileType returns null from getData() when nothing is uploaded, so calling move() on null is fatal. Check `$file instanceof UploadedFile` first. Forcing required doesn't fit an optional field, re-running handleRequest is wrong, and bypassing the form loses validation.

questions.q: Is a FileType field with mapped => false still validated by its constraints?

a.t: Yes — mapped => false only stops data-mapping; the field is still rendered, submitted and validated
No — unmapped fields skip validation entirely
Only if you also set required => true
Only when constraints are on the model class, not the field

questions.exp: mapped => false only disconnects the field from the data mapper (it is not written to the model). The field is still part of the form: rendered, submitted, and validated via its constraints option — which is exactly why the pattern is safe for uploads and plain passwords.

questions.q: What is the recommended way to name an uploaded file before move()?

a.t: Slug the original basename, append uniqid(), and use guessExtension()
Use getClientOriginalName() directly as the target path
Store the UploadedFile object on the entity and let Doctrine name it

questions.exp: Generate a safe name: slug the original filename, add uniqid() for uniqueness, and derive the extension from guessExtension() (content-based). Using the client name risks path traversal, the tmp_name is transient, and persisting the UploadedFile object (Doctrine is out of scope) is wrong.

questions.q: Which ChoiceType options render checkboxes?
questions.exp: expanded + multiple renders checkboxes; expanded + single renders radios; collapsed renders a select element.

questions.q: What does MoneyType's divisor option do?

a.t: Scales the model value (e.g. 100 lets you store integer cents)

questions.exp: The displayed amount is divided by divisor to form the model value, so 100 lets you store amounts in cents.

questions.q: For a mapped CollectionType to call the parent's adder/remover methods, set…
questions.exp: by_reference => false forces the form to call add/remove methods instead of mutating the returned collection in place, keeping associations in sync.

questions.q: Which type is out of scope here because it belongs to the Doctrine bridge?
questions.exp: EntityType lives in the Doctrine bridge and is out of scope. Use ChoiceType with explicit choices for the non-Doctrine equivalent.

questions.q: For a DateType that renders one HTML5 date input and produces a \DateTimeImmutable model, which options do you set?
questions.exp: widget controls rendering: single_text is one type=\"date\" input (best with HTML5); choice renders dropdowns and text renders three text fields. input picks the model type — datetime_immutable is the recommended value, whereas string, timestamp and array yield other model shapes.

questions.q: What is RepeatedType used for?

a.t: Rendering one inner type twice (e.g. password + confirmation) that only passes if both entries match
Rendering a dynamic list of sub-forms you can add/remove
Repeating a form submission N times server-side
Rendering the same field for every locale

questions.exp: RepeatedType renders its inner type (via the type option) twice — configured with first_options/second_options — and validates only if both values match, ideal for password confirmation. The dynamic add/remove list is CollectionType, not RepeatedType.

questions.q: Which statements about PasswordType and button types are correct? (choose 2)

a.t: PasswordType is not re-rendered with its value by default (always_empty => true)
SubmitType/ButtonType/ResetType are not part of the mapped form data
PasswordType always re-renders the submitted value for convenience
SubmitType values are written to the data_class object

questions.exp: PasswordType defaults to always_empty => true, so the field renders blank after submit for safety. Buttons (Submit/Button/Reset) are unmapped — they carry no data — though SubmitType lets you detect the clicked button via getClickedButton().

questions.q: In which direction does reverseTransform() run?

a.t: It never runs for view transformers

questions.exp: transform() converts toward the view (display); reverseTransform() converts toward the model (submission). Reversing these is the classic trap.

questions.q: addModelTransformer() converts between which representations?
questions.exp: Model transformers bridge model<->norm; view transformers bridge norm<->view. Pick a model transformer when the underlying type changes.

questions.q: What should a transformer throw when input cannot be converted?
questions.exp: TransformationFailedException is caught by the form and turned into a field-level invalid state showing the field's invalid_message, not a 500.

questions.q: On submit, which transformers run first?

a.t: Only model transformers run on submit

questions.exp: On submission data flows view -> norm -> model, so view transformers' reverseTransform runs before model transformers' reverseTransform.

questions.q: In a DataTransformer, what should transform(null) return when the model value is unset?

a.t: '' (an empty string the widget can display)

questions.exp: On display, transform(null) fires for an unset model value and should return '' so the input renders cleanly and later value comparisons hold; returning null can make the widget render oddly. Throwing is for genuinely unconvertible input on reverseTransform, not for a normal empty value.

questions.q: An optional text field with a custom transformer reports 'invalid' whenever it is left blank. What is the likely cause?

a.t: reverseTransform('') runs the parser on an empty string and throws TransformationFailedException; guard for ''/null and return the empty model value first
The field needs a NotBlank constraint removed
transform() must return null for empty values
Model transformers cannot handle optional fields

questions.exp: An empty submission arrives as '' (or null) at reverseTransform(); if you parse it instead of short-circuiting, you raise a spurious TransformationFailedException and the field is marked invalid. Guard the first line for emptiness and return the model's empty value (null/[]/0). This is a format-handling bug, not a validation constraint issue.

questions.q: You need a field whose view is an id string but whose model is a domain object. Which transformer slot fits?

a.t: A model transformer (the underlying type changes: id string <-> object)
Either — the slot makes no difference
A PRE_SET_DATA listener instead of any transformer

questions.exp: Use a model transformer when the type of the underlying object changes (id <-> rich object); it bridges model<->norm. A view transformer is for pure string formatting (norm<->view). The slot matters because it determines where in the pipeline the conversion runs and what the norm data looks like.

questions.q: What is the correct order of the submit-phase form events?
questions.exp: Submission dispatches PRE_SUBMIT (raw view data), SUBMIT (normalized), then POST_SUBMIT (bound model), in that order.

questions.q: What is the correct order of the set-data-phase form events?
questions.exp: Setting data (on create/populate) dispatches PRE_SET_DATA then POST_SET_DATA. There is no SET_DATA constant.

questions.q: On PRE_SUBMIT, what does $event->getData() return?

a.t: The raw submitted view data (an array/string)

questions.exp: PRE_SUBMIT fires before transformation, so the data is the raw request values — not your object.

questions.q: To add a field based on the submitted value, which event do you listen on?
questions.exp: Fields must be added before binding. PRE_SUBMIT exposes the raw submitted value while the form is still mutable (dynamic/dependent fields).

questions.q: Which event does the validator form extension hook to run validation?
questions.exp: Validation runs after data is bound to the model, via a POST_SUBMIT listener. There is no PRE_VALIDATE/POST_VALIDATE in FormEvents.

questions.q: In a PRE_SUBMIT listener you read the submitted country. Which line is safe?
questions.exp: PRE_SUBMIT data is the raw request array, so a blank field is simply an absent key — read it with ?? null to avoid an undefined-key warning. Treating the data as an object (->getCountry()) is wrong: it is not transformed yet, and the model on the form is not yet populated from this submission.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a real FormEvents constant?
questions.exp: There is no PRE_VALIDATE (nor POST_VALIDATE) in FormEvents. The five constants are PRE_SET_DATA, POST_SET_DATA, PRE_SUBMIT, SUBMIT and POST_SUBMIT; validation is simply a POST_SUBMIT listener registered by the validator extension.

questions.q: How do you attach a reusable event subscriber to a form?

a.t: Implement FormEventSubscriberInterface and tag it form.subscriber
Add a #[AsFormSubscriber] attribute to the class
Register it under framework.form.subscribers in YAML

questions.exp: Form subscribers implement the EventDispatcher's EventSubscriberInterface (the Form component has no dedicated FormEventSubscriberInterface) declaring getSubscribedEvents(), and are added with $builder->addEventSubscriber(). There is no #[AsFormSubscriber] attribute or framework.form.subscribers config for this.

questions.q: Which method declares the types a form type extension applies to?
questions.exp: getExtendedTypes() is static and returns an iterable of type FQCNs. It replaced the removed singular getExtendedType().

questions.q: With autoconfiguration enabled, how is a type extension registered?

a.t: Automatically, via the form.type_extension tag on FormTypeExtensionInterface services
By calling addTypeExtension() in a controller

questions.exp: Symfony auto-tags implementers of FormTypeExtensionInterface with form.type_extension. There is no dedicated attribute for this in core.

questions.q: What is the effect of returning FormType::class from getExtendedTypes()?

a.t: The extension applies to every form type (all descend from FormType)
It applies only to the root form

questions.exp: Because all types inherit from FormType, the extension attaches to every form — powerful for global concerns but risky to overuse.

questions.q: Which attribute registers a form type extension in core Symfony?

a.t: There is none — core has no #[AsFormTypeExtension]; registration is by interface + getExtendedTypes() (autoconfig) or a manual tag

questions.exp: Unlike #[AsEventListener] or #[AsCommand], form type extensions have no dedicated attribute in core. Autoconfiguration tags FormTypeExtensionInterface services with form.type_extension, and getExtendedTypes() tells the registry which types to attach them to; a manual form.type_extension tag with extended_type is the fallback when autoconfiguration is off.

questions.q: A type extension defines `public function getExtendedType(): string { return FileType::class; }` but never applies. What is wrong?

a.t: The singular getExtendedType() was removed; you must implement the static getExtendedTypes(): iterable returning [FileType::class]
FileType cannot be extended; only FormType can
You must also return the parent chain from getExtendedType()

questions.exp: Registration keys off the static getExtendedTypes(): iterable; the old singular getExtendedType() no longer exists, so the extension is never matched to a type. Any type (including FileType) can be extended, and the method is static/public.

questions.q: With autoconfiguration disabled, which services.yaml tag correctly registers an extension for FileType?
questions.exp: Without autoconfiguration you must both use the form.type_extension tag and supply the extended_type attribute (the FQCN of the extended type) — it is not inferred from getExtendedTypes() in the manual case. form.type is for form types, and form.extension is not a real tag.

questions.q: Which of the following statements are true about creating a custom form type? (select all that apply)

a.t: buildForm() receives a FormBuilderInterface — the form does not exist yet, so you cannot read submitted data there
Without a data_class option, a compound form's getData() returns an array, not an object
getBlockPrefix() — not getName() — determines the Twig block names used for theming
configureOptions() must return a plain array of default options
getName() is the method that controls Twig theming block names

questions.exp: buildForm() works on a FormBuilderInterface before any FormInterface exists; without data_class the data mapper falls back to an array; and getBlockPrefix() drives theming block resolution. configureOptions() configures an OptionsResolver instance rather than returning an array, and getName() was removed long ago in favour of getBlockPrefix().

questions.q: Which of the following statements are true about form submission handling? (select all that apply)

a.t: Calling isValid() on a form that was never submitted throws a LogicException — guard with isSubmitted() first
handleRequest() silently ignores a request whose HTTP method does not match the form's method option
For a PATCH form, clearMissing is false, so fields missing from the submission keep their existing value
Validation runs while handleRequest() parses the request, before any form events fire
handleRequest() automatically redirects the user after a successful submission

questions.exp: isValid() on an unsubmitted form throws a LogicException; a method mismatch means the form is simply treated as not submitted; and PATCH implies clearMissing = false for partial updates. Validation actually fires as a POST_SUBMIT listener, not during request parsing, and the redirect after success is your controller's responsibility.

questions.q: Which of the following statements are true about CSRF protection in Symfony forms? (select all that apply)

a.t: CSRF protection is enabled by default and adds a hidden _token field that is checked on submission
The CSRF token is validated on PRE_SUBMIT by the CsrfValidationListener, before data transformation
The default csrf_token_id is always the literal string 'form', regardless of the form type
Stateless CSRF tokens (stateless_token_ids) still require an active session to work
The default CSRF field name is 'csrf_token'

questions.exp: CSRF protection is on by default via a hidden _token field, and the token check runs on PRE_SUBMIT via CsrfValidationListener. The default token id is the form's block prefix (not a fixed 'form' string) unless csrf_token_id is set, the default field name is _token, and stateless_token_ids uses SameOriginCsrfTokenManager with no session needed.

questions.q: Which of the following statements are true about data transformers? (select all that apply)

a.t: transform() converts model data to view data for display; reverseTransform() converts submitted view data back to model data
Model transformers bridge model↔norm data, while view transformers bridge norm↔view data
A TransformationFailedException thrown during reverseTransform() marks the field invalid instead of causing a 500 error
On submission, model transformers run before view transformers
transform() is the method invoked to process the user's submitted input

questions.exp: transform() is the model→view direction and reverseTransform() the view→model direction; model transformers sit between model and norm data while view transformers sit between norm and view data; and a TransformationFailedException surfaces as the field's invalid_message rather than a 500. On submit the order is view→norm→model, so view transformers run first, and submitted input goes through reverseTransform(), not transform().

questions.q: Which of the following statements are true about form events? (select all that apply)

a.t: The data available in PRE_SUBMIT is the raw view data (array/string), not your model object
Fields can only be added or removed in the PRE_* events, before submit binds them
FormEvents defines PRE_VALIDATE and POST_VALIDATE constants for hooking into validation
The submit sequence is SUBMIT → PRE_SUBMIT → POST_SUBMIT
POST_SET_DATA fires after the form has been submitted

questions.exp: PRE_SUBMIT exposes the raw submitted array/string before any transformation, and dynamic field changes are only possible in PRE_SET_DATA/PRE_SUBMIT before binding. There are no PRE_VALIDATE/POST_VALIDATE events — validation is itself a POST_SUBMIT listener — the submit order is PRE_SUBMIT → SUBMIT → POST_SUBMIT, and POST_SET_DATA belongs to the data-setting sequence, not submission.

questions.q: Which of the following statements are true about rendering forms in Twig? (select all that apply)

a.t: form_end() renders all remaining unrendered fields by default, including the hidden CSRF token
form_row() renders the label, widget, errors and help text for a field
form_errors(form) on the root form shows form-level errors; per-field errors require form_errors(form.field)
form_widget() renders the field's label together with its control
Passing render_rest: false to form_end() still outputs the CSRF token automatically

questions.exp: form_end() emits remaining fields (hidden ones and the CSRF _token) unless render_rest is disabled; form_row() bundles label + widget + errors + help; and error display is split between the root form and individual fields. form_widget() outputs only the control itself, and with render_rest: false you must render the CSRF field yourself.

questions.q: Which of the following statements are true about handling file uploads with Symfony forms? (select all that apply)

a.t: form_start() adds enctype="multipart/form-data" automatically, but only when the form contains a file field
getClientOriginalName() and getClientMimeType() return untrusted, client-supplied values
An unmapped FileType field is still validated, and you read it via $form->get('x')->getData()
FileType fields provide the upload as a plain string path to the temporary file
Setting maxSize on the File constraint raises PHP's upload_max_filesize ini limit

questions.exp: Multipart encoding is only set when a file field is present; the client-provided name and MIME type must never be trusted (use guessExtension()/getMimeType() instead); and unmapped fields are validated and fetched with ->get('x')->getData(). FileType yields an UploadedFile object (not a string path), and the File constraint is capped by — it can never override — PHP's upload_max_filesize/post_max_size limits.

questions.q: Which Cache-Control value does a Symfony Response emit when you set no caching information at all?
questions.exp: ResponseHeaderBag::computeCacheControlValue() defaults to "no-cache, private" when nothing is configured. It is safe (shared caches will not store it) but gives no caching benefit — you must opt in with public/max-age. It is not "no-store" (that forbids storage entirely) nor an empty header (Symfony always renders a value).

questions.q: Which caches honour the s-maxage directive?

a.t: Shared caches only (proxies and the reverse proxy)
None — it is a request-only directive

questions.exp: s-maxage sets freshness for shared caches. Browsers (private caches) ignore it and fall back to max-age / Expires. It is a response directive, not a request one, and every cache honouring it would be max-age, not s-maxage.

questions.q: You call $response->setPublic() and then $response->setPrivate(). What is emitted?
questions.exp: public and private are mutually exclusive; setPrivate() removes the public flag, so the later call wins. You can never emit "public, private", and no exception is thrown — the header bag simply keeps the last intent.

questions.q: What does the response header 'Vary: Accept-Language' instruct a cache to do?

a.t: Store a separate copy keyed by each distinct Accept-Language value
Reject requests that lack an Accept-Language header

questions.exp: Vary adds the named request header(s) to the cache key, so each variant is stored and served independently. It never rejects requests or translates content. Vary:* or Vary:Cookie effectively disables shared caching by exploding the key space.

questions.q: Given #[Cache(public: true, maxage: 3600, vary: ['Accept-Language', 'Accept-Encoding'])] on an action, which raw headers result?

a.t: Cache-Control: public, max-age=3600 and Vary: Accept-Language, Accept-Encoding
Cache-Control: public, s-maxage=3600 only (Vary is ignored by the attribute)
Only Vary is set; maxage on the attribute is dev-only

questions.exp: maxage maps to max-age (all caches), public opts into shared caching, and vary is emitted verbatim as a comma-separated Vary header. maxage is not s-maxage (that is the smaxage option), the response stays public not private, and the attribute fully supports vary.

questions.q: Why is Vary: Cookie on a shared-cacheable response almost always a mistake? (choose 2)

a.t: Each distinct cookie value becomes its own cache entry, so session cookies yield near-zero shared hits
It explodes the cache key space, defeating the purpose of a shared cache
It causes the reverse proxy to throw an InvalidArgumentException
It automatically strips the Set-Cookie header

questions.exp: Vary:Cookie adds the cookie value to the cache key; with per-user session cookies almost every request is unique, so the shared cache stores one entry per user and reuses nothing. It neither throws nor strips Set-Cookie. The right fix is to keep the shell public and isolate the per-user part with ESI.

questions.q: A reverse proxy (gateway cache) such as Symfony HttpCache or Varnish is a shared cache.
questions.exp: A reverse proxy / gateway cache serves many users, so it is a shared cache you own and deploy in front of the app — it therefore honours s-maxage. Only the browser is a private cache.

questions.q: A page is marked public with s-maxage=60 but still calls $request->getSession() and reads a cookie. What is the risk behind a CDN?

a.t: The CDN may store one user's personalized page and serve it to other users
Nothing — sessions automatically add Vary: Cookie
The response is silently downgraded to private by Symfony
The CDN refuses to cache any response that touched the session

questions.exp: A public response with a shared TTL is storable by any shared cache regardless of the session it read; the CDN can leak one user's page to another. Symfony does not auto-add Vary:Cookie nor auto-downgrade to private. The Symfony reverse proxy protects you only because its private_headers default includes Cookie — a generic CDN does not. Keep such pages private/uncached or pull the personal part via ESI.

questions.q: What does the Cache-Control directive 'no-cache' mean?

a.t: The response may be stored but must be revalidated before every reuse
The response must never be stored anywhere
The response is private to the browser

questions.exp: no-cache permits storage but forces revalidation on each reuse. The directive that forbids storing at all is no-store. It says nothing about freshness duration or private/shared scope.

questions.q: Besides setting s-maxage, what side effect does $response->setSharedMaxAge(600) have?

a.t: It also sets max-age=600 for the browser

questions.exp: A shared TTL is meaningless on a private response, so setSharedMaxAge() sets the public flag as well. It does not touch max-age (browsers still have no freshness), adds no must-revalidate, and sets no Expires.

questions.q: For a shared cache, which freshness source takes precedence?
questions.exp: Shared caches resolve freshness as s-maxage > max-age > Expires. A private cache starts at max-age since it ignores s-maxage. Expires is the lowest-priority HTTP/1.0 fallback, and header order is irrelevant.

questions.q: How do you emit a must-revalidate directive from a Response object?

a.t: It is added automatically by no-cache

questions.exp: There is no dedicated setter; Response::mustRevalidate() is a getter returning bool (calling it with an argument is a type error, and it never mutates state). Use setCache(['must_revalidate' => true]) or #[Cache(mustRevalidate: true)]. no-cache does not imply must-revalidate.

questions.q: Which #[Cache] options accept a relative date string like '1 hour' as well as an integer?

a.t: None — all durations must be integers

questions.exp: Those numeric-duration options accept an int (seconds) or a relative date string parsed via DateTimeImmutable. expires is a date string (an absolute moment), while public/private are booleans, not durations.

questions.q: What happens when you call $response->setCache(['s_maxage' => 300, 'foo' => true])?

a.t: An InvalidArgumentException is thrown because 'foo' is not an allowed key
s-maxage=300 is set and 'foo' is silently ignored
A custom header Foo: true is added
A deprecation is triggered but the call succeeds

questions.exp: setCache() validates its keys against a fixed whitelist (etag, last_modified, max_age, s_maxage, public, private, immutable, must_revalidate, no_cache, no_store, no_transform, proxy_revalidate, stale_while_revalidate, stale_if_error). An unknown key throws InvalidArgumentException immediately — nothing is set and no header is added. This is unlike setting a raw stray header string.

questions.q: A controller explicitly calls $response->setMaxAge(0) and the action also has #[Cache(maxage: 3600)]. Which wins, and why?

a.t: max-age=0 wins — CacheAttributeListener runs late on RESPONSE (prio -10) and does not override headers already set explicitly
max-age=3600 wins — the attribute always overrides controller code
An exception is thrown for the conflict
Both are emitted as max-age=0, max-age=3600

questions.exp: CacheAttributeListener applies expiration directives on KernelEvents::RESPONSE at priority -10 (late) but only fills in values the controller has not already set, so an explicit setMaxAge(0) stays. The attribute never blindly overrides, never throws for this, and Cache-Control cannot carry two max-age values.

questions.q: Cache-Control: no-cache tells caches never to store the response.
questions.exp: False. no-cache permits storing but requires revalidation before every reuse. The directive that forbids storage entirely is no-store — the single most common Cache-Control misconception.

questions.q: What does Cache-Control: stale-while-revalidate=30 let a cache do?

a.t: Serve the stale response for up to 30 s while it revalidates in the background
Extend the fresh lifetime by 30 s
Serve stale for 30 s only if the origin returns an error
Force revalidation every 30 s regardless of freshness

questions.exp: stale-while-revalidate lets a cache immediately answer with a stale copy while it refreshes asynchronously, hiding origin latency. Serving stale only on origin errors is stale-if-error; it does not extend freshness nor schedule periodic revalidation.

questions.q: When Response::isNotModified() returns true, what has it done to the response?

a.t: Set the status to 304 and removed the body and content headers
Nothing — it only returns a boolean
Sent the response to the client immediately

questions.exp: isNotModified() mutates the response in place (status 304, strips the body and content-related headers like Content-Type/Length) and returns a bool. It never throws or sends the response — you still return it yourself. Assuming it is pure (returns bool only) is the classic trap.

questions.q: A request carries both If-None-Match and If-Modified-Since. Which one decides the 304?

a.t: Both are ignored and a 200 is always returned

questions.exp: When an ETag is supplied it governs the comparison; Last-Modified alone only decides when no ETag is present. The two are not compared by magnitude, and a 200 is not forced.

questions.q: Using #[Cache(etag: 'post.getContent()')], what value is actually sent as the ETag?

a.t: The SHA-256 hash of the evaluated expression
The raw return value of getContent()
A weak ETag of the whole rendered body

questions.exp: CacheAttributeListener evaluates the expression on kernel.controller_arguments and SHA-256-hashes the result before using it as the ETag, so it can point at large content safely. The string is an expression (not a literal), and the raw value is never sent verbatim.

questions.q: How do you produce a weak ETag with the Response API?
questions.exp: The second boolean argument to setEtag() prefixes the value with W/. There is no setWeakEtag() method and no weak_etag setCache key; passing 'W/abc' yourself would double the prefix. Conditional GET uses weak comparison regardless of which form you emit.

questions.q: With #[Cache(lastModified: 'post.getUpdatedAt()')], when can a 304 be returned?

a.t: Before the controller body runs, during kernel.controller_arguments
Only after the controller has fully rendered the response

questions.exp: CacheAttributeListener evaluates the expression on CONTROLLER_ARGUMENTS (priority 10) and, if the request is up to date, replaces the controller so a 304 is returned without running the body. That is precisely the CPU/render saving the model exists for; it does not wait for RESPONSE or terminate.

questions.q: Consider: $response->setEtag(sha1($post->getContent())); if ($response->isNotModified($request)) { return $response; } return $this->render('post.html.twig', ['post' => $post], $response); — what is the benefit when If-None-Match matches?

a.t: A bodyless 304 is returned and the template is never rendered
The template is rendered, then discarded, and a 304 is sent
A 200 with the full body is always returned

questions.exp: isNotModified() sets 304 and strips the body when the ETag matches, and the early return short-circuits before render() runs — so no template work happens at all. If you called render() first you would lose that saving. It never sends twice; you return the response once.

questions.q: A developer sets $response->setLastModified(new \DateTimeImmutable()) but 304s never happen. Why?

a.t: The validator is the current time, so it never equals the client's If-Modified-Since value
setLastModified() requires a string, not a DateTimeImmutable
Last-Modified is ignored unless an ETag is also set
DateTimeImmutable is not supported; only DateTime works

questions.exp: Using now() as the validator means every response looks freshly modified, so If-Modified-Since can never match and you always get 200. Use the resource's real modification time (e.g. an entity's updatedAt). setLastModified() accepts any \\DateTimeInterface (immutable included), and Last-Modified works without an ETag.

questions.q: A 304 Not Modified response must be sent without a message body.
questions.exp: True. A 304 carries no message body — the client already holds the bytes. Symfony enforces this: isNotModified() strips the body and content headers when it sets the 304 status.

questions.q: Which conditional request header does a client send to revalidate an ETag?
questions.exp: ETags round-trip via If-None-Match for a conditional GET. If-Modified-Since pairs with Last-Modified (a date), while If-Match and If-Range serve write concurrency and range requests, not cache revalidation of a GET.

questions.q: Which directive does a browser ignore when managing its own private cache?
questions.exp: The browser is a private cache; it honours max-age/Expires, no-store and immutable, but ignores s-maxage, which targets shared caches only.

questions.q: A normal browser reload (not hard reload) typically sends which request directive?
questions.exp: A reload asks caches to revalidate via max-age=0 (a 304 is possible), whereas a hard reload sends no-cache to force a full refetch. no-store and only-if-cached are unrelated to reload behaviour. Confusing reload with hard reload is a common exam trap.

questions.q: What is the recommended header combination for a fingerprinted (content-hashed) asset?
questions.exp: A fingerprinted URL never changes content, so cache it long-term in every cache and skip revalidation with immutable. A new build yields a new URL. no-store/no-cache would defeat caching, and s-maxage alone would leave the browser uncached.

questions.q: Which request is eligible to be served from the browser cache?
questions.exp: Only safe methods (GET, HEAD) are cacheable; unsafe methods (POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE) always hit the origin and may invalidate cached entries for the target URL.

questions.q: To detect whether a client forced a revalidation, which reads the request's Cache-Control correctly?
questions.exp: HeaderBag exposes hasCacheControlDirective()/getCacheControlDirective() on request headers; the directive value is a string, so max-age is compared to '0'. There is no Request::isNoCache() or getCacheControl(), and get('Cache-Control') returns a plain string, not an object.

questions.q: What does the immutable directive buy for a fresh, fingerprinted asset in the browser?

a.t: The browser skips revalidation while the response is still fresh, even on a normal reload
The asset is cached forever regardless of max-age
Shared caches refuse to store it
It forces the connection to HTTPS

questions.exp: immutable tells the browser the body will not change during its freshness window, so even F5 (which normally sends max-age=0) will not revalidate. It does not extend caching beyond max-age, does not block shared caches, and has nothing to do with TLS.

questions.q: A user says 'I reloaded but still see the old CSS.' What is the cache-level cause and the real fix?

a.t: A normal reload only revalidates (max-age=0); a 304 keeps the old bytes. Fix by serving the CSS under a content-hashed URL
The browser cache is corrupt; the fix is to disable caching entirely
s-maxage is too high; lower it so the browser refreshes
The server must send no-store on every asset

questions.exp: A normal reload sends max-age=0, so the browser revalidates; an unchanged ETag/Last-Modified yields 304 and the stale bytes stay. A hard reload (no-cache) would refetch, but the durable fix is cache busting via a new (fingerprinted) URL. s-maxage is ignored by the browser, and no-store throws away all caching benefit.

questions.q: What does the request directive Cache-Control: only-if-cached ask a cache to do?

a.t: Return a cached copy if available, otherwise respond 504 without contacting the origin
Always revalidate the cached copy with the origin
Store the response only if it is cacheable
Accept a stale response up to a given age

questions.exp: only-if-cached forbids any origin request: the cache serves a stored entry or returns 504 (Gateway Timeout). Revalidating is no-cache/ max-age=0, and accepting stale up to N seconds is max-stale=N.

questions.q: What is Symfony\Component\HttpKernel\HttpCache\HttpCache?

a.t: A reverse-proxy kernel that wraps your application kernel
A Twig extension for cache tags
A compiler pass that caches the container

questions.exp: HttpCache implements HttpKernelInterface and TerminableInterface and wraps the real kernel, acting as an in-PHP shared gateway cache. It is not a PSR-6 pool, a Twig extension, or a compiler pass.

questions.q: By default, which request header makes the Symfony reverse proxy treat a request as private?
questions.exp: The private_headers option defaults to Authorization and Cookie; requests carrying them skip the shared cache, protecting authenticated responses. Accept/User-Agent/Referer have no such role by default.

questions.q: Which header lets you inspect whether the reverse proxy served a cache hit?
questions.exp: HttpCache writes a trace to the trace_header (default X-Symfony-Cache), e.g. "GET /: fresh", "miss", or "store". Age reports elapsed seconds, not hit/miss, and the other header names are invented.

questions.q: What is the simplest way to enable the reverse proxy in Symfony 8?
questions.exp: framework.http_cache: true wraps the kernel automatically. The alternative is wrapping it manually in public/index.php with the FrameworkBundle HttpCache subclass. There is no compiler pass or #[AsHttpCache] attribute, and Varnish is a separate external proxy.

questions.q: Which interfaces does HttpCache implement, and what is its constructor shape?

a.t: HttpKernelInterface and TerminableInterface; __construct(HttpKernelInterface $kernel, StoreInterface $store, ?SurrogateInterface $surrogate = null, array $options = [])

questions.exp: HttpCache is both an HttpKernelInterface (so it can handle requests) and TerminableInterface (so terminate() propagates). Its constructor takes the wrapped kernel, a StoreInterface, an optional SurrogateInterface (Esi/Ssi) and an options array. It is not a PSR-6 pool nor an event subscriber.

questions.q: A visitor sends Cache-Control: no-cache to force a reload through the Symfony reverse proxy. What happens by default?

a.t: It is ignored — allow_reload defaults to false, so the client cannot force a bypass
The proxy always refetches from the backend on no-cache
The proxy throws an error for unauthorized reload

questions.exp: allow_reload (client no-cache) and allow_revalidate (client max-age=0) both default to false, because letting any client force a bypass invites abuse. So a hard reload does not blow past the shared cache unless you opt in. Nothing is deleted and no error is raised.

questions.q: What does this config do? framework: { http_cache: { enabled: true, trace_header: X-Symfony-Cache, default_ttl: 0 } }

a.t: Wraps the kernel with HttpCache, sets the trace header name, and applies no default freshness when a response gives none
Forces a 0-second TTL on every response regardless of its headers
Only renames the trace header without enabling caching

questions.exp: enabled: true wraps the kernel; trace_header sets the debug header name; default_ttl is the TTL used ONLY when a response carries no freshness info — 0 means such responses are not cached by default, but responses that do set s-maxage/max-age are still cached normally. It does not override explicit freshness nor disable caching.

questions.q: A page sets s-maxage=60 but logged-in users never get a shared-cache hit from HttpCache. Why, and how do you still cache the anonymous view?

a.t: Their session Cookie is in private_headers, so the request is treated as private; move per-user parts into ESI so the shell stays anonymous/cacheable
s-maxage is too low; raising it will cache logged-in requests
HttpCache never caches HTML, only assets
The response must be marked private to be cached

questions.exp: Logged-in requests carry a session Cookie, which is in the default private_headers, so HttpCache treats them as private and neither serves from nor stores in the shared cache. Anonymous requests are cached. Raising s-maxage changes nothing, HttpCache caches any cacheable response, and private means no shared caching at all — instead isolate per-user bits with ESI fragments.

questions.q: The default HttpCache Store is a distributed store shared across servers out of the box.
questions.exp: False. The default Store (Symfony\\Component\\HttpKernel\\HttpCache\\Store) is a filesystem store keyed by URL + Vary, using digest and lock files. There is no built-in distributed/shared store — that is a reason to use Varnish or a CDN at scale.

questions.q: When does the render_esi Twig function actually emit an <esi:include> tag?

a.t: Only when a surrogate advertises ESI capability; otherwise it renders the fragment inline

questions.exp: The ESI renderer checks the Surrogate-Capability header. Without a surrogate it falls back to inline rendering so the same template works everywhere. It is not always-on, not dev-only, and not tied to content type.

questions.q: What is the primary benefit of ESI over full-page caching?

a.t: Each fragment can be cached with its own independent lifetime
It encrypts fragments end to end
It removes the need for any reverse proxy

questions.exp: ESI caches fragments as separate entries, so a long-lived shell can coexist with short-lived or per-user fragments on one page. It provides no encryption or compression, and it actually requires a surrogate (reverse proxy) to work.

questions.q: Which component processes <esi:include> tags?

a.t: The reverse proxy / surrogate (Symfony HttpCache or Varnish)
The PHP engine at render time

questions.exp: ESI is a surrogate feature; the gateway cache fetches each include as a sub-request and stitches the results, caching each on its own terms. Twig/PHP only emit the tag, and the browser never sees or resolves it.

questions.q: Why does Symfony sign _fragment URIs (UriSigner)?

a.t: To prevent attackers forging arbitrary fragment requests

questions.exp: Fragment URIs are signed with the application secret (via UriSigner) so only legitimately generated fragment calls are honoured by the kernel. Signing is a security measure, not compression, push, or ETag computation.

questions.q: What is the minimal config to make render_esi emit real ESI tags that get processed?

a.t: framework.esi: true AND a running surrogate (framework.http_cache: true or Varnish)
Nothing — ESI is on by default in Symfony 8

questions.exp: You need ESI enabled (framework.esi: true) AND a surrogate to advertise the capability and process the includes — the Symfony reverse proxy (framework.http_cache: true) or Varnish. Enabling only one of them means render_esi falls back to inline rendering; ESI is not on by default.

questions.q: Without ESI, adding a #[Cache(smaxage: 5)] fragment to an s-maxage=3600 page collapses the whole page to a 5-second TTL. Which mechanism causes this?

a.t: ResponseCacheStrategy reduces the master TTL to the minimum of all embedded (inline) fragment TTLs
The #[Cache] attribute overrides the parent controller's headers
The kernel discards s-maxage whenever a sub-request runs
Twig strips Cache-Control from embedded responses

questions.exp: When a fragment is rendered inline into the master response, ResponseCacheStrategy merges freshness by taking the MINIMUM TTL, so the 5-second fragment caps the page. ESI avoids this by caching the fragment as a separate entry, leaving the shell's long TTL intact. It is not an attribute override, a kernel discard, or Twig stripping headers.

questions.q: Which Twig call embeds a controller as an ESI fragment?
questions.exp: render_esi() wraps a controller() reference and delegates to the fragment handler, which emits <esi:include> when a surrogate is present (else inline). There is no esi(), include_esi(), or 'esi:' render prefix in Twig — the pair is render()/render_esi()/render_ssi().

questions.q: What is the near-identical alternative to ESI for servers like nginx or Varnish that speak Server Side Includes?

a.t: SSI, via render_ssi(), the Ssi surrogate and framework.ssi

questions.exp: SSI is the sibling of ESI: same mixed-freshness idea, exposed through render_ssi(), the Ssi surrogate class and framework.ssi. hinclude is a pure client-side AJAX approach (no caching goal), and the others are unrelated.

questions.q: You set framework.esi: true but run no reverse proxy. A page uses render_esi for a fragment. What happens?

a.t: The fragment renders inline on every request — no separate caching, no benefit, but the page still works
An exception is thrown because no surrogate is configured
The <esi:include> tag is sent raw to the browser

questions.exp: With no surrogate advertising ESI capability, render_esi silently falls back to inline rendering, so the fragment is embedded and re-rendered each request — correct output, but none of the per-fragment caching benefit. No exception is thrown and no raw <esi:include> reaches the browser (that only happens if a broken proxy fails to process it).

questions.q: Which of the following statements are true about cache types and Cache-Control? (select all that apply)

a.t: A Symfony response with no explicit caching headers defaults to Cache-Control: no-cache, private
s-maxage is honoured only by shared caches — the browser ignores it
setPublic() and setPrivate() are mutually exclusive: the last call wins and removes the other directive
Adding Vary: Cookie is the recommended way to make a shared cache efficient
max-age applies only to private (browser) caches

questions.exp: Symfony's conservative default is no-cache, private, so shared caching is strictly opt-in; s-maxage targets shared caches only; and you can never end up with both public and private on one response. Vary: Cookie makes a shared cache near-useless because nearly every user has a distinct key, and max-age applies to all caches — s-maxage is the shared-only directive.

questions.q: Which of the following statements are true about the expiration caching model? (select all that apply)

a.t: setSharedMaxAge() also marks the response public — no separate setPublic() call is needed
For a shared cache the freshness precedence is s-maxage > max-age > Expires
no-cache instructs caches to never store the response
Response provides a setMustRevalidate() setter for the must-revalidate directive
The #[Cache] attribute overrides caching headers you set explicitly in the controller

questions.exp: setSharedMaxAge() implies public since s-maxage only makes sense for shared caches, and shared caches resolve freshness as s-maxage > max-age > Expires. no-cache means "revalidate before reuse" (never-store is no-store), mustRevalidate() is only a getter — emit the directive via setCache(['must_revalidate' => true]) or #[Cache] — and the #[Cache] attribute is applied late without overriding explicit controller headers.

questions.q: Which of the following statements are true about the validation caching model? (select all that apply)

a.t: isNotModified() mutates the response into a 304, strips the body, and returns a bool — you must still return the response yourself
When both If-None-Match and If-Modified-Since are sent, the ETag comparison takes precedence
A 304 Not Modified response must not carry a message body
The expression in #[Cache(etag: ...)] is used verbatim as the ETag header value
isNotModified() sends the 304 response to the client itself

questions.exp: isNotModified() only mutates the Response (304 + stripped body/content headers) and reports a bool — returning it to the kernel is still your job — ETag beats Last-Modified when both conditional headers are present, and 304 responses are bodiless by definition (Symfony enforces it). The #[Cache] etag expression is SHA-256 hashed before becoming the header, and nothing is sent automatically by isNotModified().

questions.q: Which of the following statements are true about Edge Side Includes (ESI)? (select all that apply)

a.t: When no surrogate advertises ESI capability, render_esi() silently renders the fragment inline
Each ESI fragment can carry its own TTL, allowing mixed freshness on a single page
Fragment URIs are signed with the UriSigner to prevent forged _fragment requests
ESI include tags are processed by the browser when it receives the page
render_esi() only works with Varnish — Symfony's HttpCache cannot process ESI tags
