questions.exp: render_esi() degrades gracefully to inline rendering without a surrogate, ESI's whole point is per-fragment TTLs instead of the shortest fragment capping the page's TTL, and _fragment URIs are signed for security. Processing happens in the reverse proxy — either Symfony's own HttpCache (via the Esi surrogate) or Varnish — never in the browser.

questions.q: Which of the following statements are true about Symfony's HttpCache reverse proxy? (select all that apply)

a.t: HttpCache is a shared cache, so it prefers s-maxage over max-age when computing freshness
Requests carrying a Cookie or Authorization header are treated as private by default and bypass the shared cache
allow_reload and allow_revalidate are enabled by default so clients can force a cache bypass
The default HttpCache Store persists entries in Redis
HttpCache is activated purely by registering a service tag — it never wraps the kernel

questions.exp: As a shared/gateway cache HttpCache follows s-maxage first, and its private_headers default (Cookie, Authorization) keeps authenticated traffic out of the shared cache. allow_reload/allow_revalidate are off by default, the default Store writes to the filesystem, and HttpCache is a kernel wrapper (framework.http_cache: true or wrapping in public/index.php), implementing HttpKernelInterface and TerminableInterface.

questions.q: Which of the following statements are true about client-side (browser) caching? (select all that apply)

a.t: The browser's private cache ignores s-maxage; only max-age and Expires govern it
Cache-Control is also a request header — clients can send directives like no-cache, max-age=0 or only-if-cached
Only responses to safe methods are cached — a POST response is never served from the browser cache
A normal reload and a hard reload send identical cache directives to the server
The back/forward cache (bfcache) re-issues a full network request on back navigation

questions.exp: s-maxage is shared-cache-only so the browser ignores it, Cache-Control request directives let the client steer caches independently of response semantics, and browser caching is restricted to safe methods. A normal reload roughly means max-age=0 (revalidate) while a hard reload means no-cache (full refetch), and bfcache restores the page instantly from memory without a network round trip.

questions.q: Which component decides whether a request is served over HTTP/2? (choose one)

a.t: The web server / reverse proxy via ALPN negotiation

questions.exp: Protocol negotiation happens at the TLS/web-server layer (ALPN). PHP only observes the negotiated version via $request->getProtocolVersion().

questions.q: HTTP is best described as: (choose one)

a.t: A protocol that always requires TLS

questions.exp: HTTP is a stateless application-layer protocol; state is layered on with cookies/sessions, and TLS is optional (HTTPS).

questions.q: Which Request method returns the negotiated HTTP protocol version (e.g. HTTP/2)? (choose one)
questions.exp: getScheme() returns http/https; getProtocolVersion() returns the version string from SERVER_PROTOCOL.

questions.q: In a Symfony 8 app, HTTP/2 server push is the recommended way to preload sub-resources and 103 Early Hints should be avoided. True or false?
questions.exp: It is the reverse. HTTP/2 server push is effectively dead — browsers have dropped support — and the modern replacement for hinting sub-resources is the 103 Early Hints informational response. The claim also mislocates the decision: push/version selection is a web-server concern, not a PHP one.

questions.q: At the front controller, which call builds the Request object from PHP's superglobals? (choose one)
questions.exp: public/index.php calls Request::createFromGlobals(), which reads $_GET, $_POST, $_SERVER, $_COOKIE and $_FILES once into the typed bags. Request::create() builds a synthetic request from explicit arguments (used in tests/sub-requests), and there is no createFromRequest() factory for this purpose.

questions.q: An app sits behind a TLS-terminating reverse proxy that forwards X-Forwarded-Proto: https, yet $request->isSecure() returns false. What is the most likely cause? (choose one)

a.t: Trusted proxies were not declared, so Symfony ignores X-Forwarded-* headers
isSecure() only reads getScheme(), which is always http
isSecure() requires HTTP/2 to return true
PHP terminated TLS but did not tell Symfony

questions.exp: For security, Symfony trusts X-Forwarded-* (including -Proto) only from proxies registered via Request::setTrustedProxies() (or framework.trusted_proxies). Until then isSecure() reflects the direct connection (plain HTTP from the proxy) and returns false. PHP never terminates TLS; the edge does.

questions.q: On a keep-alive connection, why is the first request typically slower than the ones that follow it? (choose one)

a.t: It pays for DNS resolution plus the TCP and TLS handshakes before any HTTP byte flows; later requests reuse the warm connection
PHP compiles the controller only on the first request
The first request always uses HTTP/1.1 and later ones upgrade to HTTP/2
The server caches the response body after the first hit

questions.exp: The first exchange must complete DNS → TCP 3-way handshake → TLS handshake before the HTTP request is even sent. Subsequent requests on the same keep-alive (HTTP/1.1) or multiplexed (HTTP/2/3) connection skip that setup. The HTTP version is fixed for the life of the connection, and body caching is a separate concern.

questions.q: A POST must be redirected while preserving its method and body. Which status code? (choose one)
questions.exp: 307 (temporary) and 308 (permanent) preserve method and body; 301/302 may switch to GET, and 303 forces GET.

questions.q: The user is authenticated but lacks permission for a resource. Which status? (choose one)
questions.exp: 401 means unauthenticated (send WWW-Authenticate); 403 means authenticated but not authorized — re-authenticating will not help.

questions.q: Response::HTTP_UNPROCESSABLE_ENTITY corresponds to which numeric code? (choose one)
questions.exp: The constant keeps the RFC 4918 name 'Unprocessable Entity' but is code 422, the correct code for validation errors on a well-formed body.

questions.q: A rate limit is exceeded. Which status code and companion header are correct? (choose one)
questions.exp: 429 signals rate limiting; Retry-After advertises when the client may try again.

questions.q: You issue a 302 (instead of 303) after a successful POST. What is the real-world risk? (choose one)

a.t: Some clients may re-issue the request as POST, causing a duplicate submission
The browser will refuse the redirect entirely
The body is always stripped, so nothing can go wrong

questions.exp: 302's method-handling is historically ambiguous, so a client may repeat the POST on the redirect. 303 See Other is unambiguous: it forces a GET to the target, implementing Post/Redirect/Get and preventing resubmission on refresh. 307 would also preserve POST — the opposite of what you want here.

questions.q: Which status codes preserve the original request method and body when redirecting? (choose 2)
questions.exp: 307 (temporary) and 308 (permanent) are the method-and-body-preserving redirects. 302 may be downgraded to GET by clients and 303 always forces GET, so neither is safe when a non-GET method must survive the redirect.

questions.q: You call new Response('', Response::HTTP_CREATED) without a reason phrase. How does Symfony fill the reason phrase? (choose one)

a.t: setStatusCode() looks the code up in the public static Response::$statusTexts map
It queries the web server for the canonical phrase
It always leaves the reason phrase empty
It reads the phrase from the HTTP_* constant name

questions.exp: Response::$statusTexts is a public static array mapping each known code to its reason phrase; setStatusCode() consults it when no explicit text is supplied. An unknown code simply yields an empty phrase (still valid). The HTTP_* constants are plain integers and carry no text themselves.

questions.q: What happens when you call $response->setStatusCode(600)? (choose one)

a.t: It throws \InvalidArgumentException because the code is outside 100–599
It silently clamps the value to 599
It stores 600 with an empty reason phrase

questions.exp: setStatusCode() validates that the code is within the HTTP range 100–599 and throws \\InvalidArgumentException otherwise — a common gotcha when a code is computed dynamically. It neither clamps nor stores out-of-range values.

questions.q: 401 Unauthorized means the user is authenticated but lacks permission. True or false?
questions.exp: 401 actually means *not authenticated* — credentials are missing or invalid, and the server must send a WWW-Authenticate header. The 'authenticated but not allowed' case is 403 Forbidden, where re-authenticating will not help. The name 'Unauthorized' is a long-standing misnomer.

questions.q: Where does the Router place matched route parameters on the Request? (choose one)
questions.exp: The attributes bag (ParameterBag) holds framework/route data such as _route, _controller and path parameters — not the query string.

questions.q: Which class backs $request->query, $request->request and $request->cookies? (choose one)
questions.exp: query, request and cookies are InputBag (scalar-restricted); attributes is a plain ParameterBag, server is ServerBag, headers is HeaderBag.

questions.q: Which method reads the submitted body regardless of JSON vs form content type? (choose one)
questions.exp: getPayload() returns an InputBag from the parsed body (decoding JSON or reading form data); getContent() returns the raw unparsed body string.

questions.q: Which method reports the request format derived from the body's Content-Type header in Symfony 8? (choose one)
questions.exp: getContentType() was removed; the current method is getContentTypeFormat(), which maps the incoming Content-Type to a Symfony format (e.g. 'json'). getRequestFormat() reads the _format attribute, and getPreferredFormat() negotiates from the client's Accept header — different concerns entirely.

questions.q: Why does InputBag (query/request/cookies) reject reading an array where a scalar is expected? (choose one)

a.t: InputBag restricts values to scalars/arrays-of-scalars/null and throws BadRequestException on a type mismatch, hardening against malicious nested input
ParameterBag also throws in the same case
It silently casts the array to its first element

questions.exp: InputBag extends ParameterBag but narrows the contract to user-supplied data: get() accepts only scalars/null and raises a BadRequestException (HTTP 400) when handed an unexpected array, blocking parameter-pollution style attacks. A plain ParameterBag (used by attributes) imposes no such restriction. Use all('key') to intentionally read array values.

questions.q: Route parameters such as {id} are read from $request->query. True or false?
questions.exp: Route parameters live in $request->attributes (a ParameterBag), written by the Router — not in $request->query, which mirrors $_GET (the URL query string). Reading {id} via query returns null; use $request->attributes->get('id').

questions.q: A request handler crashes with a TypeError only when the X-Trace-Id header is absent, on the line strtoupper($request->headers->get('X-Trace-Id')). What is the cause and fix? (choose one)

a.t: HeaderBag::get() returns null for a missing key; guard with ?? or supply a default before calling a string function
get() throws when the header is missing; wrap it in try/catch
Headers are only readable via $_SERVER; the bag is empty
get() returns an empty array, breaking strtoupper()

questions.exp: HeaderBag::get(string $key, mixed $default = null) returns null when the key is absent — a normal lookup miss, not an error. Passing null to strtoupper() triggers the TypeError. Guard with $request->headers->get('X-Trace-Id') ?? '' or pass a default. Typed InputBag getters (getString etc.) coalesce to a zero value, but HeaderBag::get() is nullable.

questions.q: Which Response class streams an on-disk file and supports HTTP range requests? (choose one)
questions.exp: BinaryFileResponse streams a file without buffering it in memory and supports Range requests and X-Sendfile.

questions.q: What does Response::prepare() do? (choose one)

a.t: Makes the response compliant with the request (charset, body for HEAD/304, protocol version)
Sends the headers and body to the client
Validates that the status code is in range

questions.exp: prepare() normalises the response against the incoming Request; send() (sendHeaders + sendContent) actually transmits it.

questions.q: $response->headers is an instance of which class? (choose one)
questions.exp: ResponseHeaderBag extends HeaderBag and adds cookie management plus Cache-Control normalisation.

questions.q: You create new Response('hi') and set no cache headers. What Cache-Control does ResponseHeaderBag emit by default? (choose one)

a.t: no header is sent at all

questions.exp: When you set no cache directives, ResponseHeaderBag computes a sensible default of 'no-cache, private', so a bare response is never stored by shared caches. Calling setPublic()/setMaxAge()/setSharedMaxAge() changes this. It is not 'no-store', and a Cache-Control header is always present.

questions.q: In Symfony 8, where does the makeDisposition() helper for a Content-Disposition header live? (choose one)
questions.exp: makeDisposition() now lives on HeaderUtils; the old ResponseHeaderBag::makeDisposition() was removed. For file responses you can also use BinaryFileResponse::setContentDisposition(), which delegates to the same logic — but the static helper itself is on HeaderUtils.

questions.q: You must serve a 2 GB file for download without exhausting memory. Which approach is correct? (choose one)

a.t: Return a BinaryFileResponse (or StreamedResponse) so the bytes are streamed, not buffered
Base64-encode the file into a JsonResponse
Increase memory_limit and use a plain Response

questions.exp: new Response(file_get_contents(...)) loads the whole file into memory and will exhaust it. BinaryFileResponse streams a file already on disk (and adds Range and X-Sendfile support), while StreamedResponse streams generated output. Both keep memory flat regardless of size.

questions.q: Response::prepare() transmits the status line, headers and body to the client. True or false?
questions.exp: prepare() only normalises the response against the request (charset, Content-Type/Length, stripping the body for HEAD/204/304, aligning the protocol). Transmission is done by send(), which calls sendHeaders() then sendContent(). The kernel calls prepare() automatically before send().

questions.q: Which set contains only idempotent methods? (choose one)
questions.exp: GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent (repeating yields the same state); POST and PATCH are not.

questions.q: By default in Symfony 8, is the _method parameter honoured? (choose one)

a.t: No — http_method_override defaults to false and must be enabled

questions.exp: You must enable framework.http_method_override (or call Request::enableHttpMethodParameterOverride()); it applies to POST only.

questions.q: Which method is both safe and idempotent? (choose one)
questions.exp: GET reads with no side effects (safe) and repeats identically (idempotent); PUT is idempotent but not safe.

questions.q: After a successful method override, what does getRealMethod() return for a POST+_method=PUT request? (choose one)
questions.exp: getMethod() returns the overridden verb (PUT) while getRealMethod() returns the raw transport method (POST).

questions.q: A candidate claims PATCH is always idempotent like PUT. Why is this wrong? (choose one)

a.t: PATCH applies a partial change that may differ when repeated (e.g. an increment delta), so it is generally not idempotent
PATCH is safe, so idempotency is irrelevant
PATCH is never allowed to have a body
PATCH and PUT are identical in every respect

questions.exp: PUT replaces a resource wholesale, so sending the same body twice leaves the same state (idempotent). PATCH describes a partial modification; a delta such as 'add 1' applied twice yields a different result, so PATCH is generally not idempotent. Neither PATCH nor PUT is safe — both change state.

questions.q: Which configuration enables the _method override on POST forms? (choose one)
questions.exp: The key is framework.http_method_override (default false). It makes Symfony honour a _method field (or X-HTTP-Method-Override header) on POST requests, rewriting the method to PUT/PATCH/DELETE. The other keys do not exist.

questions.q: Which HTTP methods are considered safe? (choose 3)
questions.exp: Safe methods do not change server state: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS (and TRACE). POST is neither safe nor idempotent. All safe methods are idempotent, but the converse is false — PUT and DELETE are idempotent yet not safe.

questions.q: What are the exact conditions under which Symfony applies the method override? (choose one)

a.t: Only on a POST request, only when enabled, and only to the values PUT, PATCH or DELETE
On any request whenever a _method field is present
On GET and POST, to any value including GET

questions.exp: The override fires only when http_method_override is enabled, only on a POST transport request, and rewrites the method solely to PUT/PATCH/DELETE. Other transports are never rewritten, which is why getRealMethod() still reports POST.

questions.q: SameSite=None is only accepted by browsers when the cookie is also: (choose one)
questions.exp: SameSite=None requires the Secure attribute; otherwise browsers reject the cookie.

questions.q: Which attribute prevents JavaScript from reading a cookie? (choose one)
questions.exp: HttpOnly hides the cookie from document.cookie, mitigating XSS token theft.

questions.q: A cookie with neither Expires nor Max-Age is: (choose one)

a.t: a session cookie deleted when the browser closes

questions.exp: With no lifetime attribute a cookie is a session cookie, removed when the browser session ends.

questions.q: The Symfony Cookie object is immutable. What does Cookie::create('a')->withValue('b') require? (choose one)

a.t: Using the returned instance — with* returns a new Cookie
Nothing; it mutates the original in place
Passing the value to the constructor only

questions.exp: Cookie is immutable; every with* method returns a new instance, so the result must be captured or the change is lost.

questions.q: A cookie set with Path=/app and Domain=.example.com is not deleted by $response->headers->clearCookie('session'). Why? (choose one)

a.t: clearCookie() defaults to path '/' and no domain, so the expiry targets a different scope and the original survives
Cookies can only be deleted client-side via JavaScript
You must call setCookie() with an empty value instead

questions.exp: A browser keys cookies by name plus path plus domain. clearCookie() emits a past-dated Set-Cookie, but with its default path '/' and no domain it does not match the original (Path=/app, Domain=.example.com), so the browser expires a non-existent cookie and keeps the real one. Fix: clearCookie('session', '/app', '.example.com').

questions.q: Which framework configuration sets the session cookie's SameSite policy to Lax and hides it from JavaScript? (choose one)

a.t:
framework:
    session:
        cookie_samesite: lax
        cookie_httponly: true

framework:
    cookie:
        samesite: lax
        httponly: true

framework:
    session:
        samesite: lax
        httponly: true

questions.exp: Session cookie behaviour is configured under framework.session with the cookie_* keys: cookie_samesite (strict|lax|none), cookie_httponly, and cookie_secure (often 'auto'). Symfony's defaults are already HttpOnly: true and SameSite: lax. The other key shapes do not exist.

questions.q: What does the __Host- cookie name prefix force the browser to require? (choose one)

a.t: Secure, no Domain attribute, and Path=/ — the strictest scoping the browser enforces
A matching Domain attribute and Max-Age
Nothing; the prefix is purely cosmetic

questions.exp: A cookie named __Host-... is accepted only if it is Secure, has no Domain attribute (so it is locked to the exact host), and uses Path=/. This is the strongest same-origin scoping the browser guarantees, preventing subdomain injection. The related __Secure- prefix only requires the Secure flag.

questions.q: Symfony's session cookie defaults to HttpOnly: true and SameSite: lax. True or false?
questions.exp: Symfony ships secure session-cookie defaults: HttpOnly is true (JavaScript cannot read the session id) and SameSite is lax (mitigating most CSRF via cookies while still allowing top-level GET navigations). cookie_secure typically defaults to 'auto' (Secure when the request is HTTPS).

questions.q: Which caching model can avoid contacting the server entirely? (choose one)
questions.exp: While a copy is fresh (within max-age), the cache serves it with no request; validation always sends a conditional request.

questions.q: The s-maxage directive applies to: (choose one)
questions.exp: s-maxage is honoured only by shared caches and overrides max-age there.

questions.q: What does Response::isNotModified($request) do on a validator match? (choose one)

a.t: Returns true and turns the response into a bodyless 304
Only reads headers without changing the response

questions.exp: It compares the request's conditional headers and, on a match, sets the status to 304 and removes the body.

questions.q: Which statement correctly contrasts freshness and validation caching? (choose one)

a.t: Freshness (max-age) can serve with no request; validation (ETag/Last-Modified) always sends a conditional request that may return 304
Validation avoids the request while fresh; freshness always revalidates
Both always contact the server on every request
ETag is a freshness header and max-age is a validation header

questions.exp: Freshness uses Cache-Control: max-age/s-maxage (and Expires); while fresh the cache answers with zero round-trips. Validation uses ETag/If-None-Match and Last-Modified/If-Modified-Since — it always asks, but the server can reply 304 Not Modified with no body. The models are complementary, not interchangeable.

questions.q: Which attribute declaratively marks a controller's response public and cacheable for one hour in shared and private caches? (choose one)
questions.exp: Symfony\\Component\\HttpKernel\\Attribute\\Cache exposes public, maxage, smaxage, expires, etag and lastModified. #[Cache(public: true, maxage: 3600, smaxage: 3600)] sets Cache-Control: public, max-age=3600, s-maxage=3600. The other attributes do not exist.

questions.q: To cache a public page in a CDN for 10 minutes without letting the browser cache it long-term, which setter do you use? (choose one)

a.t: setSharedMaxAge(600) (plus setPublic()), which emits s-maxage honoured only by shared caches
setMaxAge(600), which targets shared caches only
setExpires(), which only affects the browser

questions.exp: setSharedMaxAge() writes s-maxage, obeyed only by shared caches (CDN/proxy) and it implies public. setMaxAge() targets any cache including the browser, so it is the wrong tool here. setPrivate() would forbid shared caching entirely.

questions.q: A default Symfony Response is storable by a shared cache (CDN/proxy) out of the box. True or false?
questions.exp: A default response carries Cache-Control: no-cache, private, so shared caches will not store it. You must opt in with setPublic()/setSharedMaxAge() (or #[Cache(public: true)]). Marking user-specific responses public would leak data across users.

questions.q: getPreferredLanguage(['en','de']) returns: (choose one)

a.t: the best of en/de for this client

questions.exp: With a whitelist it intersects the client's ordered languages with your supported list and returns the best match.

questions.q: What does getAcceptableContentTypes() return? (choose one)

a.t: MIME types ordered by client preference

questions.exp: It returns raw MIME types best-first; getPreferredFormat() returns Symfony format names.

questions.q: In an Accept header, what does q=0 mean for an option? (choose one)
questions.exp: A quality value of 0 explicitly marks that media type or language as unacceptable.

questions.q: Which response header ensures a shared cache stores one entry per representation? (choose one)
questions.exp: Vary lists the request headers that change the response, so caches key each variant separately.

questions.q: What is the key difference between getPreferredFormat() and getAcceptableContentTypes()? (choose one)

a.t: getPreferredFormat() returns a Symfony format name (e.g. 'json'); getAcceptableContentTypes() returns raw MIME types
They are aliases returning the same value
getPreferredFormat() returns MIME types; getAcceptableContentTypes() returns formats

questions.exp: getPreferredFormat() maps the client's Accept header to a short Symfony format (html, json, xml, csv...), best for a match expression. getAcceptableContentTypes() returns the raw MIME strings ordered by preference. Confusing format names with MIME types is a classic trap.

questions.q: Given AcceptHeader::fromString('text/html;q=0.9, application/json;q=1.0'), what does $accept->first()?->getQuality() return? (choose one)

a.t: 0.9 — items are returned in string order
null — first() only works on a single-value header
true — first() returns a boolean like has()

questions.exp: AcceptHeader parses and sorts items by quality (descending), so first() returns the AcceptHeaderItem for application/json (q=1.0) and getQuality() gives 1.0. The nullsafe operator guards the empty-header case where first() would return null.

questions.q: A proxy sometimes serves the JSON representation of /articles/7 to a browser expecting HTML. What is the most likely fix? (choose one)

a.t: Add Vary: Accept (via $response->setVary(['Accept'])) so the cache keys each representation separately
Set Cache-Control: private so the proxy never caches
Send the Accept header on the response
Switch to getRequestFormat() in the controller

questions.exp: Without Vary, a shared cache stores one entry for the URL and may replay the wrong representation. setVary(['Accept']) tells caches the response varies by the Accept header, so each variant is stored separately. Marking it private would just disable caching; Accept is a request header, not a response one.

questions.q: How does getRequestFormat() differ from getPreferredFormat()? (choose one)

a.t: getRequestFormat() returns the format from the _format attribute (e.g. a route suffix); getPreferredFormat() negotiates from the client's Accept header
They both read the Accept header
getRequestFormat() returns a MIME type, getPreferredFormat() a locale

questions.exp: getRequestFormat(?string $default = 'html') returns the format stored in the _format request attribute (set e.g. by a /path.{_format} route), while getPreferredFormat() computes the best format from the client's Accept header. Mixing the two is a common mistake.

questions.q: What is the safe way to pick a locale from the browser's Accept-Language? (choose one)
questions.exp: The whitelist form guarantees a supported locale; the others may return one you do not support.

questions.q: What sets the request locale when a route defines {_locale}? (choose one)
questions.exp: LocaleListener reads the _locale attribute and calls setLocale(); LocaleAwareListener then propagates it to LocaleAware services.

questions.q: What does framework.enabled_locales configure? (choose one)

a.t: The whitelist of locales the application accepts and generates

questions.exp: enabled_locales restricts valid locales (routing _locale, translation compilation); default_locale sets the fallback.

questions.q: Which configuration makes Symfony guess the request locale from Accept-Language automatically, bounded to en and fr, with no custom listener? (choose one)
questions.exp: set_locale_from_accept_language: true tells Symfony to set the request locale from Accept-Language when no _locale is present, constrained to enabled_locales. No custom kernel.request listener is needed. The other keys do not exist.

questions.q: The browser sends Accept-Language: es, en;q=0.8 and the app supports only ['en','fr']. What does getPreferredLanguage(['en','fr']) return? (choose one)

a.t: en — es is unsupported, so the next acceptable option in the whitelist (en, q=0.8) wins
es — the client's top choice always wins
fr — the first entry of the whitelist is always returned

questions.exp: getPreferredLanguage intersects the client's ordered languages with your whitelist. es is not supported, so it is skipped; en (q=0.8) is the best remaining acceptable option and is returned. With a whitelist it never returns an unsupported locale, and it falls back to the first list entry only if none match.

questions.q: After the request locale is set, how does it reach services like the Translator? (choose one)

a.t: LocaleAwareListener pushes it into every service implementing LocaleAwareInterface
Twig broadcasts it during template rendering
The Router injects it into the container parameters

questions.exp: LocaleListener sets the request locale; LocaleAwareListener then calls setLocale() on every service tagged/implementing Symfony\\Contracts\\Translation\\LocaleAwareInterface (e.g. the Translator). For a scoped switch you use LocaleSwitcher. Services do not read superglobals.

questions.q: Why is calling getPreferredLanguage() with no argument risky for locale detection? (choose one)

a.t: It returns the client's top language unfiltered, which may be a locale you do not support (e.g. pt-BR)
It always throws when Accept-Language is present
It ignores the Accept-Language header entirely
It returns an array instead of a string

questions.exp: Without a whitelist, getPreferredLanguage() returns the client's single highest-ranked language regardless of what your app supports, so you may get an unsupported locale and break translations/routing. Always pass your supported list so the result is bounded.

questions.q: When is an HttpClient request actually performed? (choose one)

a.t: Lazily, on first read of status/headers/content

questions.exp: request() returns a lazy ResponseInterface; the transfer completes on first access, which enables free concurrency.

questions.q: What does ResponseInterface::getContent() do on a 500 response by default? (choose one)
questions.exp: By default getContent()/toArray() throw on 3xx/4xx/5xx; pass false (or the throw option) to read the body without throwing. getStatusCode() never throws.

questions.q: Which type should you type-hint to autowire an HTTP client? (choose one)
questions.exp: Depend on the HttpClientInterface contract; the framework selects the concrete transport (curl or native).

questions.q: Which class lets you test API integration code without any network traffic? (choose one)
questions.exp: MockHttpClient returns canned MockResponse objects (or a callback) with no real HTTP requests.

questions.q: What does this test assert? $client = new MockHttpClient(new MockResponse('{"id":42}')); $data = $client->request('GET', 'https://api.test/x')->toArray(); (choose one)

a.t: $data === ['id' => 42], produced from the canned body with no network call
It performs a real GET to api.test and decodes the live body
It throws because MockResponse needs an explicit http_code

questions.exp: MockHttpClient serves the supplied MockResponse without any network; toArray() JSON-decodes the body to ['id' => 42]. MockResponse defaults to HTTP 200, so no exception is thrown, and toArray() returns an array, not the raw string.

questions.q: Which framework configuration defines a scoped client that prefixes a base URI and bearer token for one API? (choose one)

a.t:
framework:
    http_client:
        scoped_clients:
            github.client:
                base_uri: 'https://api.github.com/'
                auth_bearer: '%env(GITHUB_TOKEN)%'

questions.exp: Scoped clients are declared under framework.http_client.scoped_clients; each named entry (e.g. github.client) applies its base_uri, headers and auth only to matching URLs. The framework registers a service you autowire by variable name ($githubClient). The other shapes are invalid.

questions.q: Reading each response's getContent() inside the loop that fires the requests makes the batch slow. Why? (choose one)

a.t: Reading the body blocks until that transfer completes, so requests run sequentially instead of concurrently
getContent() opens a second connection per call
request() is synchronous, so the loop cannot help
toArray() must be used to enable concurrency

questions.exp: request() is lazy/async: firing them all first lets transfers overlap. But calling getContent() on a response forces that transfer to finish before the next request() runs, serialising the batch. Fire all requests first, then read (or iterate $client->stream($responses)) to keep concurrency.

questions.q: You call toArray() on a 204 No Content response (empty body). What happens? (choose one)

a.t: It throws a JsonException because an empty string is not valid JSON — guard by checking the status/empty body first
It returns null for the empty body

questions.exp: getContent() on an empty body returns '' (not null), but toArray() tries to JSON-decode that '' and throws JsonException. There is no silent null. Guard with a 204/empty check before decoding, e.g. if (204 === $r->getStatusCode() || '' === $r->getContent(false)) return [];.

questions.q: Which of the following statements are true about HTTP methods? (select all that apply)

a.t: PUT and DELETE are idempotent but not safe
GET and HEAD are the methods that are cacheable by default
The _method override only applies to POST requests and is disabled by default
POST is idempotent, so repeating it is always harmless
Request::getMethod() returns the raw method and ignores any method override

questions.exp: Safe methods are a subset of idempotent ones: PUT/DELETE change state but repeating them yields the same result, and only GET/HEAD are cacheable by default. The _method override requires http_method_override to be enabled and only fires on POST. POST (like PATCH) is neither safe nor idempotent, and getMethod() is the override-aware effective method — getRealMethod() returns the raw one.

questions.q: Which of the following statements are true about HTTP status codes? (select all that apply)

a.t: 307 and 308 redirects preserve the original request method and body
A 303 See Other redirect always forces the follow-up request to use GET
401 means the user is authenticated but lacks permission for the resource
422 Unprocessable Entity is meant for syntactically malformed requests

questions.exp: 307/308 are the method-preserving redirects (unlike 301/302, which user agents may rewrite to GET), and 303 explicitly forces GET — the classic POST/redirect/GET pattern. 401 means unauthenticated (403 is the not-authorized case), 422 targets well-formed but semantically invalid requests (malformed syntax is 400), and setStatusCode() throws for codes outside 100–599.

questions.q: Which of the following statements are true about the Symfony Request object and its parameter bags? (select all that apply)

a.t: Route parameters are stored in the attributes bag, not in query
query, request and cookies are InputBag instances, while attributes is a ParameterBag
getPayload() reads the request body regardless of its content type
getContentType() is the current method for reading the request's format

questions.exp: Route/application data lives in attributes (a ParameterBag), while the user-input bags query/request/cookies are scalar-only InputBag instances, and getPayload() is the content-type-agnostic body reader. $request->request maps to the $_POST body (query maps to $_GET), and getContentType() was removed in favour of getContentTypeFormat().

questions.q: Which of the following statements are true about the Symfony Response object? (select all that apply)

a.t: prepare() strips the body for HEAD requests and for 204/304 responses
A freshly created Response gets Cache-Control: no-cache, private by default
send() delegates to sendHeaders() and then sendContent()
$response->headers is a plain HeaderBag with no special cookie handling
makeDisposition() is a method on ResponseHeaderBag

questions.exp: prepare() normalises the response against the request — including removing the body for HEAD/204/304 — the conservative default Cache-Control is no-cache, private, and send() is sendHeaders() followed by sendContent(). $response->headers is actually a ResponseHeaderBag that manages cookies and normalises Cache-Control, and makeDisposition() lives on HeaderUtils.

questions.q: Which of the following statements are true about cookies in Symfony/HTTP? (select all that apply)

a.t: A cookie with SameSite=None must also be marked Secure, or browsers drop it
The Symfony Cookie object is immutable — each with*() call returns a new instance
Omitting both Expires and Max-Age produces a session cookie deleted when the browser closes
clearCookie() deletes the cookie no matter which path/domain it was set with
Symfony session cookies default to SameSite=Strict

questions.exp: SameSite=None is only valid together with Secure; the immutable Cookie API means forgetting to reassign a with*() result is a silent no-op; and without Expires/Max-Age the cookie only lives for the browser session. clearCookie() must match the original path/domain or the cookie survives, and Symfony's session cookie defaults are HttpOnly: true with SameSite=Lax, not Strict.

questions.q: Which of the following statements are true about HTTP content negotiation? (select all that apply)

a.t: A q=0 quality value in an Accept header means that representation is unacceptable
getPreferredLanguage($locales) returns the best match within the list you pass, not just the client's top language
getPreferredFormat() returns a raw MIME type string such as application/json
Shared caches parse the Accept header themselves, so a Vary header is unnecessary on negotiated responses
Response gzip compression should normally be implemented inside your PHP controllers

questions.exp: q=0 explicitly marks a representation as unacceptable rather than merely low priority, and getPreferredLanguage() intersects the client's preferences with the locale list you provide. getPreferredFormat() maps Accept to a Symfony format name (json, html) — raw MIME types come from getAcceptableContentTypes() — negotiated responses must send Vary or shared caches will mis-serve, and gzip is typically handled by the web server/proxy.

questions.q: Which of the following statements are true about the Symfony HttpClient component? (select all that apply)

a.t: request() is lazy/asynchronous — the transfer only completes when you first read the status, headers or content
getContent() and toArray() throw on 3xx–5xx responses by default, while getStatusCode() never throws
MockHttpClient with MockResponse lets you test HTTP interactions without any network access
You should type-hint the concrete CurlHttpClient class in your services for best performance
Options defined on a scoped client apply to every request the client makes, whatever the URL

questions.exp: Responses are lazy so firing several requests before reading gives free concurrency; the content readers throw HTTP exceptions by default (pass false / throw: false to read error bodies) while getStatusCode() is always safe; and MockHttpClient keeps tests offline. You should depend on the HttpClientInterface contract, not a concrete transport, and scoped-client options only apply to URLs matching the scope/base URI.

questions.q: What does MessageBusInterface::dispatch() return?
questions.exp: dispatch() always returns the (possibly stamped) Envelope. A handler's return value is available via $envelope->last(HandledStamp::class)->getResult(). It never returns the value directly because a routed (async) message is not handled in this process at all — only the Envelope exists yet.

questions.q: A message is routed to an async transport. During dispatch() in the web process, the handler…

a.t: does not run — SendMessageMiddleware serializes and sends it, stopping the bus
runs immediately and is also queued
runs only if a worker is currently active

questions.exp: When a message is routed to a transport, SendMessageMiddleware adds a SentStamp, sends the envelope and stops the pipeline; a worker handles it later. It is not handled twice, and a running worker is irrelevant to the dispatching process. NoHandlerForMessageException only occurs when no handler exists for a synchronously handled message.

questions.q: DelayStamp(5000) delays delivery by how long?
questions.exp: DelayStamp is expressed in milliseconds, so 5000 means 5 seconds. The classic trap is to read it as seconds; the retry strategy's initial delay is likewise in milliseconds.

questions.q: After a message exhausts its configured retries, where does it go?

a.t: Back to the front of the same queue forever

questions.exp: Once max_retries is reached the envelope is sent to the failure_transport, where messenger:failed:show/retry can inspect and requeue it. Without a failure transport the message would be lost, which is why configuring one is a best practice.

questions.q: Which middleware locates and invokes the handler(s), adding a HandledStamp?
questions.exp: HandleMessageMiddleware resolves handlers for the message type, calls them, and records each result in a HandledStamp. SendMessageMiddleware only routes/sends to transports (and may stop the bus before Handle runs).

questions.q: How do you make a failing handler skip retries and go straight to the failure transport?
questions.exp: UnrecoverableMessageHandlingException marks the failure as non-retryable, so the worker sends the message to the failure transport immediately. A handler's return value never influences retries, and there is no stopPropagation() on an Envelope.

questions.q: Which attribute marks a service as a message handler in Symfony 8?
questions.exp: Symfony\\Component\\Messenger\\Attribute\\AsMessageHandler registers an invokable service (or a specific method) as a handler for its typed message argument. The other names do not exist in the component.

questions.q: What is the purpose of DispatchAfterCurrentBusStamp?

a.t: Defer delivery of a message dispatched inside a handler until the current handling finishes successfully
Send the message to every bus in the application
Add a delay equal to the current bus latency
Retry the message on the next bus in a chain

questions.exp: It prevents dispatching side-effect messages (e.g. a confirmation email) before the surrounding work commits, so a failure/rollback cancels them. It has nothing to do with delays, multi-bus fan-out, or retries.

questions.q: True or False: routing a message to the sync:// transport skips the middleware pipeline.
questions.exp: False. sync:// still runs the full middleware stack (validation, transactions, handler discovery) — it simply handles the message immediately in the same process instead of enqueueing it. Treating sync:// as "no bus" is a common exam trap.

questions.q: A dispatched message throws NoHandlerForMessageException. What is the most likely cause?

a.t: The handler class is missing #[AsMessageHandler] (or its __invoke argument type does not match the message)
The failure transport is not configured

questions.exp: Handlers are discovered by autoconfiguration of the #[AsMessageHandler] attribute and matched by the typed argument of __invoke(). Missing the attribute (or a mismatched/imported type) means no handler is registered. Worker state, failure transport and message immutability are unrelated to handler resolution.

questions.q: Which statements about Messenger buses are correct? (choose 2)

a.t: The default bus service is messenger.bus.default
You can define multiple buses, each with its own ordered middleware list
All buses in an app must share a single global middleware list
The command/query/event bus split is enforced by the component

questions.exp: Messenger ships one default bus (messenger.bus.default) but supports many, each configured with its own middleware — so a command bus can wrap handlers in a transaction while an event bus does not. The command/query/ event convention is just that: a convention, not enforced by the code.

questions.q: During messenger:consume, which event is dispatched when a handler throws an exception?
questions.exp: The worker loop dispatches WorkerMessageReceivedEvent, then on success WorkerMessageHandledEvent (ack) or on exception WorkerMessageFailedEvent (reject/retry). WorkerRunningEvent fires between receives and WorkerStoppedEvent on shutdown — neither signals a handler failure.

questions.q: With retry_strategy delay: 1000 and multiplier: 2, what are the delays before the 1st, 2nd and 3rd retry?

a.t: 1000 ms, 2000 ms, 4000 ms (delay × multiplier per attempt)

questions.exp: MultiplierRetryStrategy multiplies the initial delay by the multiplier for each successive attempt: 1000, 1000×2=2000, 2000×2=4000 (capped by max_delay if set). It is exponential, not constant or linear, and starts at the configured delay, not delay×multiplier.

questions.q: An order handler dispatches an 'order confirmed' email message, but the email is sent even when the surrounding DB transaction rolls back. What fixes this?

a.t: Dispatch the email message with DispatchAfterCurrentBusStamp so it is delivered only after the current handler finishes successfully
Add a DelayStamp so the email is sent 5 seconds later
Throw UnrecoverableMessageHandlingException in the email handler
Route the email to the sync:// transport

questions.exp: DispatchAfterCurrentBusStamp defers the inner dispatch until the current message finishes handling successfully, so a rollback cancels the email. A delay only postpones sending, the unrecoverable exception affects the email's own retries, and sync routing would send it immediately during the transaction.

questions.q: $envelope->last(HandledStamp::class) returns null. Which situation explains this best?

a.t: The message was routed to an async transport, so it has not been handled in this process yet
The handler returned null, so no HandledStamp was created
dispatch() failed and returned null instead of an Envelope
HandledStamp only exists on the query bus

questions.exp: A handler that returns null still produces a HandledStamp (its result is null) — so last() returning null means no such stamp exists, i.e. the message was sent async and not handled here. dispatch() always returns an Envelope (never null), and HandledStamp is not query-bus-specific. This is why the nullsafe ?-> guards 'not handled here', distinct from 'handled, returned null'.

questions.q: Which serializer does a Messenger transport use by default to serialize the envelope?
questions.exp: By default transports use Transport\\Serialization\\PhpSerializer, which calls PHP's serialize(). The Symfony Serializer transport serializer is opt-in and recommended for cross-language/cross-app interop, but it is not the default.

questions.q: In a custom middleware, code placed AFTER the $stack->next()->handle($envelope, $stack) call runs…

a.t: On the way out — after the inner middleware and the handler have executed
Never — the call terminates the middleware
Before any other middleware in the stack
Only if the message was routed async

questions.exp: The middleware stack is a russian-doll chain: code before $stack->next()->handle() runs on the way in, and code after it runs on the way out once the rest of the pipeline (including the handler) has returned. This lets a middleware wrap the whole handling (e.g. open/commit a transaction).

questions.q: After a deploy, long-running workers keep executing the old code. Which approach fixes this for zero-downtime deploys?

a.t: Run messenger:stop-workers on deploy and let a supervisor restart workers, ideally combined with --time-limit/--memory-limit
Restart the database so workers reconnect with new code
Add a DelayStamp to every message
Increase max_retries so old workers eventually give up

questions.exp: Workers bootstrap the kernel once and keep it in memory, so new code is only picked up after a restart. messenger:stop-workers signals running workers to finish the current message and exit; a process manager then restarts them with the new code. --time-limit/--memory-limit make them recycle regularly. The other options don't reload the worker's code.

questions.q: How do you retrieve a synchronous handler's return value after MessageBusInterface::dispatch()?

a.t: The value is returned directly by dispatch()

questions.exp: dispatch() returns an Envelope. For a single sync handler you read its result via the HandledStamp: $envelope->last(HandledStamp::class)->getResult(). Use HandleTrait to unwrap it in a query bus. Envelope has no getResult() and the bus does not cache a "last result".

questions.q: What information does a RedeliveryStamp carry on a retried message?

a.t: The current retry count (and timing), so the retry strategy knows how many attempts have happened
The DSN of the failure transport
The fully-qualified class name of the handler that failed
A cryptographic signature of the payload

questions.exp: RedeliveryStamp records the retry count (and redelivery timestamp). The worker reads it to compare against max_retries and to compute the next delay via the retry strategy. Handler identity is on HandlerFailedStamp, not here.

questions.q: Inside a custom middleware, how do you pass the envelope on to the rest of the stack?
questions.exp: A MiddlewareInterface::handle() implementation calls $stack->next()->handle($envelope, $stack) to invoke the next middleware. Code before that call runs on the way in; code after it runs on the way out. Re-dispatching via the bus would restart the whole pipeline.

questions.q: Which built-in transport handles a message immediately in the same process, without a queue?
questions.exp: sync:// processes the message synchronously during dispatch. in-memory:// keeps messages in memory for tests, while doctrine/amqp/redis are real asynchronous transports consumed by a worker.

questions.q: In framework.messenger.routing, mapping App\Message\SmsNotification to 'async' means…

a.t: SendMessageMiddleware sends that message class to the 'async' transport instead of handling it in-process
The message is handled by every transport named async
It only affects messages dispatched from the CLI

questions.exp: routing maps a message class (or interface/parent) to one or more transport names. A routed message is serialized and sent to that transport rather than handled synchronously. A message with no routing entry is handled immediately.

questions.q: Which options let 'messenger:consume' stop a worker gracefully for zero-downtime deploys?

a.t: --limit (max messages) and --time-limit (max seconds), optionally with memory limits

questions.exp: A long-running worker is stopped cleanly with --limit / --time-limit (and --memory-limit). Combined with a process manager and messenger:stop-workers, this enables graceful restarts on deploy.

questions.q: Under a transport's retry_strategy, what does the 'multiplier' option control?

a.t: The factor by which the delay grows between successive retries (exponential backoff)
The number of parallel workers spawned
How many transports share the message
The maximum number of messages fetched per poll

questions.exp: retry_strategy defines max_retries, delay (initial, ms), multiplier (delay is multiplied by this each attempt) and max_delay to cap it, producing exponential backoff before the failure transport is used.

questions.q: Which transport is intended specifically for functional tests, asserting dispatched messages without a broker?

a.t: The in-memory transport (in-memory://), inspected via getSent()

questions.exp: in-memory:// keeps envelopes in memory instead of sending them, so a test can fetch the transport from the container and assert on getSent(). It is reset between tests via the messenger reset behaviour.

questions.q: Symfony\Contracts\Cache\CacheInterface::get() runs its callback…

a.t: only on a cache miss, then stores and returns the value
never — you must call save() yourself
only when the beta factor is INF

questions.exp: The callback computes the value on a miss; the result is persisted and returned. It also provides probabilistic early-expiration stampede protection. Running on every call would defeat caching, and unlike PSR-6 you do not call save() manually.

questions.q: Which statement about PSR-6 vs PSR-16 is correct?

a.t: PSR-6 (pools/items) supports deferred saves and, via TagAwareAdapter, tags; PSR-16 (SimpleCache) does not
PSR-16 supports tags but PSR-6 does not

questions.exp: PSR-16 SimpleCache is a thin key/value API with no items, deferred saves or tags. PSR-6 uses CacheItem objects and supports tags through a TagAwareAdapter as well as expiration.

questions.q: Cache stampede protection in Symfony Cache is implemented by…

a.t: probabilistic early expiration controlled by the $beta factor
a global mutex acquired on every key
duplicating the value across all adapters

questions.exp: As an item nears expiry, one request is probabilistically chosen to recompute early while others serve the cached value ($beta=INF forces it, 0 disables it). There is no per-key mutex.

questions.q: Which adapter keeps entries only for the current process (ideal for tests)?
questions.exp: ArrayAdapter stores items in memory for the current request/process only, so nothing persists across requests — useful for deterministic tests.

questions.q: Your CacheInterface::get() callback returns null on the first call. What happens on the next call before expiry?

a.t: null is returned as a cache hit; the callback is NOT run again
The callback runs again because null means a miss
A CacheException is thrown for storing null

questions.exp: null is a valid cached value: the contracts API stores whatever the callback returns and treats it as a hit until it expires. get() never uses null to mean 'miss' — that is exactly the PSR-6 footgun (getItem()->get() returning null for both absent and stored-null) that the callback API avoids. Caching 'no result' as null is fine, but it counts as a hit.

questions.q: A pool is declared with `tags: true` in cache.yaml. What does this enable?

a.t: Tagging items with $item->tag([...]) and evicting groups via invalidateTags([...])
Sharing the pool across all servers

questions.exp: `tags: true` wraps the pool in a TagAwareAdapter implementing TagAwareCacheInterface, so items can carry tags and invalidateTags() evicts all items with a given tag — invalidation by concern rather than by key. Calling $item->tag() on a non-tag-aware pool errors.

questions.q: True or False: passing $beta = INF to CacheInterface::get() forces the value to be recomputed immediately.
questions.exp: True. $beta = INF forces early expiration, so the callback runs and the value is refreshed on this call. $beta = 0 disables early expiration entirely; the default (null) picks a sensible probabilistic value.

questions.q: Using the raw PSR-6 API, how do you distinguish a stored null value from a missing key?

a.t: Check $item->isHit() — get() returns null for both cases

questions.exp: With PSR-6, CacheItemInterface::get() returns null both for an absent key and for a genuinely stored null, so you must call isHit() to tell them apart. The contracts callback API sidesteps this ambiguity; there is no hasKey() or miss exception.

questions.q: In serialize(), which stage runs first?

a.t: The normalizer (object to array), then the encoder (array to string)

questions.exp: serialize() normalizes the object to an array/scalars, then encodes that to a string. deserialize() reverses it: decode then denormalize.

questions.q: #[Groups(['read'])] on a property takes effect when…
questions.exp: Group filtering only applies when matching groups are passed in the context; otherwise the group attribute has no effect and all fields are (de)serialized.

questions.q: Which normalizer reads and writes private properties directly via reflection?
questions.exp: PropertyNormalizer accesses object properties directly (including private), whereas ObjectNormalizer uses accessors and the constructor, and GetSetMethodNormalizer uses only get/set methods. JsonEncoder is an encoder, not a normalizer.

questions.q: By default, what is the Serializer's circular reference limit before it throws?

a.t: 1 (unless a circular reference handler or #[MaxDepth] is set)

questions.exp: The default circular reference limit is 1; beyond it a CircularReferenceException is thrown unless a CIRCULAR_REFERENCE_HANDLER or MaxDepth is configured.

questions.q: A UserDto has #[Groups(['read'])] #[SerializedName('full_name')] on $name and #[Ignore] on $passwordHash. What is the JSON when serialized with context ['groups' => ['read']]?

a.t: {"full_name":"..."} plus any other read-group fields; passwordHash is omitted
All properties, because groups are ignored during serialization
An empty object, because #[Ignore] hides everything

questions.exp: With the read group in context, only read-group properties are emitted; $name is renamed to full_name by #[SerializedName], and #[Ignore] drops passwordHash entirely regardless of group. Groups are honoured only because they are passed in the context.

questions.q: What does the framework.serializer.default_context option skip_null_values: true do?

a.t: Omits properties whose value is null from the serialized output
Throws when a property is null
Converts null to an empty string
Only affects deserialization of missing keys

questions.exp: By default a null property is serialized as \"key\":null. Setting AbstractObjectNormalizer::SKIP_NULL_VALUES (skip_null_values) omits those keys from the payload. The classic bug is a consumer treating an absent key as an error rather than 'the value was null'.

questions.q: A private property with no getter is missing from the JSON produced by the default ObjectNormalizer. Why, and how do you fix it?

a.t: ObjectNormalizer uses accessors; add a getter (or use PropertyNormalizer, which reads properties directly)
The property must be marked #[Groups] to appear
You must call serialize() with the 'private' => true context
Private properties can never be serialized in Symfony 8

questions.exp: ObjectNormalizer reads via getters/issers/hassers and the constructor, so a private property without an accessor is invisible. Provide a getter or switch to PropertyNormalizer, which uses reflection to read properties directly. Groups filter fields but do not expose accessorless private properties.

questions.q: In which environment is .env.local NOT loaded?
questions.exp: .env.local is intentionally skipped in the test environment so tests run from committed defaults and stay reproducible.

questions.q: What does `composer dump-env prod` produce, and what is the effect?

a.t: .env.local.php — Symfony loads it directly and skips parsing .env* files
Nothing; it only validates env vars

questions.exp: The whole .env* cascade is compiled to a plain PHP array in .env.local.php, which Symfony loads directly, avoiding DotEnv parsing on each request.

questions.q: ExpressionLanguage::compile() returns what?

a.t: A string of PHP source code

questions.exp: compile() transpiles an expression to PHP source you can cache/reuse, while evaluate() interprets the expression and returns its value.

questions.q: A .env file sets DATABASE_URL, but a real OS environment variable DATABASE_URL is also exported. Which wins?

a.t: The real OS environment variable — DotEnv never overrides an existing real env var

questions.exp: Real OS environment variables always take precedence; the DotEnv cascade (.env → .env.local → .env.<env> → .env.<env>.local) only fills values not already set in the real environment. Later .env* files override earlier ones but never a real env var.

questions.q: What is the result of ExpressionLanguage::compile('1 + a', ['a'])?
questions.exp: compile() emits PHP source, turning the variable name a into $a: "(1 + $a)". It does not evaluate anything (so no undefined-variable error) — use evaluate('1 + a', ['a' => 5]) to get the value 6.

questions.q: Which class merges every config source and validates it against a bundle's Configuration tree?
questions.exp: Processor::processConfiguration() merges all sources and validates them against the tree returned by the Configuration class, applying defaults and constraints. TreeBuilder only defines the schema; FileLocator finds files.

questions.q: Which composer flag excludes require-dev packages when deploying to production?
questions.exp: `composer install --no-dev` skips require-dev packages (profiler, PHPUnit, etc.). Add --optimize-autoloader (or --classmap-authoritative) to build an optimised classmap and cut per-class filesystem stat calls.

questions.q: You changed a YAML config file and redeployed to prod, but the change has no effect. Why?

a.t: Prod loads the compiled container as-is and does not auto-detect config changes; you must clear/warm the cache on deploy
Prod re-reads YAML on every request, so a restart is needed
YAML config is ignored in prod; only PHP config works
APP_DEBUG must be 1 for config to reload

questions.exp: In prod the compiled container in var/cache/prod is loaded as-is with no freshness checks (those exist only in debug), so config changes require cache:clear + cache:warmup on deploy. Enabling APP_DEBUG in prod is unsafe and not the fix.

questions.q: Why set opcache.validate_timestamps=0 in production?

a.t: To skip per-request file-modification checks and always serve cached bytecode (reset opcache on deploy instead)
To force recompilation on every request

questions.exp: With immutable deploys, disabling timestamp validation maximises opcache hits by not stat-ing files each request. Because opcache then never notices new files, you must reset opcache (or the PHP process manager) on each deploy so the new bytecode is loaded.

questions.q: Which ordered command sequence is correct for a from-scratch prod deploy?

a.t: composer install --no-dev --optimize-autoloader → composer dump-env prod → cache:clear → cache:warmup → reset opcache
cache:warmup → composer install → dump-env prod → go live

questions.exp: You install prod deps first, compile the env cascade with dump-env prod, then clear and warm the cache so the first live request is fast, and finally reset opcache. Warming before installing, or shipping dev deps / APP_DEBUG=1, are wrong.

questions.q: What does `cache:clear` run, by default, in addition to removing stale cache?

a.t: The cache warmers (CacheWarmerInterface) that pre-build the container, routing, Twig cache and metadata

questions.exp: cache:clear removes stale cache and then runs the CacheWarmerInterface warmers to pre-build the container, routing matcher/generator, Twig template cache and validator/serializer metadata. cache:warmup warms without clearing. Migrations, workers and composer are separate steps.

questions.q: True or False: leaving APP_DEBUG=1 in production is acceptable as long as the profiler is disabled.
questions.exp: False. APP_DEBUG=1 enables verbose error pages that leak stack traces and internals, re-enables freshness checks and other overhead, and generally exposes the app. Production must run APP_DEBUG=0.

questions.q: Which Process constructor auto-escapes each argument?
questions.exp: The array form escapes each element automatically. fromShellCommandline() runs a raw shell string and does not escape, risking command injection if you interpolate untrusted input.

questions.q: What does Process::run() return?
questions.exp: run() blocks until completion and returns the exit code; use getOutput() for stdout and mustRun() to throw a ProcessFailedException on failure.

questions.q: What is the default Process timeout?
questions.exp: The default timeout is 60 seconds; pass null to setTimeout() to disable it. Exceeding it throws a ProcessTimedOutException.

questions.q: You build a command from user input using Process::fromShellCommandline('convert '.$userInput). What is the risk and the fix?

a.t: Command injection — use the array constructor new Process(['convert', $userInput]) so each argument is auto-escaped
None; fromShellCommandline escapes arguments for you
It only fails on Windows; add a shebang

questions.exp: fromShellCommandline runs the string through /bin/sh with no escaping, so untrusted input can inject shell metacharacters. The array constructor escapes each element as a single argument, eliminating the injection vector. This is unrelated to timeouts or platform.

questions.q: Which call runs a process and throws automatically on a non-zero exit code?

a.t: mustRun() — it throws ProcessFailedException on failure
run() — it throws ProcessFailedException on failure
start() — it throws immediately on failure
wait() — it converts the exit code into an exception

questions.exp: mustRun() behaves like run() but throws ProcessFailedException when the process exits non-zero. run() simply returns the integer exit code and you check isSuccessful() yourself; start()/wait() are for async execution.

questions.q: LockInterface::acquire() called with no argument is…

a.t: non-blocking — it returns false immediately if the lock is held
blocking — it waits until the lock is free
throwing an exception if the lock is held

questions.exp: acquire() defaults to non-blocking; pass true to block until the resource becomes available (store permitting). It returns a boolean false when held, it does not throw, so `if (!$lock->acquire()) { return; }` is the correct guard.

questions.q: Which lock store provides mutual exclusion across multiple servers?
questions.exp: Flock and Semaphore stores are local to one machine, and InMemoryStore is per-process (tests). Shared stores like Redis (or a database store) coordinate locks across servers.

questions.q: Why call refresh() during a long critical section?

a.t: To extend the lock's TTL so it is not considered expired mid-job
To release then reacquire the lock
To switch to a different store
To convert it to a shared lock

questions.exp: Locks have a TTL to avoid deadlocks after crashes. refresh() prolongs it so a still-working owner keeps exclusivity; without it another process could acquire the lock after the TTL, breaking mutual exclusion.

questions.q: Which is the correct guard to skip work another process is already doing?
questions.exp: Non-blocking acquire() returns false when the resource is held, so !$lock->acquire() is the idiomatic early-return guard. It does not return null and does not throw on contention (only blocking acquire(true) may throw LockConflictedException). Forgetting to check the boolean means entering the critical section unprotected.

questions.q: What is the default TTL of a lock created via LockFactory::createLock($resource)?

a.t: 300 seconds (5 minutes), with autoRelease on by default

questions.exp: createLock(string $resource, ?float $ttl = 300.0, bool $autoRelease = true) defaults to a 300 second TTL and releases the lock when the Lock object is destroyed. Long jobs should raise the TTL and call refresh() to avoid premature expiry.

questions.q: With Messenger routing configured for emails, MailerInterface::send() will…

a.t: dispatch a SendEmailMessage to be delivered by a worker
throw if no worker is running
render but not send the email

questions.exp: When SendEmailMessage is routed to a transport, send() enqueues it; a worker delivers it later, giving async sending plus retries. It does not throw if a worker is down — the message just waits in the queue.

questions.q: Which class renders Twig templates into an email body?
questions.exp: TemplatedEmail (in the Twig bridge) carries htmlTemplate()/textTemplate() and context(); a body renderer turns them into MIME parts before sending. Plain Email has no template support.

questions.q: How is an inline (embedded) image referenced from an email's HTML body?

a.t: Via a cid: reference produced by embed()/embedFromPath()
Only as an absolute external URL
As a base64 data: URI hand-written by the developer

questions.exp: embed()/embedFromPath() add a DataPart addressed with cid:, which the HTML body references (e.g. ).

questions.q: In the Mailer, how does the Envelope differ from the message headers?

a.t: The Envelope holds the actual sender/recipients used for the SMTP conversation; headers (From/To) render in the visible message
They are the same object with two names
The Envelope stores the HTML body; headers store attachments
The Envelope is only used for async delivery

questions.exp: Mailer's Envelope (sender + recipients) drives the transport's SMTP exchange, whereas the message headers (From, To, Subject) are what the recipient sees. They can legitimately differ (e.g. bounce address vs visible From), which is a common exam distinction.

questions.q: Which configuration makes emails send asynchronously via Messenger?

a.t: Route Symfony\Component\Mailer\Messenger\SendEmailMessage to a transport in messenger routing (and run a worker)

questions.exp: Async delivery comes from routing SendEmailMessage to a Messenger transport and consuming it with a worker. MAILER_DSN chooses the delivery transport (SMTP/API), not sync-vs-async, and there is no framework.mailer.async flag.

questions.q: What does public/index.php return under the Runtime component?

a.t: A callable that produces the application object (e.g. a Kernel)
Nothing — it echoes the output directly
The exit code as an int

questions.exp: index.php returns a callable; autoload_runtime.php resolves its arguments, invokes it, then a RunnerInterface handles/sends/terminates. It never calls handle() itself.

questions.q: Which environment variable selects the runtime class?
questions.exp: APP_RUNTIME (or composer.json extra.runtime.class) chooses the RuntimeInterface implementation; the default is SymfonyRuntime, which extends GenericRuntime.

questions.q: Which class does the default SymfonyRuntime extend?
questions.exp: SymfonyRuntime extends the framework-agnostic GenericRuntime, adding Symfony-aware resolvers/runners (inject Request, SymfonyStyle, console Input/Output; run a Kernel or console Application). It is not a kernel.

questions.q: How does the argument `array $context` in the index.php closure get populated?

a.t: The runtime's resolver autowires it from $_SERVER (env vars like APP_ENV/APP_DEBUG)
You must call getenv() yourself inside the closure
Symfony injects it from services.yaml parameters
It is always an empty array in Symfony 8

questions.exp: RuntimeInterface::getResolver() builds a resolver that inspects the callable's typed arguments and supplies them — array $context comes from $_SERVER (env), and it can also inject Request, InputInterface, etc. You therefore never read $_SERVER manually in the entry point.

questions.q: ClockInterface::now() returns what type?
questions.exp: now() returns an immutable DatePoint (a \\DateTimeImmutable subclass). Tests swap the NativeClock for a MockClock to freeze or advance time.

questions.q: Which clock lets tests freeze or advance time without a real delay?

a.t: MockClock — you set the time and its sleep() advances virtual time

questions.exp: MockClock is constructed with a fixed time and its sleep() advances time virtually (no real waiting), perfect for TTL/expiry tests. NativeClock is the real prod clock; MonotonicClock is for durations.

questions.q: Which clock is best for measuring elapsed durations and is immune to system clock changes?
questions.exp: MonotonicClock uses a high-resolution monotonic source unaffected by NTP or manual clock adjustments, so duration diffs stay accurate. Wall-clock NativeClock can jump; MockClock is for tests; DatePoint is a date type, not a clock.

questions.q: True or False: you should guard ClockInterface::now() with a nullsafe operator because it may return null with a frozen MockClock.
questions.exp: False. now() is typed : \\DateTimeImmutable and always returns a DatePoint, even with a frozen MockClock, so ?-> is unnecessary. The real bug is comparing a MockClock time against a live new \\DateTime() — read time from the clock on both sides.

questions.q: Which object does VarDumper's VarCloner produce before rendering?
questions.exp: The cloner captures the variable into an immutable, depth-limited Data object, which a CliDumper or HtmlDumper then renders — separating capture from output.

questions.q: What does dd() do that dump() does not?

a.t: It writes the dump to a log file
It serializes the value to JSON

questions.exp: dd() means 'dump and die': it dumps then calls exit, halting the script. dump() records the variable and lets execution continue (the dump is shown in the toolbar/collector).

questions.q: What unit does StopwatchEvent::getDuration() use, and when is the debug.stopwatch service available?

a.t: Milliseconds; the service exists only when debug/the profiler is enabled
Seconds; always available in every environment

questions.exp: getDuration() returns milliseconds, and the autowirable debug.stopwatch service is only registered in debug (dev/test). Injecting Stopwatch in prod therefore causes a wiring error.

questions.q: A service that autowires Symfony\Component\Stopwatch\Stopwatch works in dev but fails to boot in prod. Why?

a.t: The debug.stopwatch service exists only in debug mode, so the dependency is missing in prod
Stopwatch requires the profiler bundle in prod

questions.exp: Stopwatch's framework service is registered only when debug is enabled, so in prod there is nothing to inject and the container fails. Use it for ad-hoc dev profiling only; for prod metrics use real observability.

questions.q: An uncaught exception that does NOT implement HttpExceptionInterface produces which status code?
questions.exp: Only HttpExceptionInterface carries a custom status code; any other throwable defaults to HTTP 500 via the error controller.

questions.q: What does the ErrorHandler component do with a PHP warning or notice?

a.t: Converts it into a catchable \ErrorException via set_error_handler()
Writes it directly into the response body

questions.exp: ErrorHandler registers set_error_handler() to throw \\ErrorException for PHP errors (warnings, notices, fatals via a shutdown function), making them catchable. It does not turn them into HttpExceptions.

questions.q: Which serializable object represents a throwable for rendering and logging?
questions.exp: Throwables are normalised into a FlattenException — a serializable snapshot (class, message, status, trace) that error renderers (HTML/JSON/XML) turn into output and that is safe to log. HttpException is a throwable, not the snapshot.

questions.q: In a controller, which throw produces a 404 rendered by the framework error controller?

a.t: throw new NotFoundHttpException('...') — it implements HttpExceptionInterface with status 404
return new Response('', 404) is required; exceptions always give 500

questions.exp: NotFoundHttpException implements HttpExceptionInterface, so the error controller maps it to 404 via getStatusCode(). A plain \\RuntimeException or \\InvalidArgumentException does not carry a status and becomes 500. You do not need to build the Response manually.

questions.q: When does the Web Profiler collect data for a request?

a.t: On kernel.response, with late collectors running at kernel.terminate

questions.exp: Profiler::collect() runs on kernel.response, invoking each DataCollector; LateDataCollectorInterface::lateCollect() runs later at terminate for data not complete during the response.

questions.q: Which service tag registers a custom data collector (with a toolbar/panel)?

a.t: data_collector (with a `template` attribute for the panel)

questions.exp: The data_collector tag wires a DataCollectorInterface; supplying a `template` attribute makes its toolbar badge and panel appear. Autoconfigure applies the tag automatically for services implementing the interface.

questions.q: A custom collector storing a PDO connection in $this->data breaks profile storage. Why?

a.t: $this->data is serialized to storage (via VarDumper's cloner); a live connection/resource is not serializable
PDO is banned from all services

questions.exp: Profiles are persisted per token, so $this->data must be serializable — store scalar/array (VarDumper-clonable) data, not live resources like a PDO connection or an entity with a connection. Implement reset() for worker reuse.

questions.q: Your metric is only complete after the response is sent. Which interface should the collector implement?

a.t: DataCollectorInterface only; collect() runs after terminate

questions.exp: Normal collect() runs on kernel.response, too early for post-response data (final dumps, cache calls). LateDataCollectorInterface::lateCollect() runs later at terminate, when that data is complete.

questions.q: Which mechanism does Symfony 8 use for translation pluralization?

a.t: ICU MessageFormat, e.g. {count, plural, one {…} other {# …}}

questions.exp: ICU MessageFormat handles plural/select rules with locale-aware categories (one/few/many/other); the old pipe syntax is legacy.

questions.q: What does the translator return when a message id has no translation in the active locale or its fallbacks?

a.t: The message id itself (and it is logged in dev)

questions.exp: A missing translation returns the untranslated id, not an error or empty string, so the UI degrades gracefully. In dev the miss is logged so you can fix the catalogue.

questions.q: Which class returns the localized display name of a country code?
questions.exp: Countries::getName() reads the bundled ICU dataset and returns the name in the current/requested locale. Related classes are Languages, Locales, Currencies and Timezones. The other namespaces do not exist.

questions.q: What is the default translation domain, and what file naming applies ICU formatting?

a.t: Default domain is messages; the +intl-icu suffix (messages+intl-icu.<locale>.yaml) enables ICU formatting
Default domain is default; ICU is always applied to every file
Default domain is translations; ICU needs a .icu extension
There is no default domain; you must always pass one

questions.exp: When no domain is passed, trans() uses messages; validators and security are separate domains. ICU MessageFormat is applied to catalogues named with the +intl-icu suffix — forgetting it means ICU rules are not parsed.

questions.q: What makes Filesystem::dumpFile() safe against partial reads?

a.t: It writes to a temporary file then atomically renames it into place
It acquires an flock on the file
It buffers writes in memory forever

questions.exp: dumpFile() writes to a temp file and renames it, so a reader always sees either the old content or the complete new content, never a half-written file. appendToFile(), by contrast, is not atomic.

questions.q: Which Finder method defines the directories to search?
questions.exp: Finder::in() sets the search directories; without it the Finder throws. It yields Symfony SplFileInfo objects with helpers like getRelativePathname().

questions.q: How does Symfony\Component\Filesystem\Filesystem signal a failed operation (e.g. copy())?

a.t: It throws an IOExceptionInterface (it does not return false)
It returns false, like the native PHP functions
It triggers a PHP warning only
