questions.exp: Requirements are compiled into the route regex, so a non-matching value means the route is skipped — it is a matching concern, not validation. There is no 400 from routing itself.

questions.q: Which two declarations are exactly equivalent?
questions.exp: The inline <...> syntax is sugar for a matching entry in the requirements array. defaults is unrelated (it sets values, not patterns).

questions.q: What is the default regex applied to a placeholder that has no requirement?
questions.exp: Placeholders match any characters except the / separator by default; use .+ to span multiple segments.

questions.q: How do you allow a single parameter to capture several path segments (slashes)?
questions.exp: The default [^/]+ stops at a slash; requiring .+ lets the token match across path segments.

questions.q: You write requirements: {id: '^\d+$'} to constrain an id. What is wrong?

a.t: Requirement regexes are implicitly anchored; adding ^ and $ is wrong
You must also add anchors to the path
The regex must be double-quoted to work

questions.exp: RouteCompiler substitutes the placeholder with a named capture group over the whole token, so the requirement is already anchored. Adding ^/$ injects them inside the group and breaks matching. Likewise, avoid capturing groups — use (?:...) if grouping is needed.

questions.q: Two routes share the path shape /blog/{x}: blog_show has {slug} (default [^/]+) declared first, blog_paged has {page<\\d+>} declared second. Which route matches /blog/42?

a.t: blog_show — the first route matches /42 as a slug, shadowing the numeric route
blog_paged — the numeric requirement always wins
Both — the matcher runs both controllers

questions.exp: Matching is first-match-wins in declaration order. Because blog_show's {slug} defaults to [^/]+, it also matches 42, so it captures /blog/42 before the numeric route is ever tried. Declare the numeric route first to disambiguate.

questions.q: In YAML, which block restricts a {slug} placeholder to lowercase letters, digits and hyphens?
questions.exp: The YAML key is `requirements`, a map of placeholder name to regex. `defaults` sets values, and there are no `constraints`/`validation` keys in a route definition — validation is a separate component.

questions.q: How does RouteCompiler represent /blog/{page<\d+>} in the CompiledRoute regex?

a.t: As a named capture group, e.g. #^/blog/(?P<page>\d+)$#sD
As two separate regexes joined at runtime
It is not compiled; the requirement is checked in the controller

questions.exp: RouteCompiler::compile() extracts each {name} token and substitutes it with a named capture group using its requirement (or [^/]+ by default), producing a single anchored regex. Named groups are how the matcher maps captured values back to parameter names.

questions.q: Which placeholder is optional (matches /blog and /blog/N) with default 1 and digits only?
questions.exp: The inline order is {name<requirement>?default}: the requirement comes first, then ? and the default value.

questions.q: generateUrl('blog', ['page' => 1]) where page defaults to 1 produces?
questions.exp: The generator omits a trailing segment whose value equals its default, yielding the canonical shortest URL. This keeps generated URLs stable and avoids duplicate-content variants.

questions.q: In the path /{a}/{b}, which placeholder can be made optional?

a.t: b only, because it is the trailing placeholder

questions.exp: Only trailing placeholders can be optional; a gap in the middle cannot be located by the matcher. RouteCompiler emits nested optional groups from the tail, so an optional a with a required b is impossible.

questions.q: What default value does the placeholder {slug?} declare?
questions.exp: A bare ? with no value after it sets the default to null.

questions.q: Why is the inline placeholder {page?1<\d+>} wrong?

a.t: The requirement must precede the ?: it should be {page<\d+>?1}
You cannot combine a requirement and a default
The default must come before the placeholder name

questions.exp: The inline grammar is strictly {name<requirement>?default}. Putting ?1 before the <\\d+> requirement is a syntax error / misparse. Requirement and default can absolutely be combined — just in the right order.

questions.q: For path /archive/{year<\\d+>}/{month}, which YAML makes month optional and null when absent?
questions.exp: A trailing placeholder becomes optional by having a default; setting it to null in the defaults array is the array-form equivalent of the inline {month?}. '' is an empty string, not null, and there is no `optional` key.

questions.q: For /blog/{page<\d+>?1}, what does generateUrl('blog_list', ['page' => 3]) produce?
questions.exp: The segment is only omitted when the value equals the default (1). Since 3 differs, the generator emits the full /blog/3.

questions.q: What is the default reference type of UrlGeneratorInterface::generate() / generateUrl()?
questions.exp: By default the generator returns a root-relative path; ABSOLUTE_URL adds the scheme and host.

questions.q: generateUrl('blog_show', ['id' => 42, 'utm' => 'x']) produces what?
questions.exp: Parameters that are not route placeholders are appended as query string arguments.

questions.q: Which type defines the constants ABSOLUTE_URL, ABSOLUTE_PATH, NETWORK_PATH, RELATIVE_PATH?
questions.exp: The reference-type constants are declared on UrlGeneratorInterface.

questions.q: Why might a console command generate URLs like http://localhost/... ?

a.t: There is no request context, and framework.router.default_uri is not set
Because the route lacks a methods option

questions.exp: Outside a web request the generator falls back to the RequestContext defaults; configure router.default_uri for correct absolute URLs.

questions.q: Which Twig function outputs an absolute URL?
questions.exp: url() maps to ABSOLUTE_URL; path() maps to the default ABSOLUTE_PATH.

questions.q: What does UrlGeneratorInterface::NETWORK_PATH produce for blog_show id 42?
questions.exp: NETWORK_PATH emits a scheme-relative URL beginning with //, letting the browser reuse the current scheme. ABSOLUTE_URL includes the scheme, ABSOLUTE_PATH is root-relative, and RELATIVE_PATH gives something like ../42.

questions.q: Generating a URL for a route name that does not exist throws which exception?
questions.exp: generate() first looks up the route by name and throws RouteNotFoundException when it is missing. InvalidParameterException is thrown later, when a passed value fails a requirement. ResourceNotFoundException/MethodNotAllowedException belong to matching, not generation.

questions.q: A route declares schemes: ['https'], the current context is http, and you call generateUrl() with the default ABSOLUTE_PATH. What is returned?

a.t: An absolute https URL — generation is upgraded because a path cannot switch scheme

questions.exp: When the target route's scheme differs from the context, the generator must emit an absolute URL with the correct (https) scheme, overriding the requested ABSOLUTE_PATH — a path-only URL could not change scheme.

questions.q: What is framework.router.default_uri used for?

a.t: Supplying scheme/host/base-path to the RequestContext when there is no request (CLI, Messenger)
Rewriting all generated paths to that URI
Configuring the default HTTP method for routes

questions.exp: RequestContext is normally populated from the incoming Request. In CLI or a queue worker there is no request, so the generator uses default_uri to build correct absolute URLs instead of http://localhost.

questions.q: A route path is /blog/. A GET request to /blog results in?

a.t: A direct match with no redirect

questions.exp: RedirectableUrlMatcher issues a 301 to the canonical trailing-slash URL for safe (GET/HEAD) methods.

questions.q: A POST to /blog when the route is defined as /blog/ yields?
questions.exp: Redirecting a POST would alter the method, so the matcher returns 405 rather than a trailing-slash redirect. The auto-redirect is GET/HEAD only.

questions.q: Which RedirectController action redirects to another route by name?
questions.exp: redirectAction targets a route name and forwards parameters; urlRedirectAction targets a literal path or URL.

questions.q: In a RedirectController route config, permanent: true means which status code?
questions.exp: permanent toggles a 301; the default is a 302.

questions.q: You want /docs to redirect (302) to the literal path /docs/intro via RedirectController. Which controller + default do you use?
questions.exp: urlRedirectAction targets a literal path/URL via the `path` default; redirectAction targets a route name via the `route` default. Mixing the action with the wrong default key does not work.

questions.q: What status code does $this->redirectToRoute('blog_show', ['id' => $id]) return by default?
questions.exp: redirectToRoute() builds a RedirectResponse with a 302 by default; pass a third status argument (e.g. 301) to change it. Use controller-level redirects when the target depends on logic/data.

questions.q: For a RedirectController route, where is the 30x response actually produced?

a.t: In the controller — it returns a RedirectResponse like any normal action
In the matcher, which emits the redirect before any controller runs

questions.exp: A redirect route is an ordinary route whose _controller is RedirectController; the kernel runs it and it returns a RedirectResponse. The matcher only produces redirects itself in the special trailing-slash / scheme cases.

questions.q: Why is permanent: true (301) a poor choice for a temporary or A/B redirect?

a.t: Browsers cache 301s aggressively, so you cannot easily change the target later
301 is not a valid redirect status

questions.exp: A 301 tells clients the move is permanent, so browsers cache it hard and may not re-request the old URL. Use 302 (the default) while a target is still in flux.

questions.q: Which request attribute holds the name of the matched route?
questions.exp: The matcher injects _route (the matched name) and _route_params (the placeholder values) into the request attributes.

questions.q: What does the special _format parameter do when matched?

a.t: Sets the request format, influencing the response Content-Type
Only appears in the URL with no effect

questions.exp: RouterListener applies _format via Request::setRequestFormat(), driving content negotiation.

questions.q: What does #[Route(stateless: true)] primarily do?

a.t: Asserts the route must not use the session (warns in debug if it does)
Makes the route match any HTTP method

questions.exp: It flags accidental session usage during development, raising UnexpectedSessionUsageException in debug; important for cacheable and API endpoints. It is an assertion, not a hard prod block.

questions.q: Where does the special _fragment parameter take effect?
questions.exp: _fragment is honoured by the generator and ignored by the matcher (a URL fragment is never sent to the server).

questions.q: Which component copies the matcher's output parameters into $request->attributes?

a.t: The UrlMatcher itself writes directly to the Request

questions.exp: UrlMatcher::match() returns an array (route defaults + captured placeholders + _route/_route_params); RouterListener, a kernel.request subscriber, copies each entry into the request attribute bag. ControllerResolver and ArgumentResolver then consume _controller and the args later.

questions.q: How do you read the matched route name inside a controller or listener?
questions.exp: _route (and _route_params) are read-only outputs stored in the request attribute bag by RouterListener. There is no Request::getRoute() helper, and it is not a query parameter.

questions.q: For path /api/items.{_format} serving only JSON or XML defaulting to JSON, which config is correct?
questions.exp: _format is a normal special parameter: a default gives it a value when the extension is absent, and a requirement whitelists the allowed formats. Without the requirement, items.exe would match. Formats are never HTTP methods.

questions.q: Should you set _route or _route_params yourself in a route's defaults?

a.t: No — they are read-only outputs injected by the matcher; you only read them
Yes — _route sets the route name used for generation
Only _route_params may be set; _route is reserved

questions.exp: _route and _route_params are outputs the matcher writes; setting them in defaults is meaningless and would be overwritten. They exist for logging, subscribers and debugging.

questions.q: What is the default regex applied to a host placeholder like {sub}?
questions.exp: Host labels are separated by dots, so a host token matches any non-dot characters by default (contrast with the path default [^/]+).

questions.q: During matching, when is the host constraint checked?
questions.exp: matchCollection() tests the compiled host regex against RequestContext::getHost() first; only if it matches does it test the path regex.

questions.q: Generating a URL for a route bound to a different host produces?

a.t: A URL on the current host

questions.exp: A path-only URL cannot switch host, so the generator upgrades the reference type automatically.

questions.q: Which config captures a subdomain {tenant} (lowercase alphanumerics/hyphen) on example.com, defaulting to www?
questions.exp: Host placeholders obey the same requirements/defaults rules as path ones; you set the constraint and a base default on the route's `host`. There is no `subdomain`/`domain` key, and the host belongs in `host`, not `path`.

questions.q: How is the host constraint stored on a CompiledRoute?

a.t: As a second, separate regex (getHostRegex) and its own token list
Merged into the single path regex
As a plain string compared with ===
It is not compiled; the host is checked at runtime by DNS

questions.exp: RouteCompiler compiles `host` into its own regex and token list on the CompiledRoute, kept separate from the path regex, so matchCollection() can test host and path independently at negligible cost.

questions.q: Why should host constraints be written in lowercase?

a.t: The context host is normalized to lowercase, so an uppercase regex will not match
Uppercase hosts are rejected with a 400
Host matching is always case-insensitive, so it does not matter

questions.exp: RequestContext lowercases the incoming host. A case-sensitive constraint like Admin.Example.com would then fail against admin.example.com. Write host patterns in lowercase.

questions.q: For host '{tenant}.example.com', what does generateUrl('tenant_home', ['tenant' => 'acme'], UrlGeneratorInterface::ABSOLUTE_URL) produce (current host example.com)?
questions.exp: The tenant placeholder fills the host label, and because the requested host differs from the current one an absolute URL on acme.example.com is produced. tenant is a host placeholder, so it is not appended as a query arg.

questions.q: How do you apply one host to a whole imported controller directory?

a.t: Set host: on the YAML resource import (alongside prefix/name_prefix)
It is not possible; host must be per-route

questions.exp: Import-level options — host, prefix, name_prefix — cascade to every route in the imported resource, so you avoid repeating host: on each action.

questions.q: A route's condition expression evaluates to false. What is the result?

a.t: 404 — the route is simply not matched

questions.exp: A false condition means the route does not match; matching continues and may end in a 404. It is not authorization, so it never produces a 403.

questions.q: Which variables/functions are available inside a routing condition expression?
questions.exp: The routing expression provider exposes the RequestContext (context), the Request (request), and the env()/service() functions.

questions.q: Do conditions affect URL generation with generateUrl()?

a.t: Yes, generation fails if the condition is false

questions.exp: There is no request to evaluate during generation, so conditions never influence generated URLs.

questions.q: To reference service('x') in a routing condition, service x must…
questions.exp: Only services tagged routing.condition_service are exposed to the routing expression language. Visibility/base class are irrelevant.

questions.q: Which condition matches only when the request query string contains a 'preview' key?
questions.exp: Inside a condition, `request` is the HttpFoundation Request, so request.query.has('preview') is the idiomatic check. `query` alone is not a variable, and there is no bare has() function.

questions.q: How are route conditions executed at request time?

a.t: As pre-compiled PHP closures baked into the dumped matcher (not runtime eval)
Via eval() of the expression string on each request
They are evaluated once at boot and cached as booleans

questions.exp: The framework compiles all conditions ahead of time through ExpressionLanguage and the routing ExpressionLanguageProvider, so the dumped matcher contains compiled closures. UrlMatcher::handleRouteRequirements() runs them after host/path match — no per-request eval, and they cannot be reduced to a constant because they depend on the live request.

questions.q: Why is a routing condition a poor substitute for a security voter/authorization check?

a.t: A failed condition is a 404 (route not matched), not a 403, and cannot show a login page
Conditions cannot read the request at all
Conditions run after the controller, too late to deny access

questions.exp: Conditions are a matching filter: failing one just hides the route (404), so there is no 403 and no way to trigger authentication. Use Security voters for authorization.

questions.q: You tag a service #[AsRoutingConditionService(alias: 'feature_checker')]. How do you call its isEnabled() method in a condition?
questions.exp: The alias becomes the argument to the service() function; you then call methods on the returned object and can pass request. There is no bare identifier, @ syntax or container variable in routing expressions.

questions.q: A route allows only GET. A POST to that same path returns?

a.t: 405 Method Not Allowed (with an Allow header)

questions.exp: When the path matches but the method is not allowed, the matcher throws MethodNotAllowedException, producing a 405 with an Allow header. It is not a 404 — the path did match.

questions.q: A route declared with methods: ['GET'] also matches which verb automatically?
questions.exp: HttpKernel handles HEAD as a bodyless GET, so GET routes also match HEAD. Declaring HEAD explicitly is redundant.

questions.q: An http request hits a route restricted with schemes: ['https']. What happens?

a.t: It is redirected to the https URL

questions.exp: The RedirectableUrlMatcher redirects a scheme mismatch to the correct scheme rather than rejecting it — contrast with a wrong method, which is a 405.

questions.q: For a form's _method field to influence which route matches, you must…

a.t: Do nothing — it is enabled by default

questions.exp: Method override is opt-in; once enabled, getMethod() returns the overridden verb that the matcher uses. It is not on by default.

questions.q: A DELETE-only route /tags/{id} gets a GET. What does the 405 response's Allow header contain?

a.t: DELETE — the verbs permitted by the matched path
GET — the verb that was requested

questions.exp: On a 405 the matcher collects the allowed methods of the matching path and returns them in the Allow header (DELETE here), telling the client which verbs are valid.

questions.q: How do you make one route accept both PUT and PATCH?
questions.exp: methods accepts a list of verbs; any listed verb matches. A single route can serve several verbs — no pipe syntax or extra flags needed.

questions.q: Are HTTP method names in the methods option case-sensitive?

a.t: No — matching is case-insensitive, though uppercase is conventional

questions.exp: Method matching is case-insensitive, but you should write verbs in uppercase by convention for readability and debug:router clarity.

questions.syl: Routing → User's locale guessing & localized routes
questions.q: Does Symfony guess the user's locale from the Accept-Language header by default?

a.t: No — you must enable set_locale_from_accept_language or do it manually

questions.exp: Locale precedence is a matched _locale, then the sticky session locale, then default_locale; Accept-Language is opt-in. To honour it, read Request::getPreferredLanguage($available) or enable the option.

questions.syl: Routing → User's locale guessing & localized routes
questions.q: A #[Route(path: ['en' => '/about', 'fr' => '/a-propos'])] produces what?

a.t: One route per locale, each carrying its _locale default
A single route matching both paths
A redirect between the two paths
An error — arrays are not allowed

questions.exp: A localized path array expands at load time into one Route per locale, each with defaults['_locale'] set and a _locale requirement.

questions.syl: Routing → User's locale guessing & localized routes
questions.q: Matching a route that sets the _locale parameter causes what?

a.t: Request::setLocale() is called via the LocaleListener
Nothing until you read the value

questions.exp: _locale is a special parameter applied by the LocaleListener on kernel.request, which calls Request::setLocale().

questions.syl: Routing → User's locale guessing & localized routes
questions.q: How do you generate the French variant of a localized route named app_about?
questions.exp: Pass the _locale special parameter to select a localized variant; omit it to reuse the current request locale.

questions.syl: Routing → User's locale guessing & localized routes
questions.q: Which config exposes /{_locale}/blog restricted to en, fr or de and defaulting to en?
questions.exp: The _locale placeholder is constrained by a requirement whitelist and given a default. Omitting the requirement lets any /xx/blog match; there is no top-level locale: list on a route. (Inline requirement is valid too, but a default is still needed for it to be optional at the root.)

questions.syl: Routing → User's locale guessing & localized routes
questions.q: What goes wrong if /{_locale}/blog has no _locale requirement?

a.t: Any segment matches _locale, so /xx/blog or /foo/blog wrongly match
Symfony injects a default en|fr requirement automatically

questions.exp: Without a requirement, _locale keeps the default [^/]+ and matches any label, so invalid locales like /xx/blog match. Always whitelist _locale with a requirement.

questions.syl: Routing → User's locale guessing & localized routes
questions.q: Which two listeners cooperate to apply and propagate the request locale?

a.t: LocaleListener (sets Request locale from _locale) and LocaleAwareListener (propagates it to locale-aware services)

questions.exp: LocaleListener reads _locale on kernel.request and calls setLocale(); LocaleAwareListener then propagates the locale to locale-aware services such as the translator. RouterListener only copies matcher output into attributes.

questions.syl: Routing → User's locale guessing & localized routes
questions.q: For route app_help at /{_locale}/help, what does generateUrl('app_help', ['_locale' => 'es']) produce?
questions.exp: _locale is a real placeholder in the path, so it fills the {_locale} segment giving /es/help — not a query string, and not the default en.

questions.q: Which console command simulates matching a specific URL and explains rejections?
questions.exp: router:match runs a TraceableUrlMatcher against the given path and reports which routes matched or why they failed.

questions.q: After changing route definitions in the prod environment you must…
questions.exp: The compiled router (url_matching_routes.php / url_generating_routes.php) is built at cache warmup and is not auto-refreshed in prod.

questions.q: Which files hold the compiled router in the cache directory?
questions.exp: The CompiledUrlMatcherDumper and CompiledUrlGeneratorDumper write these two files that the Router loads at runtime.

questions.q: router:match /blog/hello reports no match, but the page works for real GET requests. What is the likely cause?

a.t: You omitted --method=GET, so the default context did not reproduce the real request
The route is missing from url_generating_routes.php

questions.exp: router:match builds a RequestContext from the options you pass; without --method/--host/--scheme it may not reproduce the real request and can report a no-match (or a method rejection) that does not happen in production. Pass the exact conditions.

questions.q: In debug:router output, a route shows Scheme=ANY and Host=ANY. What does that mean?

a.t: The route has no scheme/host constraint, so it matches any scheme and host
The route only matches literally the host 'ANY'
The route requires both HTTP and HTTPS simultaneously

questions.exp: ANY is the compiled view's way of saying no constraint was set for that column; such a route matches regardless of scheme/host. It is not a literal value.

questions.q: Why do new routes appear immediately in dev but not in prod?

a.t: In dev the router tracks route files as cache resources and rebuilds when they change; prod does not
Dev disables the compiled router entirely
Prod reads routes from the database
Dev and prod share the same cache, so it is a timing issue

questions.exp: In dev, route files are registered as cache resources so Symfony detects changes and rebuilds the compiled matcher/generator automatically. In prod the cache is warmed once (cache:clear/warmup) and not auto-refreshed.

questions.q: Which command rebuilds the compiled router after editing routes in prod?
questions.exp: cache:clear (or cache:warmup) in the prod env runs the RouterCacheWarmer and regenerates url_matching_routes.php / url_generating_routes.php. The other commands do not exist.

questions.q: Where in the web profiler can you see the matched _route for the current request?

a.t: The Routing panel (linked from the web debug toolbar)
It is never shown in the profiler

questions.exp: The profiler's Routing panel shows the matched _route and its parameters for the current request, so you do not need dump() calls to find them.

questions.q: Which of the following statements are true about route parameter requirements? (select all that apply)

a.t: The inline syntax {id<\d+>} is exactly equivalent to requirements: {id: '\d+'}
A URL that violates a requirement simply fails to match that route (typically ending in a 404), never a 400 from routing
A placeholder without a requirement matches [^/]+ by default, so it cannot span path segments
Requirement regexes must be anchored manually with ^ and $ to work
A failing requirement makes the router return a 400 Bad Request

questions.exp: Inline <...> is syntactic sugar for a requirements entry, and because the requirement is compiled into the route regex a violating value just does not match — matching moves on and usually ends in a 404. The default token pattern is [^/]+ (use .+ to cross slashes). Requirements are implicitly anchored, so adding ^/$ is wrong, and routing never produces a 400 for a bad parameter.

questions.q: Which of the following statements are true about HTTP method matching in Symfony routing? (select all that apply)

a.t: A request whose path matches but whose verb is not allowed gets a 405 Method Not Allowed with an Allow header
A route declaring methods: ['GET'] also matches HEAD requests automatically
A scheme mismatch on an https-only route also returns a 405
A form's _method field overrides the HTTP method for routing by default, with no configuration

questions.exp: When host and path match but the verb does not, the matcher throws MethodNotAllowedException, surfaced as a 405 listing the allowed verbs, and GET routes match HEAD because HttpKernel serves HEAD as a bodyless GET. A scheme mismatch is handled differently — the redirectable matcher redirects to the correct scheme — and the _method override only works after calling Request::enableHttpMethodParameterOverride().

questions.q: Which of the following statements are true about URL generation? (select all that apply)

a.t: The default reference type is ABSOLUTE_PATH, producing a root-relative path like /blog/42
Parameters that do not correspond to a route placeholder are appended to the generated URL as a query string
The reference-type constants (ABSOLUTE_URL, NETWORK_PATH, ...) are defined on UrlGeneratorInterface
The Twig functions path() and url() are interchangeable — both emit absolute URLs
In a console command, ABSOLUTE_URL automatically picks up the production host without any configuration

questions.exp: generateUrl() defaults to ABSOLUTE_PATH, left-over (non-placeholder) parameters become the ?key=value query string, and the constants live on UrlGeneratorInterface. In Twig, path() maps to ABSOLUTE_PATH while url() maps to ABSOLUTE_URL, and in CLI there is no request, so absolute URLs fall back to http://localhost unless framework.router.default_uri is configured.

questions.q: Which of the following statements are true about the special underscore routing attributes? (select all that apply)

a.t: _route and _route_params are read-only outputs injected by the matcher into the request attributes
_format sets the request format via Request::setRequestFormat(), influencing the response Content-Type
_fragment only takes effect during URL generation (appended as #fragment); it plays no role in matching
Setting _route in a route's defaults changes what $request->attributes->get('_route') returns
stateless: true hard-blocks all session usage in production

questions.exp: The matcher injects _route/_route_params and RouterListener copies them into request attributes for you to read, _format drives content negotiation and the default Content-Type, and _fragment is honoured only by the generator. You never set _route yourself, and stateless: true is an assertion that raises an UnexpectedSessionUsageException warning in debug — not a hard production block.

questions.syl: Routing → User's locale guessing & localized routes
questions.q: Which of the following statements are true about localized routes and locale guessing? (select all that apply)

a.t: A #[Route] whose path is a locale => path map expands into one route per locale, each carrying the matching _locale default
Symfony does not guess the locale from the Accept-Language header by default; that behaviour is opt-in
framework.default_locale takes precedence over a _locale parameter matched in the URL
generateUrl() always uses the default locale unless you rebuild the router

questions.exp: Localized path arrays are expanded at load time into per-locale routes with a _locale default, and Accept-Language parsing requires opting in via set_locale_from_accept_language (or reading getPreferredLanguage() yourself). The precedence is matched _locale first, then the sticky session locale, then default_locale, and generation reuses the current request's locale unless you pass _locale explicitly.

questions.q: Which of the following statements are true about host (domain) matching? (select all that apply)

a.t: A host placeholder like {tenant} matches [^.]+ by default — a single label that cannot contain dots
The host regex is tested before the path regex when matching a route
Generating a URL for a route on a different host produces an absolute (or network) URL automatically
Host placeholders cannot have requirements or defaults; only path placeholders support them
A path-only (relative) URL can switch subdomains as long as the route declares a host

questions.exp: Host tokens use the dot as separator, so they default to [^.]+ instead of [^/]+, and matchCollection() checks the compiled host regex before even trying the path. Because a path-only URL cannot change host, the generator upgrades cross-host links to absolute/network URLs. Host placeholders obey the same requirements/defaults rules as path placeholders — that is how a missing subdomain can default to www.

questions.q: In Symfony 8, where are a Passport's badges validated?

a.t: In the Firewall listener before routing

questions.exp: authenticate() only builds the Passport. Badge resolution and credential verification happen on CheckPassportEvent (UserProviderListener, CheckCredentialsListener, CsrfProtectionListener…).

questions.q: What is the status of enable_authenticator_manager in Symfony 8?

a.t: Removed — the authenticator system is the only one
Required and must be set to true

questions.exp: The key existed and was deprecated in 7.x; Symfony 8 removed it entirely because the legacy authentication system is gone.

questions.q: A stateless firewall (stateless: true) does NOT do which of these?

a.t: Persist the token in the session via ContextListener
Create a token for the current request

questions.exp: Stateless firewalls skip the ContextListener, so nothing is stored or restored between requests; each request re-authenticates.

questions.q: An authenticator's supports() returns null. What does that mean?

a.t: Authenticate lazily when the token is needed

questions.exp: null means 'unsure — call me lazily'. Many stateless authenticators use it so authentication is deferred until required.

questions.q: During a successful login, in which order does the AuthenticatorManager dispatch these events?
questions.exp: authenticate() builds the Passport; CheckPassportEvent listeners then resolve the badges; createToken() runs; AuthenticationTokenCreatedEvent is the last chance to swap/decorate the token; the token is stored; finally LoginSuccessEvent fires (invoking onAuthenticationSuccess()). On error a LoginFailureEvent is dispatched instead. Any ordering that runs LoginSuccessEvent before the passport is checked, or creates the token before CheckPassportEvent, contradicts the manager's pipeline.

questions.q: A controller runs $security->getUser()->getUserIdentifier() and fatals on some requests. What is the cause?

a.t: On an anonymous request getUser() returns null, so calling a method on null fatals; guard with ?->, ?? or an IsGranted check
getUser() throws an AccessDeniedException for guests
TokenStorage is not registered as a service

questions.exp: Security::getUser() returns ?UserInterface — it is null whenever no token holds a user (a truly anonymous request, or a lazy firewall whose token was never read). Dereferencing null is a fatal error. Guard with $user?->…, a ?? fallback, or an earlier #[IsGranted('IS_AUTHENTICATED_FULLY')] / denyAccessUnlessGranted() so $user is guaranteed non-null past that point. getUserIdentifier() is very much part of the 8.0 interface, and getUser() never throws for guests — it simply returns null.

questions.q: True or False: a firewall with stateless: true restores the authenticated token from the session on the next request.
questions.exp: False. stateless: true means the ContextListener is not registered, so no token is written to or restored from the session. Each request starts with empty token storage and must re-authenticate (e.g. re-read the bearer token). Session-backed restore is a property of stateful firewalls only.

questions.q: Which check can pass a subject to voters?
questions.exp: Only the isGranted()/#[IsGranted]/denyAccessUnlessGranted() path carries a subject. access_control is URL-based and cannot pass a subject.

questions.q: A #[IsGranted] check fails for an unauthenticated user. What happens?

a.t: The entry point starts authentication (e.g. login redirect)

questions.exp: An AccessDeniedException for an unauthenticated user is converted to the entry point response; an authenticated-but-unauthorized user gets a 403.

questions.q: isGranted() ultimately delegates the decision to which interface?
questions.exp: AuthorizationChecker reads the current token from TokenStorage, then calls AccessDecisionManager::decide().

questions.q: On a logged-out request, what does isGranted('ROLE_ADMIN') do internally?

a.t: The AuthorizationChecker substitutes a NullToken and voters run; RoleVoter finds no matching role and it returns a clean false
It throws because the token in storage is null
It returns true because no access_control rule restricts it
It redirects to the firewall entry point

questions.exp: When TokenStorage holds no token, AuthorizationChecker substitutes a NullToken rather than crashing, and voting proceeds normally. RoleVoter finds ROLE_ADMIN is not present, so the decision is false — not an exception. (AuthenticatedVoter denies the IS_AUTHENTICATED_* attributes for a NullToken, while PUBLIC_ACCESS still grants.) Authorization never starts authentication by itself; only an AccessDeniedException handled by the firewall triggers the entry point.

questions.q: In #[IsGranted('EDIT', subject: 'post')], what does subject: 'post' do?

a.t: Passes the controller argument named $post to the voters as the subject of the EDIT decision
Names the voter class that should handle the check
Restricts the route to a {post} placeholder
Combines with EDIT to require the role EDIT_POST

questions.exp: The subject option references a controller argument by name; Symfony resolves $post and passes it to AccessDecisionManager::decide() as the subject, so a voter's voteOnAttribute() receives the actual Post instance and can apply per-object rules (ownership, state). It is not a voter name, a route requirement, or a role suffix.

questions.q: Which statement about access_control vs isGranted() is correct?

a.t: access_control is URL-based and cannot pass a subject; only isGranted()/#[IsGranted] can
access_control can pass the matched entity to voters as the subject
Both can pass a subject to voters
Neither reaches voters — access_control uses its own logic

questions.exp: access_control runs through the same AccessDecisionManager and voters as isGranted(), but it only supplies the rule's roles/allow_if — there is no subject, because it matches on the URL, not on a domain object. Per-object decisions ("can edit THIS post?") must use #[IsGranted]/denyAccessUnlessGranted() with a subject. Both do reach voters, so the "neither" option is wrong.

questions.q: Which of these funnel through AuthorizationCheckerInterface::isGranted()? (choose 3)
questions.exp: #[IsGranted], denyAccessUnlessGranted() and Twig's is_granted() are all thin wrappers over AuthorizationCheckerInterface::isGranted(), which delegates to the AccessDecisionManager and voters. loadUserByIdentifier() belongs to the authentication/provider layer (loading users), not authorization, so it does not go through isGranted().

questions.q: The password_hashers map in security.yaml is keyed by…

a.t: A user class or interface name

questions.exp: You map a user class (commonly PasswordAuthenticatedUserInterface) to an algorithm such as 'auto'.

questions.q: Two providers are defined and a firewall omits the provider key. Result?

a.t: Configuration error — the provider is ambiguous
It silently uses the first provider

questions.exp: With multiple providers there is no implicit default; each firewall must name its provider explicitly.

questions.q: Why must the dev firewall (security: false) be listed first?

a.t: Firewalls are first-match, so it must precede protecting firewalls
It sets global defaults for later firewalls

questions.exp: Firewall matching is top-to-bottom, first match wins. Listing the dev firewall first stops the profiler/assets being intercepted by login.

questions.q: For each firewall, what does SecurityExtension compile at container build time?

a.t: A FirewallContext bundling its listeners, the authenticator list, an AuthenticatorManager, and (unless stateless) a ContextListener — all indexed in a FirewallMap
A single global Firewall service shared unchanged by every firewall
One controller per firewall generated from the config
Nothing at build time — firewalls are assembled lazily on the first request

questions.exp: SecurityExtension reads the security.yaml tree and, per firewall, compiles a dedicated FirewallContext (its listeners, the list of authenticators, an AuthenticatorManager, an exception listener, and a ContextListener unless the firewall is stateless). All contexts are registered in the FirewallMap; at runtime the single Firewall listener asks the map which context matches. The work happens at compile time, not lazily per request.

questions.q: Requests under /api are being handled by the session-based main firewall instead of the stateless api firewall. What is wrong?

a.t: The catch-all main firewall is listed before api; firewalls are first-match, so api must come first
You must set enable_authenticator_manager: true for the api firewall
stateless: true disables pattern matching on that firewall
Defining two providers makes the api firewall be skipped

questions.exp: Firewalls match top-to-bottom, first match wins. A catch-all main firewall (no pattern) placed before api matches every request, so /api never reaches the stateless firewall. Move the specific ^/api firewall above main. enable_authenticator_manager no longer exists in Symfony 8, stateless does not affect matching, and multiple providers do not skip a firewall.

questions.q: Which of these are valid top-level keys under security: in Symfony 8? (choose 4)
questions.exp: providers, firewalls, access_control, password_hashers and role_hierarchy are the core keys of security.yaml. enable_authenticator_manager was removed in Symfony 8 — the authenticator system is the only one — so it is not a valid key anymore.

questions.q: How do you configure eraseCredentials behaviour in security.yaml in Symfony 8?

a.t: You don't — eraseCredentials() was removed in 8.0; strip secrets in the user's __serialize()
Add erase_credentials: true under each firewall
Set it inside the password_hashers map
It is enabled by default via the erase_credentials key

questions.exp: There is no eraseCredentials configuration key, and there never was — it was a UserInterface method. In Symfony 8 both UserInterface::eraseCredentials() and TokenInterface::eraseCredentials() were removed; the documented replacement is to strip sensitive data (the password) in your user's __serialize() method, which is what runs when the token/user is stored in the session.

questions.q: Which method loads a user by identifier in Symfony 8?
questions.exp: loadUserByUsername() was removed; the UserProviderInterface loader is loadUserByIdentifier().

questions.q: When is refreshUser() called?

a.t: On every stateful request, to re-sync the session user

questions.exp: The ContextListener refreshes the stored user on each request of a stateful firewall; a stateless firewall never calls it.

questions.q: Does a user provider verify the user's password?

a.t: No — credentials are checked on CheckPassportEvent

questions.exp: Providers only load and refresh users. CheckCredentialsListener verifies the PasswordCredentials badge.

questions.q: A custom provider does `return $repo->find($id);` in loadUserByIdentifier() and sometimes throws a TypeError. What is the fix?

a.t: find() can return null but the return type is a non-nullable UserInterface; throw UserNotFoundException when no user matches
loadUserByIdentifier() must return an array of users
The method must be renamed to loadUserByUsername()
Return false instead of the user object

questions.exp: loadUserByIdentifier(): UserInterface has a non-nullable return type. Returning null (as find() may) is a contract violation and causes a TypeError. When no user matches you must throw UserNotFoundException, which Symfony normalises to a generic BadCredentialsException so an attacker cannot distinguish "unknown user" from "wrong password". You never return null or false, and the method returns a single UserInterface, not an array.

questions.q: An admin deletes a user's account while that user is browsing under a stateful firewall. What happens on the user's next request?

a.t: refreshUser() can no longer load them and throws; the ContextListener discards the token, effectively logging them out
Nothing changes until the PHP session cookie expires
A fatal 500 error is returned on every request
The user keeps full access until they click logout

questions.exp: On each stateful request the ContextListener calls refreshUser() to re-sync the session user. A now-missing account makes refreshUser() throw (UserNotFoundException / UnsupportedUserException), so the ContextListener treats the user as unloadable, discards the token and clears storage — an immediate, clean logout. It is not a fatal error, and access does not persist until the cookie expires precisely because the user is re-checked every request.

questions.q: A provider is configured as `all_users: { chain: { providers: [in_memory, api_users] } }`. What does it do?

a.t: Tries each listed provider in order; the first that supports/loads the user wins
Merges the users from both providers into a single set
Requires the user to exist in both providers to authenticate
Picks one of the providers at random per request

questions.exp: A chain provider delegates to its sub-providers in the declared order and returns the first successful match; if none support/find the user it throws. It does not merge users, require presence in all providers, or choose randomly. Correct supportsClass()/UnsupportedUserException handling in each sub-provider is what lets the chain fall through cleanly.

questions.q: True or False: a firewall with stateless: true still calls refreshUser() on every request.
questions.exp: False. refreshUser() is invoked by the ContextListener, which only exists on stateful firewalls. A stateless firewall stores no token in the session, so there is nothing to refresh — the user is re-loaded from scratch by the authenticator on each request instead.

questions.q: How many firewalls are active for a given request?

a.t: Exactly one — the first whose matcher matches

questions.exp: The FirewallMap returns the first matching FirewallContext; matching stops there.

questions.q: What does security: false on a firewall do?

a.t: Disables the security layer for that zone (and still counts as the match)
Denies all access to that zone

questions.exp: It turns off all security listeners for matching requests (used for the profiler and dev assets) and, being first-match, prevents later firewalls from matching.

questions.q: Two firewalls should share a logged-in session. What do you configure?

a.t: The same context: name on both firewalls

questions.exp: Token sharing between firewalls requires an explicit matching context key; otherwise each firewall keeps its own token.

questions.q: What does lazy: true achieve on a firewall?

a.t: Authentication is deferred until the token is actually read
It caches the authenticated token forever
It runs all authenticators eagerly on every request

questions.exp: A lazy firewall only authenticates when the token is accessed (e.g. is_granted/getUser), so fully public pages skip auth and session loading.

questions.q: A firewall configured with `pattern: /api` unexpectedly also intercepts /my-api-docs. Why?

a.t: pattern is a regex; without a leading ^ it matches anywhere in the path. Anchor it as ^/api
Symfony matches patterns as substrings and cannot be anchored
You must also set methods: to make patterns exact

questions.exp: Firewall pattern is an unanchored regular expression, so /api matches any path containing that sequence — including /my-api-docs. Anchoring with ^ (^/api) fixes it to the start of the path. Patterns are regexes (anchorable), the doc route is unrelated to physical location, and methods: narrows HTTP verbs, not path matching.

questions.q: Given firewalls declared as main (no pattern) then api (pattern: ^/api), what happens to /api requests?

a.t: main (the catch-all) matches first, so /api never reaches the api firewall; list api first
Both firewalls run in sequence for /api
api wins because its pattern is more specific
A container compile error is thrown for overlapping firewalls

questions.exp: Firewall selection is first-match, top-to-bottom — not most-specific-wins. A patternless main firewall matches everything, so it swallows /api before the api firewall is considered. The fix is ordering: specific firewalls (^/api) before the catch-all. Symfony does not run multiple firewalls per request, nor does it error on overlap.

questions.q: When does the Firewall listener run in the kernel lifecycle?

a.t: On kernel.request at priority 8 (after routing), it asks the FirewallMap for the first matching FirewallContext
On kernel.controller, just before the controller is resolved
On kernel.response, after the action has run
On kernel.terminate, asynchronously after the response
On kernel.request but before routing, at the highest priority

questions.exp: The Firewall listener subscribes to kernel.request at priority 8, which runs after the RouterListener (routing), then queries the FirewallMap for the matching FirewallContext and runs its listeners. It is a request-phase concern, not controller/response/terminate, and it deliberately runs after routing so route attributes are available.

questions.q: Which methods does UserInterface declare in Symfony 8?
questions.exp: Symfony 8 trimmed UserInterface to two methods; eraseCredentials() and getUsername() were removed.

questions.q: How do you keep a user's password out of the session in Symfony 8?

a.t: Override __serialize() and unset the password field
It happens automatically with no code

questions.exp: eraseCredentials() was removed in 8.0; the documented replacement is to strip sensitive data in __serialize().

questions.q: isEqualTo() returns false when a stored user is refreshed. Effect?

a.t: The token is invalidated — the user is logged out

questions.exp: A negative EquatableInterface comparison on refresh tells the framework the stored identity is stale, so the token is dropped.

questions.q: Which interface declares getPassword()?
questions.exp: getPassword(): ?string is declared by PasswordAuthenticatedUserInterface, an opt-in interface — not by UserInterface (which only has getRoles() and getUserIdentifier() in 8.0). EquatableInterface adds isEqualTo(); PasswordUpgraderInterface (a provider concern) adds upgradePassword(). A token-only/SSO user may skip PasswordAuthenticatedUserInterface entirely.

questions.q: A token-only API user declares getPassword(): string. Login works, but the security layer throws a TypeError when serialising the user. Why?

a.t: Such a user has no local password, so the stored hash is null; getPassword() must be typed ?string
getPassword() must return an int hash code
The method has to be named getHash() in Symfony 8

questions.exp: PasswordAuthenticatedUserInterface::getPassword() is typed ?string precisely because passwordless accounts (OAuth/LDAP/token-only) legitimately have a null hash. Declaring a non-nullable string return type makes PHP throw a TypeError the moment null is returned during verification or serialization. The CheckCredentialsListener treats a null hash as non-verifiable. The method name and return type are fixed by the interface, and eraseCredentials() no longer exists.

questions.q: You need a user's role change to immediately end their existing sessions. What do you implement?

a.t: EquatableInterface::isEqualTo() comparing roles; returning false on refresh invalidates the token
An eraseCredentials() override that clears the roles
A kernel listener that calls logout() on every request
Setting stateless: true on the firewall

questions.exp: When a user implements EquatableInterface, the ContextListener compares the session copy with the freshly refreshed user on each request via isEqualTo(). Including getRoles() in that comparison means a role change yields false, which invalidates the token and logs the user out immediately. eraseCredentials() no longer exists; a manual logout-everywhere listener is crude; and stateless would drop sessions entirely rather than invalidate on change.

questions.q: True or False: UserInterface::getUsername() still exists in Symfony 8.
questions.exp: False. getUsername() was replaced by getUserIdentifier() (mandatory since 6.0) and no longer exists on UserInterface in Symfony 8. Use getUserIdentifier() for the login identifier the session stores and refreshUser() reloads from.

questions.q: Which password algorithm is the recommended default?
questions.exp: 'auto' selects the best available algorithm (currently bcrypt) and can adapt over time; it also enables automatic rehash on cost changes.

questions.q: Transparent password rehash on login requires…

a.t: Both migrate_from and a provider implementing PasswordUpgraderInterface
Calling password_hash() manually in the controller

questions.exp: migrate_from lets needsRehash() detect the old hash; the PasswordUpgradeBadge triggers PasswordMigratingListener, which persists the new hash via upgradePassword().

questions.q: Where is a login password actually verified?
questions.exp: The authenticator adds a PasswordCredentials badge; the listener verifies it against the hash using the configured hasher.

questions.q: Which statement about the plaintext hasher is correct?

a.t: It is intended for tests only and must never be used in production
It is a fast, secure production option
It is the default when none is configured

questions.exp: plaintext stores passwords unhashed; it exists to speed up test fixtures and is a production anti-pattern.

questions.q: A hasher entry is `algorithm: sodium, migrate_from: ['bcrypt']`. What does it mean?

a.t: Hash new passwords with sodium, but still accept existing bcrypt hashes and upgrade them on the next successful login
Reject any password stored with bcrypt
Hash with bcrypt and verify with sodium
Store each password hashed by both algorithms at once

questions.exp: The primary algorithm (sodium/Argon2id) is used to hash new passwords, while migrate_from lists legacy algorithms whose hashes are still verifiable. On a valid login against an old bcrypt hash, needsRehash() returns true and the PasswordUpgradeBadge flow rehashes with sodium and persists it — transparent, no reset. It does not reject bcrypt, swap hashing/verifying roles, or double-hash.

questions.q: A user with a very long passphrase can change the trailing characters and still log in. Which hasher is in use and why?

a.t: bcrypt — it truncates input at 72 bytes, so bytes beyond that are ignored
auto — it hashes only the first word of the input
pbkdf2 — it lowercases the input before hashing

questions.exp: bcrypt has a hard 72-byte input limit; any bytes past 72 are silently ignored, so two passphrases sharing the first 72 bytes verify identically. Very long passphrases therefore lose entropy under bcrypt. sodium (Argon2id) has no such truncation, which is one reason to prefer it for long secrets. The other options invent behaviour that does not exist.

questions.q: You set migrate_from and needsRehash() returns true, yet stored hashes are never upgraded. What is missing?

a.t: The user provider does not implement PasswordUpgraderInterface, so upgradePassword() is never called to persist the new hash
migrate_from only works with the plaintext algorithm
You must call password_hash() yourself in the controller
needsRehash() is not supported in Symfony 8

questions.exp: migrate_from + needsRehash() computes a fresh hash, but persisting it is the provider's job: only a provider implementing PasswordUpgraderInterface's upgradePassword() actually stores it (triggered by the PasswordUpgradeBadge / PasswordMigratingListener). Without it, the rehash is computed and discarded every login. migrate_from is not plaintext-only, you must not hash manually, and needsRehash() is fully supported.

questions.q: Which special attribute is broader?
questions.exp: Fully-authenticated users satisfy IS_AUTHENTICATED_REMEMBERED, but remember-me users do NOT satisfy IS_AUTHENTICATED_FULLY.

questions.q: In Symfony 8, how do you allow everyone (including not-logged-in) on a path?
questions.exp: Anonymous tokens were removed; PUBLIC_ACCESS is the attribute that opts a path out of authentication.

questions.q: An attribute 'EDITOR' (no ROLE_ prefix) is checked. How does RoleVoter treat it?

a.t: It is ignored — RoleVoter only handles ROLE_-prefixed attributes
Granted if the user has it

questions.exp: RoleVoter supports only ROLE_* attributes; unprefixed strings abstain there (a custom voter could still handle them).

questions.q: Given role_hierarchy ROLE_ADMIN: [ROLE_USER], a user with ROLE_ADMIN…

a.t: Is also granted ROLE_USER (reachable roles are expanded)

questions.exp: RoleHierarchyVoter expands reachable roles, so ROLE_ADMIN transitively includes ROLE_USER. Hierarchy flows downward.

questions.q: With role_hierarchy ROLE_ADMIN: [ROLE_USER] and ROLE_SUPER_ADMIN: [ROLE_ADMIN], which roles does a ROLE_SUPER_ADMIN user satisfy?

a.t: Every role defined anywhere in the map

questions.exp: RoleHierarchy::getReachableRoleNames() expands roles transitively: ROLE_SUPER_ADMIN reaches ROLE_ADMIN, which reaches ROLE_USER, so the user satisfies all three. Inheritance flows downward and is transitive (not just one level), but it does not grant unrelated roles that are not on the reachable path.

questions.q: Which attribute protects a 'change email' action so that a remember-me cookie is not sufficient?
questions.exp: IS_AUTHENTICATED_FULLY is granted only to users who authenticated fresh in the current session — not via a remember-me cookie. A stolen remember-me cookie satisfies IS_AUTHENTICATED_REMEMBERED and IS_AUTHENTICATED, so those would wrongly permit a sensitive identity change; PUBLIC_ACCESS allows everyone. Use _FULLY to force a fresh login for payments/identity changes.

questions.q: True or False: IS_AUTHENTICATED_ANONYMOUSLY is still a valid access attribute in Symfony 8.
questions.exp: False. Symfony 8 has no anonymous tokens, so IS_AUTHENTICATED_ANONYMOUSLY no longer exists. To open a path to everyone (including not-logged-in visitors) use PUBLIC_ACCESS instead.

questions.q: How many access_control rules apply to a request?
questions.exp: AccessMap returns the first match and evaluation stops. Order rules from specific to general.

questions.q: A rule has roles: [ROLE_A, ROLE_B]. Access is granted when the user has…
questions.exp: Multiple roles within a single access_control rule are OR-combined.

questions.q: No access_control rule matches the request. What happens?

a.t: Access is allowed (deferred to controller-level guards)

questions.exp: access_control only restricts on a matching rule; with no match there is no URL-level restriction.

questions.q: What does requires_channel: https do, and when?

a.t: Redirects matching paths to HTTPS before authentication runs
Runs only after a successful login

questions.exp: The ChannelListener enforces requires_channel before authentication, so even the login page is redirected to HTTPS.

questions.q: After adding { path: ^/, roles: PUBLIC_ACCESS } at the top of access_control, the ^/admin rule below stops protecting admin. Why?

a.t: First match wins; ^/ matches every path including /admin, so the catch-all is enforced and the admin rule is never reached
PUBLIC_ACCESS globally disables all other access_control rules
roles must be given as a list, not a string, to take effect
The admin rule needs a requires_channel to be evaluated

questions.exp: access_control is first-match, top-to-bottom. ^/ matches all paths, so placing it first means /admin hits the PUBLIC_ACCESS rule and the ^/admin rule underneath is never evaluated — admin becomes public. Order specific rules before the ^/ catch-all. PUBLIC_ACCESS is a normal attribute (it does not disable other rules), and the roles syntax/requires_channel are unrelated.

questions.q: Can an access_control rule pass the matched entity to a voter as the subject?

a.t: No — access_control has no subject; it calls AccessDecisionManager with only roles/allow_if. Use #[IsGranted] with a subject for per-object rules
Yes, via a subject: key on the rule
Yes, the matched path parameter is passed as the subject
Only when allow_if is also set

questions.exp: access_control routes through the same AccessDecisionManager and voters as isGranted(), but it is purely URL-driven: the AccessListener calls decide() with the rule's roles/expression and no subject. There is no subject: key and path parameters are not passed as subjects. Per-object decisions require #[IsGranted]/denyAccessUnlessGranted() with an explicit subject.

questions.q: A rule sets both roles: ROLE_USER and an allow_if expression. When is access granted?

a.t: Only when BOTH the role check and the expression pass (AND)
When either the role or the expression passes (OR)
Only the expression is evaluated; roles is ignored
Only roles is evaluated; allow_if is ignored

questions.exp: Within one rule, multiple roles are OR-combined, but when roles and allow_if are both present they must BOTH pass — it is an AND. (allow_if runs the expression through the ExpressionVoter.) Neither key is ignored, and combining them does not turn the rule into an OR.

questions.q: What does an authenticator's authenticate() method return?
questions.exp: authenticate() builds a Passport of badges; the token is produced later by createToken() after CheckPassportEvent resolves the badges.

questions.q: Which passport type suits a valid-API-token flow with no password to verify?
questions.exp: When the credential itself proves identity, use SelfValidatingPassport, which carries only a UserBadge — there is nothing further to check.

questions.q: In which namespace does PasswordCredentials live?
questions.exp: PasswordCredentials and CustomCredentials live under Passport\\Credentials; UserBadge, CsrfTokenBadge, RememberMeBadge, PasswordUpgradeBadge and PreAuthenticatedUserBadge live under Passport\\Badge.

questions.q: Which built-in authenticator uses a token_handler returning a UserBadge?
questions.exp: The access_token authenticator delegates to an AccessTokenHandlerInterface whose getUserBadgeFrom() validates the bearer token and returns a UserBadge.

questions.q: An authenticator adds a badge that no CheckPassportEvent listener resolves. What happens?

a.t: Passport::checkIfCompletelyResolved() throws, so authentication fails — you cannot forget to validate a badge
The badge is silently ignored and login proceeds
The token is created with the unresolved badge attached
A raw 500 with no security exception is produced

questions.exp: After CheckPassportEvent, the manager calls Passport::checkIfCompletelyResolved(), which throws if any badge was never marked resolved. This is a deliberate safety net: an unregistered/forgotten badge (e.g. a CsrfTokenBadge with no listener) fails authentication as an AuthenticationException rather than letting an unverified credential slip through. It is neither ignored nor attached to a successful token.

questions.q: Which of these live in Passport\Badge (i.e. are badges, not credentials)? (choose 3)
questions.exp: UserBadge, CsrfTokenBadge, RememberMeBadge (plus PasswordUpgradeBadge and PreAuthenticatedUserBadge) live under Passport\\Badge. PasswordCredentials — like CustomCredentials — lives under Passport\\Credentials, not Badge. This namespace split is a classic exam distinction.

questions.q: What does AbstractLoginFormAuthenticator provide that AbstractAuthenticator does not?

a.t: supports() (POST to the check path), the entry point via getLoginUrl(), and a default onAuthenticationFailure() that redirects back to the login page
A default authenticate() that verifies the password for you
A createToken() that returns a PostAuthenticationToken

questions.exp: AbstractLoginFormAuthenticator adds form-login plumbing on top of AbstractAuthenticator: supports() (POST to the check path), the entry point start() built from the abstract getLoginUrl(), and a default onAuthenticationFailure() redirecting to the login page — leaving you to write authenticate(), getLoginUrl() and onAuthenticationSuccess(). It does not verify passwords (that is CheckCredentialsListener), does not own the event listeners or the provider; and returning a PostAuthenticationToken is AbstractAuthenticator's default, which FormLoginAuthenticator overrides to a UsernamePasswordToken.

questions.q: What is the default AccessDecisionManager strategy?
questions.exp: Affirmative is the default: access is granted if at least one voter returns ACCESS_GRANTED.

questions.q: The base Voter's supports() returns false. What is the resulting vote?
questions.exp: The abstract Voter abstains for unsupported attributes/subjects; it never calls voteOnAttribute() in that case.

questions.q: All voters abstain and allow_if_all_abstain keeps its default. Result?

a.t: It depends on the user's roles

questions.exp: allow_if_all_abstain defaults to false, so if every voter abstains and no one grants, access is denied.

questions.q: What are the integer values of the voter constants?
questions.exp: These integer constants drive the strategy arithmetic in the AccessDecisionManager.

questions.q: Under the unanimous strategy, one voter denies while another grants. Outcome?

a.t: Access is denied — unanimous grants only if no voter denies
Access is granted — one grant is enough
The tie is resolved by roles

questions.exp: unanimous requires that no voter denies. A single ACCESS_DENIED blocks access regardless of grants (unlike affirmative).

questions.q: In a Voter, voteOnAttribute() starts with `if (!$user instanceof AppUser) { return false; }`. Why return false rather than abstain?

a.t: supports() already accepted the attribute, so this voter owns the decision; with no valid user it must deny — abstaining would wrongly delegate an attribute it claimed
It should really return ACCESS_ABSTAIN there instead
$token->getUser() can never be null, so the branch is dead code
It should throw an AccessDeniedException from the voter

questions.exp: By the time voteOnAttribute() runs, supports() has already said "this attribute/subject is mine", so the voter must return a real yes/no. An unauthenticated request carries a NullToken whose getUser() is null (or a user of the wrong class), so there is nobody to authorize — deny (return false). Abstaining would contradict supports(); getUser() genuinely can be null; and voters signal decisions via return values, not by throwing.

questions.q: Under the unanimous strategy, a voter returns false from voteOnAttribute() for an attribute it does not actually care about. Effect?

a.t: false is ACCESS_DENIED, which blocks access under unanimous; unrelated attributes must be filtered out in supports() so the voter abstains
false is treated as abstain and has no effect on the outcome
It throws because the attribute is unsupported

questions.exp: Returning false from voteOnAttribute() maps to ACCESS_DENIED, not abstain. Under unanimous a single deny blocks access, so a voter that "says no to what isn't mine" silently breaks authorization. The correct pattern is to reject unrelated attributes/subjects in supports(), which makes the base Voter abstain (ACCESS_ABSTAIN, no effect). abstain and deny are distinct, and an unsupported attribute does not throw.

questions.q: With access_decision_manager.strategy set to priority, how is the decision made?

a.t: The first voter that does not abstain decides the outcome
All voters must agree to grant
The majority of grants over denies wins
A single grant is always enough regardless of order

questions.exp: The priority strategy takes the vote of the first (highest-priority) non-abstaining voter as final, letting a high-priority voter short-circuit (e.g. a global "banned user" voter denying before feature voters run). "All must agree" describes unanimous, "majority" describes consensus, and "one grant is enough" describes affirmative.

questions.q: Which statements about switch_user impersonation are correct in Symfony 8? (multiple)

a.t: The default required role is ROLE_ALLOWED_TO_SWITCH
While switched, the original token is preserved inside a SwitchUserToken
SwitchUserEvent is dispatched on both switch and exit
switch_user is a global option, not a per-firewall one
While switched, isGranted() still uses the admin's roles

questions.exp: switch_user is enabled per firewall and defaults to requiring ROLE_ALLOWED_TO_SWITCH. The SwitchUserListener stores the original token inside the new SwitchUserToken (getOriginalToken()) and dispatches SwitchUserEvent for both directions. All authorization while switched uses the target user's roles — that is the point of impersonation.

questions.q: How does an impersonating user return to their own account?

a.t: Append ?_switch_user=_exit to any URL on the firewall
Log out and log back in — there is no other way

questions.exp: Exiting uses the same configured parameter (default _switch_user) with the special value _exit. The SwitchUserListener then restores the original token that was preserved inside the SwitchUserToken and redirects with the parameter stripped.

questions.q: To show an 'exit impersonation' banner, a template checks is_granted('ROLE_PREVIOUS_ADMIN'). What is the Symfony 8 verdict?

a.t: Use is_granted('IS_IMPERSONATOR') — ROLE_PREVIOUS_ADMIN is the legacy spelling
It is the recommended check in Symfony 8
Both are wrong; check app.user.impersonating instead

questions.exp: The modern attribute is IS_IMPERSONATOR, granted only when the active token is a SwitchUserToken. ROLE_PREVIOUS_ADMIN is the legacy pre-5.x style and must not appear in new code. ROLE_ALLOWED_TO_SWITCH only says the user may switch, not that they currently are switched.

questions.q: Which statements describe the DEFAULT login_throttling limiter? (multiple)

a.t: It counts failed attempts per username + IP up to max_attempts per interval
It also enforces a wider limit of 5 × max_attempts per IP across all usernames
A successful login resets the counter
It counts per session ID so proxies are irrelevant
It blocks the IP permanently after the first breach

questions.exp: DefaultLoginRateLimiter combines two limits: username+IP at max_attempts and IP alone at five times that, so attackers cannot bypass the first limit by spraying usernames. A successful login resets the counters; blocking is only for the configured interval and IP/username based, not session based.

questions.q: What must a service referenced by login_throttling.limiter implement?

a.t: AuthenticatorInterface with a supports() returning null
Nothing — it is the name of a framework.rate_limiter entry

questions.exp: The firewall needs a limiter that maps a Request to rate limiters, which is RequestRateLimiterInterface (HttpFoundation namespace); extending AbstractRequestRateLimiter and returning limiters from getLimiters() is the documented shortcut. Plain LimiterInterface instances or rate_limiter names are not accepted directly.

questions.q: True or false: login throttling rejects a throttled attempt only after the password has been verified and found wrong.

a.t: False — LoginThrottlingListener runs on CheckPassportEvent with high priority, before credentials are checked
True — it hooks LoginFailureEvent after credential verification

questions.exp: The listener consumes the rate limiter on CheckPassportEvent before the CheckCredentialsListener verifies the password, throwing TooManyLoginAttemptsAuthenticationException when the limit is exceeded. It listens to LoginSuccessEvent only to reset the counters.

questions.q: role_hierarchy maps ROLE_ADMIN: ROLE_USER. A user stores only [ROLE_ADMIN]. Which check FAILS for them?

a.t: in_array('ROLE_USER', $user->getRoles(), true) — getRoles() never expands the hierarchy

questions.exp: The hierarchy is applied only at authorization time by the RoleHierarchyVoter, so isGranted(), Twig is_granted() and access_control all pass. $user->getRoles() returns exactly the stored roles (['ROLE_ADMIN']), so raw in_array checks bypass the hierarchy — the classic exam trap.

questions.q: Where IS the configured role hierarchy taken into account? (multiple)
questions.exp: Access checks run through the AccessDecisionManager where the RoleHierarchyVoter expands roles with getReachableRoleNames(), and access_control uses the same path; you can call the RoleHierarchyInterface service yourself for the same expansion. Token and user role getters always return the raw stored roles.

questions.q: Which API expands ['ROLE_SUPER_ADMIN'] into every role it implies, transitively?
questions.exp: RoleHierarchy::getReachableRoleNames() walks the configured map recursively and is the very service the RoleHierarchyVoter uses, so results always match isGranted() behaviour. The other methods do not exist in Symfony 8.

questions.q: Votes cast: one GRANTED, one DENIED, one ABSTAIN (default flags; the granting voter has highest priority). Which strategies GRANT access? (multiple)

a.t: affirmative — at least one grant exists
consensus — the 1–1 tie falls back to allow_if_equal_granted_denied (default true)
priority — the first non-abstaining voter granted
unanimous — abstain is neutral so it grants

questions.exp: Affirmative grants on any grant; consensus with equal grants and denies uses allow_if_equal_granted_denied, which defaults to true; priority takes the first non-abstain vote, here the grant. Unanimous denies because a single ACCESS_DENIED vetoes regardless of the grant — the abstain is irrelevant to that veto.

questions.q: Strategy unanimous: voter A grants, voter B abstains, no voter denies. A colleague claims access is denied because 'not everyone agreed'. Verdict?

a.t: Access is granted — unanimous only forbids denies; abstentions are neutral
Access is denied — every voter must return ACCESS_GRANTED
Access is denied — abstain counts as a deny under unanimous

questions.exp: UnanimousStrategy returns false only if some voter denies; otherwise it grants when at least one voter granted. Abstentions never count as denies, and allow_if_equal_granted_denied is a consensus-only tie breaker. Only the all-abstain case falls back to allow_if_all_abstain.

questions.q: Every voter abstains and no access_decision_manager option was changed. What is the decision?

a.t: Denied — allow_if_all_abstain defaults to false for every strategy
An exception is thrown because no decision could be made
Granted under affirmative, denied under the others

questions.exp: When no voter casts a real vote, all four strategies fall back to the allow_if_all_abstain flag, which defaults to false, so access is denied. No exception is thrown and the strategy choice does not change this default outcome.

questions.q: Which statements about Security::login() (SecurityBundle) are correct? (multiple)

a.t: It dispatches the same authentication events as an interactive login (e.g. LoginSuccessEvent)
It accepts extra badges, e.g. new RememberMeBadge()
It returns ?Response — the authenticator's success response, if any
It silently writes a token into TokenStorage without running authenticators
It verifies the user's password before logging in

questions.exp: login() delegates to the real authenticator pipeline, so badge listeners and events (CheckPassportEvent, LoginSuccessEvent) run exactly as for an interactive login, and the authenticator's onAuthenticationSuccess() response is returned. No credentials are checked — you assert the user is already trusted (e.g. just registered).

questions.q: Calling $security->logout() from a controller action that is not the logout form throws a CSRF-related error. Fix?

a.t: Call $security->logout(false) — CSRF validation is on by default and must be skipped for non-form flows
Set logout: ~ on the firewall to remove CSRF everywhere

questions.exp: logout(bool $validateCsrf = true) validates the logout CSRF token from the request by default; a programmatic call that does not originate from the logout link must pass false. It still dispatches LogoutEvent so the configured logout listeners run.

questions.q: When do the optional parameters of Security::login($user, $authenticatorName, $firewallName) become necessary? (multiple)

a.t: $authenticatorName when the firewall registers more than one authenticator
$firewallName when logging into a firewall other than the one matching the current request
$authenticatorName always — there is no single-authenticator shortcut

questions.exp: With exactly one authenticator on the target firewall both can be omitted. Multiple authenticators make $authenticatorName mandatory (built-ins are named by config key such as 'form_login', custom ones by service id), and $firewallName is needed when the current request's firewall is not the one you want to authenticate against.

questions.q: Which base class do Symfony unit tests extend for pure, kernel-free logic?
questions.exp: Symfony ships no unit-test base class; pure unit tests extend PHPUnit's TestCase directly. No kernel is booted and no container is built.

questions.q: In PHPUnit 11/12, how do you bind a test to a data provider?
questions.exp: The @dataProvider annotation is removed; use the PHPUnit\Framework\Attributes\DataProvider attribute pointing at a public static iterable-returning method.

questions.q: You need only canned return values, with no verification of how a collaborator is called. Which double do you create?
questions.exp: A stub supplies return values but never asserts interactions. A mock adds verifiable expectations you do not need here.

questions.q: What does assertSame(1, '1') do?

a.t: Fails, because the types differ (strict === comparison)
Passes, because the values are loosely equal

questions.exp: assertSame uses ===, so int 1 and string '1' are not the same. Use assertEquals for loose (==) comparison.

questions.q: A method referenced by #[DataProvider('provide')] must be…

a.t: public static and return an array or other iterable of argument sets
a protected instance method returning a Generator only

questions.exp: PHPUnit\Framework\Attributes\DataProvider names a public static method returning an iterable (array or Generator) of argument arrays; each set becomes one parameterised run of the test.

questions.q: A test method carries both #[TestWith([1000, 'FR', 1200])] and #[DataProvider('provideRates')], where provideRates() yields two rows. How many times does PHPUnit execute that test method?

a.t: Three times — the #[TestWith] row plus the two provider rows
Twice — #[TestWith] is ignored when a #[DataProvider] is present
Once — the attributes conflict and PHPUnit uses only the first
Two times — #[TestWith] must be the only data attribute or it errors

questions.exp: #[TestWith] inlines one argument row and #[DataProvider] contributes its iterable rows; they are additive, so the method runs once per row across all data attributes (1 + 2 = 3). #[TestWith] is simply a provider that needs no separate method — it does not replace or disable #[DataProvider].

questions.q: In PHPUnit 10+, a data-provider method declared non-static (public function provide()) results in…

a.t: An error — provider methods must be public static
A silent fallback where PHPUnit instantiates the class to call it
A deprecation notice but the test still runs
Nothing — visibility and staticness are irrelevant to providers

questions.exp: PHPUnit 10+ requires data-provider methods to be public and static; a non-static provider is reported as an error, not a fallback or a mere deprecation. The provider is resolved before any test instance exists, so it cannot depend on instance state.

questions.q: True or False: PHPUnit creates a fresh instance of the test class for every test method, so state set in one test does not leak into another.
questions.exp: PHPUnit reflects over the TestCase subclass and, for each test method, builds a new instance, runs setUp(), the test, then tearDown(). Instance properties therefore never carry over between test methods; only static properties (which you should avoid) can leak state.
