questions.exp: The auto-escaping context is derived from the file extension (html, js, css, url, html_attr are available), which is why a .txt.twig template gets no escaping at all — it is not a fixed html default. Escaping happens at print time via the escaper, and |raw / {% autoescape false %} switch the protection off entirely, making them XSS holes for untrusted data. The html_attr strategy is a stricter encoder than html, not an alias.

questions.q: Which statements about Twig template inheritance are true? (select all that apply)

a.t: A template can extend exactly one parent, but can pull in blocks from many templates with {% use %}
A child template that extends a parent cannot output markup outside of blocks
parent() inside a block renders the parent template's version of that block
A template may list several parents in a single {% extends %} tag to combine layouts
{% use %} sets the referenced template as an additional parent for the hierarchy

questions.exp: Inheritance is single and vertical: one parent per template, with blocks as the overridable holes, and any child markup outside blocks is invalid. parent() extends rather than replaces a block by rendering the parent's version. {% use %} is horizontal reuse — it imports blocks only and does not set a parent, and {% extends %} accepts a single parent, never several to combine.

questions.q: Which statements about {{ include() }} in Twig are correct? (select all that apply)

a.t: Without the only keyword, the included template inherits the whole context of the parent template
With only, the local context is isolated, but the app global variable is still available
ignore missing skips a missing template but does not swallow errors raised inside an existing template
include can override blocks defined in the included template
Passing a list of templates renders every template in the list that exists

questions.exp: By default the full parent context is merged into the include; only isolates the local variables while globals such as app remain accessible. ignore missing only prevents the error for a template that does not exist — exceptions thrown inside the included template still propagate. Overriding blocks is the job of {% embed %}, not include, and a template list renders only the first template that exists.

questions.q: Which statements about the app global variable are true? (select all that apply)

a.t: app.user is null for anonymous/unauthenticated requests, so templates must not assume it exists
Reading app.flashes consumes the flash messages, so they are gone after being displayed
Accessing app.session can start the session as a side effect
app.environment exposes the operating-system environment variables
The app global can never be shadowed by a local template variable

questions.exp: app is an AppVariable instance: app.user is null when nobody is authenticated, app.flashes consumes messages when read, and app.session starts the session on access (which can defeat HTTP caching). The distractors are wrong because app.environment is the kernel environment (dev/prod), not OS variables, and defining a local variable named app shadows the global.

questions.q: Which statements about generating URLs in Twig are correct? (select all that apply)

a.t: path() generates a relative URL while url() generates an absolute URL, both from route names
Parameters that are not part of the route definition are appended to the URL as a query string
Using an unknown route name throws a RouteNotFoundException when the template is rendered
Extra parameters not defined in the route are silently dropped from the generated URL
path() is the right choice for links inside emails since mail clients resolve relative URLs

questions.exp: path() and url() both take a route name (plus parameters): path() yields a relative URL, url() an absolute one, and any parameter the route does not declare ends up in the query string rather than being dropped. An unknown route name fails at render time with RouteNotFoundException. Email bodies, canonical links and feeds leave the page context, so they need url() — relative links from path() break in mail clients.

questions.q: Which statements about translations in Twig are correct? (select all that apply)

a.t: The trans filter arguments are ordered (parameters, domain, locale)
A missing translation key does not throw; the key string itself is returned
ICU MessageFormat pluralization is only parsed for catalogues in domains with the +intl-icu suffix
transchoice is the recommended filter for pluralization in current Symfony versions
Requesting a missing translation key raises an exception at render time

questions.exp: The trans filter signature is message|trans(parameters, domain, locale) — passing the domain first is a classic mistake. Missing keys fall back to returning the key itself instead of erroring, and ICU {n, plural, ...} syntax is only interpreted for domains suffixed with +intl-icu. The transchoice filter was removed; ICU MessageFormat is the modern way to pluralize.

questions.q: What does ValidatorInterface::validate() return when the value is invalid?

a.t: An array of error message strings

questions.exp: validate() always returns a ConstraintViolationListInterface. It never returns a bool and never throws on failure; you inspect the result with count() and by iterating it.

questions.q: Which method validates a hypothetical value without changing the object?
questions.exp: validatePropertyValue() takes an explicit value and validates it against the property's constraints without touching the object. validateProperty() uses the object's current value instead.

questions.q: How is #[Assert\...] attribute metadata turned into constraints at runtime?

a.t: AttributeLoader builds ClassMetadata once, cached in a PSR-6 pool
It is re-parsed by reflection on every validate() call
It is compiled into the DI container and never changes
It is read from a database mapping table

questions.exp: LazyLoadingMetadataFactory uses AttributeLoader to reflect over the class and build ClassMetadata, which is cached (validator.mapping.cache) so the reflection cost is paid once per class.

questions.q: You call $validator->validate(null). What happens?

a.t: You get back an empty ConstraintViolationListInterface — no error, no TypeError
A TypeError, because null is not an object

questions.exp: Passing null is legal: the value is wrapped in a node, no class metadata is found, and an empty violation list comes back. Validation is values against constraints, and a bare null carries none. The trap is that a null object silently passes when you expected a required value.

a.t: 0 — Email skips null, so the unset property produces no violation
1 — the email is required and missing
1 — null is not a valid email

questions.exp: Most value constraints, Email included, skip null/empty and return no violation; only NotBlank/NotNull enforce presence. Stack NotBlank with Email when a missing value must be rejected.

questions.q: A developer writes `if ($validator->validate($dto)) { throw ...; }` and it throws even for valid objects. What is the cause?

a.t: validate() returns a ConstraintViolationList object, which is always truthy; you must check count() > 0
The DTO has a hidden constraint that always fails
You must always pass groups explicitly

questions.exp: The returned list is a non-null object, so it is truthy even when empty. Test count($violations) > 0 (or iterate); treating the list itself as a boolean is the classic mistake.

questions.q: In framework.yaml, what is the default of framework.validation.enable_attributes?

a.t: true — #[Assert\...] attribute mapping is enabled by default
false — you must enable it manually
It does not exist; mapping is always on

questions.exp: enable_attributes defaults to true, and YAML/XML files under config/validator/ are also auto-loaded. All active loaders are merged for the same class.

questions.q: A class has a #[Assert\NotBlank] attribute on $name, and a YAML mapping file adds Length to the same $name. Which constraints apply?

a.t: Both — all enabled loaders are merged; attributes do not override YAML, the constraints accumulate
Only the attribute; attributes take precedence
Only the YAML; file mapping wins
A MappingException is thrown for the conflict

questions.exp: LazyLoadingMetadataFactory merges every active loader's constraints for a class, so attribute and YAML constraints add up rather than one silently overriding the other.

questions.q: True or False: ValidatorInterface::validate() throws a ValidationFailedException when the object is invalid.
questions.exp: validate() never throws on failure and never returns a bool — it returns a ConstraintViolationListInterface. ValidationFailedException is thrown by higher-level helpers (e.g. the MapRequestPayload resolver), not by validate() itself.

questions.q: What does the #[MapRequestPayload] argument resolver do regarding validation?

a.t: It deserializes the request into the DTO and automatically validates it, producing a 422 on violations
It only deserializes; you must call the validator yourself
It validates but does not deserialize
It requires a Form to be defined

questions.exp: The argument resolver maps the request into the typed DTO and runs the validator, returning a 422 automatically when there are violations. In a controller you rarely call the validator directly; Forms invoke it during handleRequest() too.

questions.q: Which statement about NotBlank and NotNull is correct?

a.t: NotBlank rejects an empty string; NotNull accepts an empty string
They are aliases for the same check
NotNull rejects an empty string; NotBlank accepts it

questions.exp: NotBlank fails on '', [], and blank strings; NotNull only fails on a strict null, so '' and 0 pass NotNull. This is a classic exam distinction.

questions.q: To apply constraints to every element of an indexed array, which constraint do you use?
questions.exp: All applies the given constraints to each element of a collection. Collection validates the keys of an associative array; they are not interchangeable.

questions.q: A nested object's own constraints never run during validation. Why?

a.t: The property is missing #[Assert\Valid] to cascade into it
The validator cannot handle nested objects
You must call validateProperty() for nested objects
Nested objects need their own validator service

questions.exp: Cascading is opt-in: without #[Assert\\Valid] on the property, the validator does not descend into the related object, so its constraints are skipped.

questions.q: What does #[Assert\Email] report for an empty string value?

a.t: No violation — empty and null values pass most constraints
A violation, because '' is not a valid email
It depends on the charset option

questions.exp: Like Url, Regex and most value constraints, Email skips empty/null values. Combine it with NotBlank when an empty value must be rejected.

questions.q: What does #[Assert\Length(max: 10)] count by default?
questions.exp: Length counts characters using its charset (UTF-8 by default) with min/max/charset/countUnit options. To constrain the number of elements in an array use Count instead.

questions.q: How do you make GreaterThan compare against another property of the same object (e.g. endDate > startDate)?

a.t: Pass the other property as the first constructor argument
It is impossible; you must use a Callback

questions.exp: All comparison constraints (GreaterThan, LessThan, EqualTo, IdenticalTo…) accept a propertyPath option to compare against another field of the same object instead of a fixed value.

questions.q: You have an indexed array of email strings and place #[Assert\Collection([...])] on it. Why is that wrong?

a.t: Collection validates the KEYS of an associative array; to validate every element of an indexed array use All
Nothing is wrong; Collection validates each element

questions.exp: Collection maps per-key constraints for associative arrays (with Required/Optional wrappers), whereas All applies constraints to every element of an indexed collection. They are not interchangeable.

questions.q:
Given:
```php
#[Assert\When(
    expression: 'this.getType() === "premium"',
    constraints: [new Assert\NotBlank()],
)]
public ?string $vatNumber = null;
```
For a non-premium object with $vatNumber = null, what happens?

a.t: No violation — the inner NotBlank runs only when the expression is true
A violation, because NotBlank always runs
A syntax error; When cannot wrap NotBlank
The expression is ignored for null values

questions.exp: When applies its inner constraints only if the ExpressionLanguage expression evaluates to true. Here getType() is not 'premium', so NotBlank is skipped and null passes.

questions.q: #[Assert\Choice(choices: ['a','b','c'])] is placed on an array property $roles, and elements outside the list are NOT rejected. Why?

a.t: Choice validates the whole value as one choice unless multiple: true is set
You must use All instead of Choice

questions.exp: Without multiple: true, Choice checks that the value itself is one of the allowed choices. Setting multiple: true validates each element of the array (with optional min/max counts).

questions.q: Which of these constraints return NO violation for a null value? (choose three)
questions.exp: Email, Length, Range (and virtually all value constraints) bail out on null/empty and add no violation. NotNull fails on null; NotBlank fails on null/''/[]. To require and validate a value, stack the presence check with the shape check.

questions.q:
What are the defaults for allowExtraFields and allowMissingFields in:
```php
#[Assert\Collection(fields: [ 'street' => new Assert\NotBlank() ])]
public array $address = [];
```

a.t: Both default to false — extra keys and missing keys both cause violations
They default to null and are ignored

questions.exp: allowExtraFields and allowMissingFields both default to false, so Collection rejects partial or extra arrays unless you opt in. Per-field Required/Optional wrappers control whether a specific key may be absent.

questions.q: True or False: #[Assert\IsTrue] considers the integer 1 and the string '1' as passing.
questions.exp: IsTrue passes for true, 1 and '1' (a loose truthy check); IsFalse likewise passes for false, 0 and '0'. Both are commonly placed on getters.

questions.q: What causes the validator to recurse into a nested object property?

a.t: #[Assert\Valid] on the property holding the nested object
Calling validateProperty() on the nested object
A class-level Valid constraint on the parent

questions.exp: Valid marks a property for cascading; the ValidValidator tells the context to descend so the nested object's own constraints (and, for collections, each element's) are validated.

questions.q: A rule must compare two properties of the same object. Which scope fits best?

a.t: Class scope (e.g. a Callback or Expression constraint)
A property constraint on each of the two fields
It cannot be expressed with the Validator component

questions.exp: Cross-field rules need access to the whole object, so they belong on a class-target constraint such as Callback or Expression.

questions.q: A constraint on the getter isActive() reports a violation under which property path?
questions.exp: Getter constraints validate the return value of isX/getX/hasX and report under the property-ised name, so isActive() maps to 'active'.

questions.q: You place a property-target-only constraint at class scope. What happens?

a.t: A ConstraintDefinitionException is thrown — its getTargets() does not allow CLASS_CONSTRAINT
It silently validates the first property

questions.exp: A class-scope constraint must target the class (getTargets() returns CLASS_CONSTRAINT). Placing a property-target constraint at class scope raises a ConstraintDefinitionException.

questions.q: When a #[Assert\Valid] property is cascaded, which validation group is used for the nested object?

a.t: The current group being validated is passed down to the nested object
Always the nested object's own Default group
All groups defined on the nested object

questions.exp: Cascading passes the current group down. A custom group propagates as-is, so a nested object only validates its custom-group constraints if that group actually reaches it. Valid never changes groups.

questions.q: For a property holding a collection of Address OBJECTS, how do you validate each element's own constraints?

a.t: Put #[Assert\Valid] on the property; it cascades into every element
Nothing is needed; object collections cascade automatically

questions.exp: For a collection of objects, a single #[Assert\\Valid] on the property cascades into each element. All([new Valid()]) is a redundant anti-pattern; All is for applying scalar constraints to elements.
The ExecutionContext builds the property path from the traversed nodes; a cascaded collection element uses index notation, giving lines[2].price.

questions.q: You call validate($obj, groups: ['edit']). Which constraints run?

a.t: Only constraints assigned to the 'edit' group

questions.exp: Only the requested groups run. Passing a custom group does NOT implicitly include Default; list ['Default', 'edit'] if you need both.

questions.q: For a class that defines a GroupSequence, validating the 'Default' group will…

a.t: Trigger the group sequence (stepwise, stop on first failing group)
Run every constraint flat, ignoring the sequence

questions.exp: On a sequenced class, the special Default group is remapped to the sequence. To run the same constraints flat (bypassing the sequence), validate the {ClassName} group instead.

questions.q: For class App\Entity\User with no group sequence, what is the {ClassName} group?

a.t: 'User' (the short class name), equivalent to 'Default' here

questions.exp: The {ClassName} group uses the short class name. Every Default-group constraint is also in it, so with no sequence 'User' and 'Default' are equivalent.

questions.q: Which default group name does an unqualified constraint belong to?
questions.exp: The implicit group is 'Default' with a capital D; group names are case-sensitive, so 'default' would be a different (empty) group.

questions.q: In a Symfony form, how do you tell the validator to validate the bound object with the 'registration' group?

a.t: Set 'groups' on the form type's constructor

questions.exp: Forms invoke the validator during handleRequest(); the validation_groups option selects which groups run (default ['Default']). It can also be a callback for dynamic group selection.

a.t: 1 — only the 'registration' group runs, so only $password's NotBlank fires; $email's Default NotBlank is skipped
0 — Default must be requested for any violation

questions.exp: Passing a custom group does not include Default. Only registration-group constraints run, so $password fails but the blank $email (Default) is skipped. List ['Default','registration'] to get both.

questions.q: A parent cascades into a child with #[Assert\Valid] and validate() is called with the Default group. The child has a constraint only in a custom 'strict' group. Does it run?

a.t: No — only the Default group reaches the child, so its 'strict'-only constraint is skipped
Yes — Valid runs all of the child's groups
Yes — custom groups always run on cascade
Only if the child defines a group sequence

questions.exp: The cascaded group is the current one (Default). A child's custom-group constraint runs only if that custom group actually propagates to it.

questions.q: You call validate($user, groups: ['Default', 'edit']). Which constraints run? (choose two)

a.t: Constraints in every group defined on the class
Only constraints in whichever group is listed first

questions.exp: Listing both groups runs both sets. A custom group never implies Default, which is exactly why you list Default explicitly when you also need it.

questions.q: When does a group sequence stop early?

a.t: After the first group in the sequence that produces any violation
After the first individual constraint that fails
Only after all groups have run

questions.exp: Each group runs fully, but the sequence halts after the first group that yields a violation, so later (often more expensive) groups are skipped.

questions.q: Inside a class's #[Assert\GroupSequence], how do you reference the class's own basic constraints?
questions.exp: Referencing 'Default' inside its own sequence would loop, because Default is remapped to the sequence. Use the {ClassName} group to mean the class's Default-group constraints run flat.

questions.q: What must a class annotated with #[Assert\GroupSequenceProvider] provide?

a.t: It must extend the GroupSequence class

questions.exp: The provider attribute delegates to getGroupSequence() from GroupSequenceProviderInterface, evaluated on each validation so the sequence can depend on the object's state.

questions.q: A class defines #[Assert\GroupSequence(['User','Strong'])]. You call validate($user, groups: ['User']). What runs?

a.t: The class's Default-group constraints flat, WITHOUT the sequence (bypassing stop-on-first-fail)
The full sequence, stopping on the first failing group
Nothing, because 'User' is remapped to the sequence

questions.exp: Validating the {ClassName} group ('User') runs the class's Default constraints flat, bypassing the sequence. Only validating 'Default' triggers the sequence.

questions.q:
What does this YAML configure?
```yaml
App\Entity\Registration:
    group_sequence:
        - Registration
        - Strict
```

a.t: A group sequence: validate the Registration (class-name) group first, then Strict, stopping at the first failing group
Two independent validation runs whose violations are merged

questions.exp: group_sequence declares the ordered sequence used when validating Default. The class-name group (Registration) means the class's own Default constraints; Strict runs only if the first step passes.

questions.q: When is a #[Assert\GroupSequenceProvider] class's getGroupSequence() called?

a.t: Each time the object is validated, so the sequence can depend on the object's state
Only when invoked from the console

questions.exp: The provider is evaluated per validation, letting the returned array or GroupSequence adapt to runtime state (e.g. premium vs free account).

questions.q:
Given:
```php
#[Assert\GroupSequence(['Login', 'Strict'])]
class Login {
    #[Assert\NotBlank] public string $email = '';    // ''
    #[Assert\NotBlank] public string $password = '';  // ''
    #[Assert\Email(groups: ['Strict'])] public string $email2 = 'bad';
}
$validator->validate($login); // Default
```
Which violations are returned?

a.t: Only the two NotBlank violations from step 1 (Login); the Strict Email check never runs

questions.exp: Step 1 is 'Login' (the class's Default constraints). Both NotBlank checks fail, so the sequence halts before the 'Strict' step and the Email check on $email2 is skipped.

questions.q: What is the signature of an instance-method #[Assert\Callback]?
questions.exp: An instance callback receives the ExecutionContext and the optional payload and returns void; violations are added through the context. The static form additionally receives the object as the first argument.

questions.q: How does a callback validator register an error?
questions.exp: Violations are built and committed through the execution context. The callback's return value is ignored.

questions.q: #[Assert\Callback] is which kind of constraint?

a.t: A class-level constraint; the callback reads the whole object
A property constraint that receives the property value

questions.exp: Callback targets the class, so it does not receive a single property value; you read the object from $this or $context->getObject() and can report on any path with atPath().

questions.q: A static #[Assert\Callback] method (referenced via the callback: option) receives what as its first argument?

a.t: The object being validated (then the ExecutionContext, then the payload)

questions.exp: The static form has no $this, so its signature is (object $object, ExecutionContextInterface $context, mixed $payload). The instance form is (context, payload).

questions.q: A callback compares $this->start >= $this->end and occasionally throws a TypeError in production. What is the most likely cause?

a.t: One of the properties is null; callbacks run even when fields are unset, so you must guard against null first
The callback is missing a return value

questions.exp: Callbacks always run regardless of field state, so nullable properties are the classic callback bug. Guard with null checks (or ?-> / ??) and let each field's own NotNull enforce presence.

questions.q: A #[Assert\Callback(groups: ['checkout'])] never fires during a plain validate($obj). Why, and does it join sequences?

a.t: It runs only when the 'checkout' group is validated; being class-scoped, it also participates in group sequences like any constraint
Callbacks ignore groups; the attribute is malformed
Callbacks can never run inside groups
It runs only in the Default group regardless of the option

questions.exp: Callback honours its groups option (default Default). A non-Default callback runs only when that group is validated, and it participates in group sequences exactly like any other constraint.
atPath('stackable') relocates the violation to that field. The void return is normal — the error is committed by addViolation(), not by returning a value.

questions.q: Where must #[Assert\Callback] be placed?

a.t: On a method (or on the class via the callback: option) — never on a property

questions.exp: Callback is a class-level constraint attached to a method; placing it on a property is a mistake. Read the object via $this or $context->getObject().

questions.q: By default, which validator class validates the constraint App\Validator\Foo?
questions.exp: Constraint::validatedBy() returns static::class.'Validator' by convention. Override it only when the validator service id differs from that name.

questions.q: How do you make a custom constraint apply at class scope?

a.t: Rename the class with a 'Class' suffix

questions.exp: The validator uses getTargets() (defaulting to PROPERTY_CONSTRAINT) to decide placement. Returning CLASS_CONSTRAINT makes the validator receive the whole object as $value.

questions.q: What is the recommended first step in ConstraintValidator::validate()?

a.t: Check $constraint instanceof YourConstraint and throw UnexpectedTypeException otherwise

questions.exp: Guarding the constraint type documents intent and fails fast if the validator is mis-wired. It is the documented convention in the Symfony examples.

questions.q: What does #[HasNamedArguments] do on a custom Constraint constructor?

a.t: Passes attribute arguments as named constructor arguments (typed options)
Enables group sequences for the constraint

questions.exp: #[HasNamedArguments] (Symfony\\Component\\Validator\\Attribute) opts into typed, named-argument construction instead of the legacy options-array style; remember to forward $groups and $payload to parent::__construct().

questions.q: How is a ConstraintValidator subclass wired so you can inject dependencies (e.g. a repository) into it?

a.t: It is autoconfigured as a service tagged validator.constraint_validator (via ConstraintValidatorInterface), so normal autowiring applies
You must register it manually in services.yaml with a factory
You register a compiler pass for each validator

questions.exp: Implementing ConstraintValidatorInterface (via ConstraintValidator) triggers autoconfiguration with the validator.constraint_validator tag, so validators are services and can have dependencies autowired.

questions.q: In a custom Constraint with #[HasNamedArguments], why forward $groups and $payload to parent::__construct()?

a.t: Otherwise the constraint ignores its groups/payload, so group assignment silently stops working
It is optional decoration with no effect

questions.exp: The base Constraint stores groups and payload. Forgetting to forward them means the constraint always lands in Default and the payload is lost.

a.t: Guard the constraint type (fail fast if mis-wired) and skip null/empty so the rule composes with NotBlank
They are optional boilerplate with no effect

questions.exp: The instanceof guard documents intent and throws UnexpectedTypeException if mis-wired; the null/empty early return keeps the constraint composable with presence checks like NotBlank.

questions.q:
What does IS_REPEATABLE enable here?
```php
#[\Attribute(\Attribute::TARGET_PROPERTY | \Attribute::IS_REPEATABLE)]
final class ContainsAlphanumeric extends Constraint { /* ... */ }
```

a.t: The same constraint attribute can be applied more than once on the same property
It makes the validator re-run until it passes
It registers the constraint in every group
It allows the constraint on both properties and classes

questions.exp: IS_REPEATABLE is a native PHP attribute flag allowing multiple instances on one target. Allowing both property and class placement instead needs TARGET_CLASS in the flags AND getTargets() returning both.

questions.q: How does a ConstraintValidator obtain $this->context (the ExecutionContext)?

a.t: The validator calls initialize($context) before validate(); ConstraintValidator stores it as $this->context
It is passed as a third argument to validate()
It is a static property on ConstraintValidator

questions.exp: For each constraint the validator resolves its ConstraintValidator, calls initialize($context) (which sets $this->context on the base class) and then validate($value, $constraint).

questions.syl: Data Validation → Violations & the execution context
questions.q: When is a violation built with buildViolation() actually recorded?

a.t: Only when addViolation() is called on the builder

questions.exp: buildViolation() returns a fluent builder; nothing is added to the list until addViolation() commits it. Forgetting it makes the validator pass silently.

questions.syl: Data Validation → Violations & the execution context
questions.q: Which method returns the message with its {{ placeholders }} still unresolved?
questions.exp: getMessage() returns the interpolated message; getMessageTemplate() keeps the raw template with {{ x }} placeholders, and getParameters() holds the substitution map.

questions.syl: Data Validation → Violations & the execution context
questions.q: On the violation builder, which method attaches the error to a different property?
questions.exp: atPath() relocates the violation to a path relative to the current node, commonly used in class-level constraints to blame a specific field.

questions.syl: Data Validation → Violations & the execution context
questions.q: What is $this->context->addViolation($message, $params) a shortcut for?

a.t: buildViolation($message, $params)->addViolation() — the common case with no extra setters

questions.exp: The context's addViolation() is a convenience for the simple case; use buildViolation() when you need atPath/setCode/setInvalidValue before committing.

questions.syl: Data Validation → Violations & the execution context
questions.q: Why use setParameter('{{ value }}', ...) instead of concatenating the value into the message string?

a.t: Placeholders keep the message translatable; the {{ x }} template is interpolated later and preserved by getMessageTemplate()
setParameter is required to commit the violation
Messages cannot contain any variables otherwise

questions.exp: {{ }} placeholders filled by setParameter keep the raw template translatable and available via getMessageTemplate(); inlining values into the string breaks translation.

questions.syl: Data Validation → Violations & the execution context
questions.exp: getMessage() is interpolated; getMessageTemplate() keeps the raw {{ x }} template. getPropertyPath() returns the path (e.g. 'code').

questions.syl: Data Validation → Violations & the execution context
questions.q: A developer uses $violations[0] (works) but array_map(..., $violations) (fails). Why?

a.t: The list is a Countable/IteratorAggregate/ArrayAccess object, not a plain array; use foreach/count() or iterator_to_array()
The list is null when empty
array_map only works on associative arrays

questions.exp: ConstraintViolationList implements ArrayAccess (so [0] works) but is not an array. Iterate it, call count(), use findByCodes(), or convert via iterator_to_array() for array functions.

questions.syl: Data Validation → Violations & the execution context
questions.q: What is the purpose of the builder's setCode() value?

a.t: A stable machine-readable code for the violation, usable via findByCodes() and independent of translated text
The HTTP status code returned to the client

questions.exp: setCode() attaches a stable code (often a constant) so application code can branch on it without depending on translated message text; the list's findByCodes() filters by it.

questions.q: Which constraint passes only when the value IS strictly null?
questions.exp: IsNull requires the value to be exactly null (fails otherwise). It is the inverse of NotNull. Blank (its cousin) passes for null or ''.

questions.q: In #[Assert\GroupSequence(['A', 'B'])], if a constraint in group 'A' fails, group 'B' is…

a.t: Not validated — the sequence stops at the first group that produces a violation
Still validated, and all violations are merged
Validated only if 'A' had exactly one violation
Validated in a separate pass afterwards

questions.exp: A GroupSequence validates groups in order and stops as soon as one group yields a violation, so later groups (and their expensive checks) never run.

questions.q: A constraint declared without any explicit 'groups' option belongs to which validation group?

a.t: No group at all, so it is never validated
A group named after the property

questions.exp: Every constraint with no explicit groups is placed in the Default group, which is the group used when you call validate() without specifying groups.

questions.q: To make a single custom constraint usable on BOTH a property and a class, getTargets() should return…

a.t: an empty array to allow any target

questions.exp: getTargets() may return a single string or an array of them. Returning both PROPERTY_CONSTRAINT and CLASS_CONSTRAINT lets the same constraint be placed on a property and on a class.

questions.q: You put #[Assert\Valid] on a property holding a Collection/array of Address objects. What happens on validate()?

a.t: Each element is traversed and its own constraints are validated (cascade)
Only the first element is validated
The collection count is validated but not the elements
Nothing — Valid works only on single objects

questions.exp: Assert\Valid cascades into nested objects, and for a traversable/array it validates every element's constraints. Without it, nested objects are not validated at all.

questions.q: Which of the following statements are true about built-in validation constraints? (select all that apply)

a.t: NotBlank fails on an empty string, but NotNull lets an empty string pass because it only rejects null
Email and Url pass on an empty/null value, so they must be stacked with NotBlank when empty must be rejected
A nested object is only cascaded into when its property carries #[Assert\Valid]
NotNull also rejects empty strings and empty arrays, exactly like NotBlank
Email fails on null values, so combining it with NotBlank is redundant

questions.exp: NotBlank rejects '', whitespace-only strings, empty arrays and null, while NotNull only rejects null — so '' passes NotNull. Format constraints like Email and Url deliberately pass on empty/null (stack NotBlank to require a value), and nested objects are skipped entirely unless the property has Assert\Valid, even if the nested class defines its own constraints.

questions.q: Which statements about validation groups are correct? (select all that apply)

a.t: Constraints declared without an explicit groups option belong to the Default group
Validating with a custom group excludes the Default group unless Default is listed as well
For a class without a group sequence, the Default group and the {ClassName} group are equivalent
Passing any custom group always runs the Default group constraints in addition
Group names are case-insensitive, so 'default' and 'Default' refer to the same group

questions.exp: Unnamed constraints all land in Default, and validate($object, null, ['Registration']) runs only that group — Default must be listed explicitly to be included too. Without a group sequence, the short class-name group is just an alias of Default. Group names are case-sensitive strings, so 'default' is not the Default group.

questions.q: Which statements about #[Assert\GroupSequence] are true? (select all that apply)

a.t: The sequence stops at the first failing group, but all constraints inside that group still run
The sequence is triggered when validating the Default group, while validating {ClassName} bypasses it
Inside the sequence you must reference the short class-name group, never Default itself
The sequence stops at the very first failing constraint, skipping the rest of its group
All groups of the sequence always run, and violations from every group are collected

questions.exp: A group sequence is fail-fast per group: every constraint of the current group runs, and only if the group succeeds does the next group start. It fires when Default is validated, whereas {ClassName} performs a flat run that bypasses it — which is also why the sequence itself must list {ClassName} instead of Default (that would recurse). Halting mid-group or always running every group are both incorrect.

questions.q: Which statements about validating objects with ValidatorInterface are correct? (select all that apply)

a.t: validate() returns a ConstraintViolationListInterface and never throws on validation failure
validatePropertyValue() validates a supplied value against a property's constraints without touching the object
validate() returns true when the object is valid and false otherwise
validate() automatically throws a ValidationFailedException when violations are found
validateProperty() requires you to pass the value to check as an explicit argument

questions.exp: validate() always returns a violation list — you check count() to know whether the object is valid; it neither returns a boolean nor throws on failure. validatePropertyValue() tests an arbitrary supplied value against a property's constraints, whereas validateProperty() reads the object's current value, so no explicit value argument is passed to it.

questions.syl: Data Validation → Violations & the execution context
questions.q: Which statements about the violation builder and violations are true? (select all that apply)

a.t: buildViolation() records nothing until addViolation() is called on the builder
getMessage() returns the interpolated message, while getMessageTemplate() keeps the raw placeholders
atPath() appends to the current property path relative to the validated node
buildViolation() immediately adds the violation; addViolation() is optional
validate() returns a plain PHP array of violations that you inspect with count()

questions.exp: The builder is fluent and lazy: setParameter(), atPath(), setCode() etc. configure the violation, and only addViolation() commits it to the context. getMessage() is the interpolated text while getMessageTemplate() preserves the raw {{ placeholders }}, and atPath() is relative — it appends to the current path rather than resetting the root. The result of validation is a ConstraintViolationListInterface object (Countable/iterable), never a plain array.

questions.q: Which statements about the #[Assert\Callback] constraint are correct? (select all that apply)

a.t: Callback is a class-level constraint: the method does not receive a property value and reads the object from $this or $context->getObject()
Errors must be added through the context (e.g. $context->buildViolation()->addViolation()); the callback's return value is ignored
Callbacks honour the groups option, so a callback in a non-Default group only runs when that group is validated
Returning false from the callback marks the object as invalid
The callback receives the value of the property it is declared next to as its first argument

questions.exp: Callback targets the class, so the method inspects the whole object (via $this for instance methods or the first argument for static callbacks) and must report problems by building violations on the ExecutionContext — any returned value is discarded. Callbacks also participate fully in groups and group sequences. Returning false does nothing, and no property value is injected because it is not a property constraint.
